Chapter on Wealth (Dhanavagga) First Discourse on the Dear One (Paṭhamapiyasutta) “Monks, there are these seven kinds of wealth. What seven? The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtuous behavior, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of truth, and the wealth of peace. These, monks, are the seven kinds of wealth.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus.
"Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, possessing seven qualities, a bhikkhu is disliked and displeasing to his fellow celibates, and he is neither respected nor esteemed.
Which seven?
“Here, monks, a monk is desirous of gain, desirous of honor, and desirous of not being despised; he is shameless and lacks moral dread; he has evil desires and holds wrong view.
Possessed of these seven qualities, monks, a monk is displeasing and disagreeable to his fellow celibates, and is neither respected nor esteemed by them.
But possessed of seven other qualities, monks, a monk is pleasing and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is both respected and esteemed by them.”
“By which seven?

Here, monks, a monk does not desire gain, does not desire honor, and does not desire not being despised; he is possessed of moral shame, he is possessed of moral dread, he has few desires, and he holds right view.
Endowed with these seven qualities, monks, a monk is dear and agreeable to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, and is respected and esteemed by them.”
First. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.2 1.
The Chapter on Wealth (Dhanavagga)
The Second Discourse on the Unloved (Dutiyapiyasutta) “Bhikkhus,
possessed of seven qualities, a bhikkhu is unloved and displeasing to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, and he is neither respected nor esteemed.
By which seven?
Here, monks, a monk is desirous of gain, desirous of honor, and desirous of not being treated with contempt; he is shameless and lacks moral dread; he is envious and stingy.
Possessing these seven qualities, monks, a monk is disliked and displeasing to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, and he is neither respected nor esteemed.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses seven qualities is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed by them. What seven?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not desire gain, does not desire honor, and does not desire not to be disrespected; he is possessed of moral shame and moral dread; he is free from envy and free from avarice. Possessing these seven qualities, a bhikkhu is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed by them.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses these seven qualities is dear and agreeable to his fellow celibates, and is respected and esteemed by them. Thus was the second [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.3.

1. Dhanavagga Saṅkhittabalasutta (AN 7.3, PTS AN iv 3) “Monks, there are these five powers. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, monks, are the five powers.”
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
… “Monks, there are these seven powers.”
Which seven?
The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
These, monks, are the seven powers.
The power of faith and energy,
the powers of moral shame and dread of blame;
the power of mindfulness and concentration.
Wisdom indeed is the seventh strength;
endowed with these strengths,
the wise bhikkhu lives happily.
One who investigates phenomena with systematic attention perceives the meaning through wisdom;
it is like the extinguishing of a lamp.
“...there is liberation of the mind.
The third [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.4.

1. Dhanavagga: Vitthatabalasutta (AN 7.4, PTS AN iv 3) “Monks, there are these five powers. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, monks, are the five powers.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven powers. What seven?
The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.”
And what, monks, is the power of faith?
Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:
"Thus indeed is that Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened... the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One."
This, monks, is called the power of faith.
And what, monks, is the power of energy?

Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish his burden regarding wholesome states.
This, monks, is called the power of energy.
And what, monks, is the power of moral shame?
Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses moral shame; he feels shame at bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he feels shame at the acquisition of evil, unwholesome states.
This, monks, is called the power of moral shame.
And what, monks, is the power of moral dread?

Here, monks, the noble disciple is one who feels moral dread; he feels moral dread regarding bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he feels moral dread regarding the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states.
This, monks, is called the power of moral dread.
And what, monks, is the power of mindfulness?
Here, monks, a noble disciple is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recalls what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago.
This, monks, is called the power of mindfulness.
And what, monks, is the power of concentration?
Here, monks, a noble disciple, quite secluded from sensual pleasures...
he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
This, monks, is called the power of concentration.
And what, monks, is the power of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise;
he is endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
This, monks, is called the power of wisdom.
"These, monks, are the seven powers:
the power of faith, energy,
moral shame, and the power of moral dread."
The power of mindfulness, concentration,
and wisdom is indeed the seventh power;
by these, a bhikkhu becomes powerful.
The wise person lives happily,
investigating the Dhamma with systematic attention and seeing the meaning through wisdom.
“Just as the extinguishing of a lamp,
there is the liberation of the mind. Thus ends the fourth [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.5 1.

Dhanavagga Saṅkhittadhanasutta – The Discourse on Wealth in Brief "Bhikkhus, there are these seven kinds of wealth. What seven? The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtuous behavior, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of truth, and the wealth of peace. These, bhikkhus, are the seven kinds of wealth."
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven kinds of wealth.
What are the seven?
The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of moral shame, the wealth of moral dread, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, and the wealth of wisdom.
These, monks, are the seven kinds of wealth. [Namely:
the wealth of faith and the wealth of virtue...
Modesty and shame are wealth;
the wealth of learning, generosity,
and wisdom is indeed the seventh wealth.
Whosoever, whether woman or man, possesses these riches—
of them it is said, "He is not poor."
His life is not in vain.
Therefore, faith and virtue,
serenity and the vision of the Dhamma—
The wise person should apply themselves to it,
remembering the teaching of the Buddhas.
Thus ends the fifth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.6 1. Dhanavagga Vitthatadhanasutta – The Discourse on Detailed Wealth “Bhikkhus, there are these seven kinds of wealth. What seven? Wealth of faith, wealth of virtue, wealth of learning, wealth of generosity, wealth of wisdom, wealth of truth, and wealth of peace. And what, bhikkhus, is wealth of faith? Here, someone is endowed with faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This, bhikkhus, is called wealth of faith. And what, bhikkhus, is wealth of virtue? Here, someone abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, abstains from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This, bhikkhus, is called wealth of virtue. And what, bhikkhus, is wealth of learning? Here, someone has learned much, retained what he has learned, recited it verbally, examined it with the mind, and penetrated it well through view. This, bhikkhus, is called wealth of learning. And what, bhikkhus, is wealth of generosity? Here, someone dwells at home with a heart devoid of the stain of stinginess, freely generous, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, one devoted to charity, responsive to requests, delighting in the distribution of gifts. This, bhikkhus, is called wealth of generosity. And what, bhikkhus, is wealth of wisdom? Here, someone is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called wealth of wisdom. And what, bhikkhus, is wealth of truth? Here, someone speaks at a proper time, speaks truthfully, speaks meaningfully, speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, and speaks in accordance with the Vinaya. At the proper time, he utters words that are worth recording, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial. This, bhikkhus, is called wealth of truth. And what, bhikkhus, is wealth of peace? Here, someone is peaceful in body, peaceful in mind, and has attained peace within himself. This, bhikkhus, is called wealth of peace. These, bhikkhus, are the seven kinds of wealth.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven kinds of wealth.
What are the seven?
The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of moral shame, the wealth of moral dread, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, and the wealth of wisdom.
And what, monks, is the wealth of faith?
Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:
‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened … [as before] … an awakened one, a Blessed One.
This, monks, is called the wealth of faith.
And what, monks, is the wealth of virtue?
"Here, monks, a noble disciple abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...he abstains from the use of fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence.
This, monks, is called the wealth of virtue.
And what, monks, is the wealth of moral shame?"
"Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses a sense of shame; he feels shame for misconduct of body, speech, and mind, and he feels shame for the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states.
This, monks, is called the wealth of moral shame.
And what, monks, is the wealth of moral dread?"

"Here, monks, a noble disciple is conscientious; he is conscientious regarding bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he is conscientious regarding the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states.
This, monks, is called the wealth of conscientiousness.
And what, monks, is the wealth of learning?"
In this case, monks, a noble disciple is learned, one who has retained what he has heard, and one who has accumulated what he has heard.
Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, which proclaim the holy life in its meaning and its letter,
entirely complete and pure— such teachings as these he has heard much of, remembered, and mastered through speech.
Examined with the mind and thoroughly penetrated by right view—
this, monks, is called the wealth of learning.
And what, monks, is the wealth of generosity?

"Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure in hand, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and taking pleasure in sharing.
This, monks, is called the wealth of generosity.
And what, monks, is the wealth of wisdom?"
“Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise … [as before] … leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
This, monks, is called the wealth of wisdom.
These, monks, are the seven kinds of wealth.”
The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue,
the wealth of moral shame and dread of blame;
the wealth of learning and generosity—
Wisdom, indeed, is the seventh treasure.
For whichever woman or man possesses these treasures, [they are truly wealthy].
They say that for such a person life is not in vain;
therefore, faith and virtue—
Faith and the vision of the Dhamma—
the wise person should devote themselves to these,
remembering the teaching of the Buddhas.
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.7 1.
Dhanavagga (The Chapter on Wealth)
The Discourse to Ugga (Uggasutta).

Then Ugga, the royal minister, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Ugga, the royal minister, said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
How wealthy, Bhante, is this Migāra of the Rohaṇa clan; how much wealth he possesses; how great his fortune!
“But how wealthy, householder, is Migāra of the Rohaṇa clan? How much wealth does he possess? How great is his fortune?”
“Lord, there are hundreds of thousands of measures of gold, let alone silver.
“There is indeed this wealth, Ugga; I do not say it does not exist.
But this wealth, Ugga, is common property, shared with fire, water, kings, thieves, and unpleasant heirs.”
“Ugga, there are these seven treasures that are not shared with fire, water, kings, thieves, or unpleasant heirs.
What are the seven?
The treasure of faith, the treasure of virtue, the treasure of moral shame, the treasure of moral dread, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, and the treasure of wisdom.”
"These, Ugga, are the seven kinds of wealth that are not shared by fire, water, kings, thieves,
or unpleasant heirs: the wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue,
and the wealth of moral shame and moral dread."
Learning, wealth, and generosity,
and wisdom indeed as the seventh treasure—
for whomsoever these treasures exist,
Whether for a woman or for a man,
he is indeed one of great wealth in the world,
unconquerable by gods or humans.
Therefore, the wise person should devote themselves to faith and virtue, to confidence and the vision of the Dhamma.
"Follow the teaching of the Buddhas.
This is the seventh [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.8.

1. Dhanavagga Saṁyojanasutta (AN 7.8, PTS AN iv 7) “Bhikkhus, there are these five fetters. What five? The fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of ill will, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, and the fetter of conceit. These, bhikkhus, are the five fetters.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven fetters.
Which seven?
The fetter of attachment, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of lust for existence, and the fetter of ignorance.”
“Monks, these indeed are the seven fetters.
The eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.9

“Bhikkhus, the holy life is lived for the sake of abandoning, for the sake of cutting off, the seven fetters. Which seven?
The holy life is lived for the sake of abandoning, for the sake of cutting off, the fetter of attachment; [the fetter] of aversion … [and so on].”
of the fetter of views … of the fetter of doubt … of the fetter of conceit …
The holy life is lived for the abandoning and the eradication of the fetter of lust for existence... and the fetter of ignorance.
Indeed, monks, it is for the abandoning and the eradication of these seven fetters that the holy life is lived.

But when, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned the fetter of attachment, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising; and when he has abandoned the fetter of aversion … and the fetter of views … [as before] … then he is called a bhikkhu who is a non-returner, one who has no further existence in this world.”
the fetter of doubt … the fetter of conceit … the fetter of lust for existence …
The fetter of ignorance has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is of a nature not to arise again in the future.
This, monks, is called a monk who has cut off craving, stripped away the fetters, and through the right penetration of conceit, has made an end of suffering. Thus it was said.
The ninth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.10 1.

Dhanavagga Macchariya Sutta: Stinginess “Monks, there are these five kinds of stinginess. What five? Stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma. These, monks, are the five kinds of stinginess.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven fetters. Which seven? [The text continues with the enumeration of the seven fetters.]”
The fetter of attachment, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice.
These, monks, are the seven fetters. Thus ends the tenth [discourse].
The First Chapter on Wealth.
Its summary:
Two dear things, strength, wealth.
In brief and in detail;
lofty and likewise the fetter,
and the abandoning of stinginess.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.11 2.
Anusayavagga First Discourse on Latent Tendencies (Paṭhama-anusaya-sutta)
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
Which seven?

The underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance.
These, monks, are the seven underlying tendencies. Thus ends the first [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.12 2.

Anusayavagga Dutiyaanusayasutta (The Second Discourse on Latent Tendencies) "Bhikkhus, there are these seven latent tendencies. What seven? The latent tendency of sensual lust, the latent tendency of aversion, the latent tendency of views, the latent tendency of doubt, the latent tendency of conceit, the latent tendency of attachment to existence, and the latent tendency of ignorance. These, bhikkhus, are the seven latent tendencies."
“Bhikkhus, the holy life is lived for the sake of abandoning and cutting off the seven underlying tendencies. Which seven? [The text continues with the list of the seven underlying tendencies.]”
The holy life is lived for the abandoning and eradication of the underlying tendency to sensual lust;
for the underlying tendency to aversion … [and so on] … for the underlying tendency to views … for the underlying tendency to doubt.
The holy life is lived for the sake of abandoning and eradicating the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance.
"Monks, it is for the abandoning and eradication of these seven underlying tendencies that the holy life is lived.
And when, monks, a monk’s underlying tendency to sensual lust has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising;
[when his] underlying tendency to aversion … [and so on for the remaining five]."
the underlying tendency to views … the underlying tendency to doubt … the underlying tendency to conceit …
The underlying tendency to lust for existence...
the underlying tendency to ignorance has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
This, monks, is called a monk who has cut off craving, stripped away the fetters, and through the complete penetration of conceit, has made an end of suffering.”
The Second [Discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.13.
2. The Chapter on Latent Tendencies (Anusayavagga).
Kulasutta (AN 7.13,
PTS AN iv 10): “Bhikkhus,
possessing seven factors, a family is not fit to be approached, or, having been approached, it is not fit to sit down near them.

Which seven? They do not rise up in a pleasing manner; they do not pay homage in a pleasing manner; they do not offer a seat in a pleasing manner; they conceal what they possess; they give little even when there is much; they give coarse things even when there are refined ones; they give without respect, not with respect.
Possessing these seven factors, monks, a family is not fit to be approached if one has not already been approached, nor is it fit to be sat near if one has already been approached.
“Bhikkhus, possessing seven qualities, a family is fit to be approached even if one has not yet been visited, and once approached, it is fit to sit down with.

What are the seven? They rise in a pleasing manner; they pay homage in a pleasing manner; they offer a seat in a pleasing manner; they do not hide what they have; they give much even when they have little; they give what is excellent even when they have only the excellent; they give respectfully, not disrespectfully. Possessing these seven qualities, a family is fit to be approached even if one has not yet been visited, and once approached, it is fit to sit down with.”
“Bhikkhus, when a family possesses these seven factors, it is sufficient not to approach them; or if one has approached them, it is sufficient to sit down.
The third.

2. Anusayavagga Puggalasutta (AN 7.14, PTS AN iv 10) “Monks, there are these seven kinds of persons found existing in the world. What seven? The one who is latent with lust; the one who is latent with hatred; the one who is latent with delusion; the one who is latent with all three; the one who is free from latent tendencies toward lust; the one who is free from latent tendencies toward hatred; and the one who is free from latent tendencies toward delusion. And how, monks, is a person latent with lust? Here, monks, a certain person has not abandoned sensual desire, has not removed it, has not extinguished it, has not ended it, and has not relinquished it. This, monks, is called a person latent with lust. And how, monks, is a person latent with hatred? Here, monks, a certain person has not abandoned ill will, has not removed it, has not extinguished it, has not ended it, and has not relinquished it. This, monks, is called a person latent with hatred. And how, monks, is a person latent with delusion? Here, monks, a certain person has not abandoned ignorance regarding suffering, has not removed it, has not extinguished it, has not ended it, and has not relinquished it. This, monks, is called a person latent with delusion. And how, monks, is a person latent with all three? Here, monks, a certain person has not abandoned sensual desire, ill will, and ignorance, has not removed them, has not extinguished them, has not ended them, and has not relinquished them. This, monks, is called a person latent with all three. And how, monks, is a person free from latent tendencies toward lust? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned sensual desire, has removed it, has extinguished it, has ended it, and has relinquished it. This, monks, is called a person free from latent tendencies toward lust. And how, monks, is a person free from latent tendencies toward hatred? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned ill will, has removed it, has extinguished it, has ended it, and has relinquished it. This, monks, is called a person free from latent tendencies toward hatred. And how, monks, is a person free from latent tendencies toward delusion? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned ignorance regarding suffering, has removed it, has extinguished it, has ended it, and has relinquished it. This, monks, is called a person free from latent tendencies toward delusion.”
“Bhikkhus, these seven persons are worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation; they are an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Which seven?
One liberated in both ways, one liberated by wisdom, a body-witness, one attained to view, one liberated by faith, a Dhamma-follower, and a faith-follower.”
“Monks, these seven persons are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, and are an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Thus was the fourth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.15.

“Bhikkhus, there are these seven types of persons comparable to water, existing and found in the world.
What seven?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person who has once submerged remains submerged.
But here, monks, a certain person, having emerged, sinks down again;
here, monks, a certain person, having emerged, stands firm;
here, monks, a certain person, having emerged, looks ahead and surveys.
But here, monks, some person, having emerged, swims across;
here, monks, some person, having emerged, reaches a firm footing;
and here, monks, some person, having emerged, has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry land as a brahmin.
And how, monks, is a person one who, once submerged, remains submerged?
Here, monks, a certain person is possessed of entirely black, unwholesome qualities.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is one who, once submerged, remains submerged.
And how, monks, does a person, having emerged, sink back down?
Here, monks, a certain person emerges, thinking: "Excellent is faith in wholesome states; excellent is moral shame; ... [and so on] ...
excellent is moral dread."
“Excellent is energy… excellent is wisdom regarding wholesome states.
Yet his faith neither stands firm nor increases; it only declines. His sense of shame… [and so on]… [declines].
For him, that sense of moral dread... that energy...
and that wisdom neither stand still nor increase; they only diminish.
"In this way, monks, a person who has emerged sinks back down.
And how, monks, does a person who has emerged remain standing?
Here, monks, a certain person emerges, thinking: 'Excellent is faith in wholesome states; excellent is moral shame... [and so on].
Excellent is moral dread … excellent is energy … excellent is wisdom regarding wholesome states.
His faith neither diminishes nor increases; it remains stable.
His sense of shame … [as before] … his sense of moral dread … [as before] … remains stable.
His energy...
his wisdom neither diminishes nor increases; it remains stable.
In this way, monks, a person who has emerged stands firm.
And how, monks, does a person emerge and look with insight?
Here, monks, a certain person emerges, thinking: "Excellent is faith in wholesome states; excellent is moral shame...
[and so on] ...excellent is moral dread."
“Excellent is energy… excellent is wisdom regarding wholesome states.
With the complete destruction of the three fetters, he becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for full enlightenment.
"Thus, monks, a person emerges and sees clearly and looks about.
And how, monks, does a person emerge and cross over?
Here, monks, a certain person emerges, thinking: 'Excellent is faith in wholesome states; excellent is moral shame... [and so on].
Excellent is moral dread … excellent is energy … excellent is wisdom regarding wholesome states.

Thus, with the complete destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, one becomes a once-returner; having returned to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering.
In this way, monks, a person, having emerged, crosses over.
And how, monks, does a person, having emerged, reach a firm footing?
In this case, monks, a certain person emerges, thinking: "Excellent is faith in wholesome states; excellent is moral shame; ... [as before] ...
excellent is moral dread;
excellent is energy."
"Excellent is wisdom regarding wholesome states.
Through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, no longer subject to returning from that world.
It is in this way, monks, that a person, having emerged, reaches a firm footing.
And how, monks, is a person one who, having emerged, has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land—a brahmin?
Here, monks, a certain person emerges with the thought: "Excellent is faith in wholesome states; excellent is moral shame; ... [as before] ...
excellent is moral dread."
“Excellent is energy… excellent is wisdom regarding wholesome states.

Through the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.
"It is in this way, monks, that a person, having emerged, has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry land—a brahmin.
These, monks, are the seven types of persons comparable to water found existing in the world.
The fifth.

Anusayavagga Aniccānupassīsutta (The Discourse on Contemplating Impermanence) "Bhikkhus, when one dwells contemplating impermanence in the body, which is impermanent, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having overcome covetousness and grief for the world, the underlying tendency to sensual lust toward the body is abandoned. When one dwells contemplating suffering in what is impermanent, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having overcome covetousness and grief for the world, the underlying tendency to aversion toward what is suffering is abandoned. When one dwells contemplating non-self in what is suffering, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having overcome covetousness and grief for the world, the underlying tendency to the view of self in what is non-self is abandoned. When one dwells contemplating dispassion in what is non-self, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having overcome covetousness and grief for the world, the underlying tendency to delight in formations is abandoned. When one dwells contemplating cessation in what is dispassionate, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having overcome covetousness and grief for the world, the underlying tendency to conceit is abandoned. When one dwells contemplating fading away in what is subject to cessation, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having overcome covetousness and grief for the world, the underlying tendency to craving is abandoned. When one dwells contemplating relinquishment in what is subject to fading away, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having overcome covetousness and grief for the world, the underlying tendency to ignorance is abandoned."

“Bhikkhus, there are these seven grounds for praise. What seven?

he has a keen desire for seclusion and an undiminished love for seclusion in the future.

he has an intense desire for mindfulness and discernment and an undiminished love for mindfulness and discernment in the future;
he has an intense desire for the penetration of views and an undiminished love for the penetration of views in the future.

3. The Chapter on the Seven Vajji Practices:
The Discourse on Sārandada (Sārandadasutta) (AN 7.21, AN 7.19, PTS AN iv 16)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī at the Sārandada Shrine.

Then a large number of Licchavis approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to those Licchavis:
“Licchavis, I will teach you seven principles that prevent decline.
Listen to them and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those Licchavis replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"And what, Licchavis, are the seven principles of non-decline?
As long as, Licchavis, the Vajjis hold frequent assemblies and are devoted to frequent assemblies..."
Growth alone, Licchavis, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.
As long as the Vajjis assemble in harmony, rise in harmony, and carry out their Vajjian duties in harmony—
growth alone, Licchavis, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.

And as long, Licchavis, as the Vajjis do not enact what has not been enacted, do not abolish what has been enacted, and continue to undertake and practice the ancient Vajji traditions as they have been established—
for as long as this is so, Licchavis, growth is to be expected for the Vajjis,
not decline. And as long, Licchavis, as the Vajjis honor, respect, revere, and venerate those who are the elders among the Vajjis, and consider them worthy of being listened to;
Growth alone, Licchavis, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline. And so long, Licchavis,
as the Vajjis do not allow noble women and noble maidens to be taken by force or carried off,
growth alone, Licchavis, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.
And as long as, Licchavis, the Vajjis honor, revere, esteem, and worship those shrines of the Vajjis— both those within and those without—
and do not neglect the righteous offerings and services formerly given and performed for them;
Growth alone, Licchavis, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.
And as long as, Licchavis, the Vajjis maintain well-arranged righteous protection, defense, and security for the arahants, thinking:
"How may arahants who have not yet come to our realm come, and how may those arahants who have already come dwell in comfort within our realm"?
“Growth alone, Licchavis, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.
As long as these seven principles of non-decline endure among the Vajjis, and as long as the Vajjis are seen to conform to these seven principles of non-decline,
growth alone, Licchavis, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.”
First.

If they take up and practice the ancient Vajjian traditions as they have been established, then, Ānanda, growth alone is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.
What have you heard, Ānanda: ‘Do the Vajjis honor, respect, revere, and venerate those who are the elders among the Vajjis, and do they consider it their duty to listen to them?’”
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The Vajjis honor, respect, revere, and venerate those who are the elders among the Vajjis, and they consider it their duty to listen to them.

“As long as, Ānanda, the Vajjis honor, respect, revere, and venerate those who are the elders among the Vajjis, and as long as they consider it their duty to listen to them; for that long, Ānanda, there will surely be growth.”
“The Vajjis may be expected to prosper, Ānanda, not to decline.
What have you heard, Ānanda: ‘Do the Vajjis not live by abducting and forcibly seizing women and girls from their families?
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The Vajjis do not live by abducting and forcibly seizing women and girls from their families.’”

“As long, Ānanda, as the Vajjis do not allow women of good family and daughters of good family to stay there by force or by abduction; as long as this is so, Ānanda, growth is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.

What have you heard, Ānanda: ‘The Vajjis honor, revere, respect, and worship those shrines of the Vajjis, both internal and external, and they maintain what was formerly given and performed for them’?”
“Do they not fail to provide us with our lawful tribute?

“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The Vajjis honor, revere, esteem, and worship those shrines of the Vajjis, both internal and external; and what was formerly given and done for them, they continue to maintain.’”
“...and they do not neglect our lawful offerings.
“Ānanda, as long as the Vajjis honor, revere, esteem, and worship those Vajji shrines— both those within and those without— and continue to provide for them what was previously given...”
“They will not neglect the righteous tribute that has been performed in the past; Ānanda, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.

What have you heard, Ānanda: ‘Has the Vajjis established a righteous system of protection, defense, and security for the arahants—thinking, “How may arahants who have not yet come to the realm come, and how may those who have already come dwell in comfort within the realm?
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The Vajjis have established a righteous system of protection, defense, and security for the arahants…’”
"It will be so— that how the Arahants who have not yet come might come to the realm, and the Arahants who have already come might dwell in comfort within the realm.
"As long as, Ānanda, the Vajjis provide righteous protection, shelter, and security for the Arahants..."
‘How might future Arahants come to the realm, and how might the Arahants who have arrived dwell at ease within the realm?’—
in this case, Ānanda, only growth for the Vajjis is to be expected,
not decline. Then the Blessed One addressed Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha:
“Brahmin, on one occasion I was staying at Vesālī at the Sārandada Shrine.
There, brahmin, I taught these seven principles of non-decline to the Vajjis.
As long as, brahmin, these seven principles of non-decline endure among the Vajjis, and while these seven...”
“The Vajjis will be seen to possess those qualities that prevent decline; O Brahmin, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.
“Master Gotama, if the Vajjis were possessed of even a single quality that prevents decline, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline;
how much more so when they possess all seven qualities that prevent decline!”
"Furthermore, Master Gotama, the Vajjis are not to be attacked in battle by King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha, except by means of bribery or the sowing of dissension.
Now, Master Gotama, we must go; we have many duties and much to do.
"Do now, brahmin, as you see fit," he replied.
Then Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat and departed.
This is the second [sutta].
*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 7.23.
3. The Chapter on the Seven [Qualities] of the Vajjīs The First Discourse on the Seven [Qualities] (AN 7.22–27; AN 7.20.1, PTS AN IV 17)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you seven principles that prevent decline.
Listen to them and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, are the seven qualities that prevent decline?
As long as, bhikkhus, the bhikkhus meet frequently and are devoted to frequent meetings, growth alone is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.”

"As long as, monks, the monks assemble in harmony, rise from their meetings in harmony, and perform the duties of the Saṅgha in harmony, only growth, monks, is to be expected for the monks, not decline. As long as, monks,
the monks do not lay down what has not been laid down, do not abolish what has been laid down,
and practice by undertaking the training rules exactly as they have been laid down, only growth, monks, is to be expected for the monks."
...an increase is to be expected, not decline. And for as long, monks,

as the monks honor, respect, revere, and venerate those elder monks who have long been ordained, who have been long gone forth, who are fathers to the Saṅgha, and who are leaders of the Saṅgha— and [as long as they] toward them...
They will think it worth hearing. Monks, for monks, only growth is to be expected, not decline.
As long as monks do not fall under the power of arisen craving that leads to renewed existence, monks, for monks, only growth is to be expected, not decline.
As long as monks remain intent upon forest dwellings, monks, for monks, only growth is to be expected, not decline.
“Monks, as long as monks establish mindfulness within themselves, thinking:
‘How may well-behaved fellow practitioners who have not yet arrived come here, and how may those well-behaved fellow practitioners who have already arrived dwell in comfort?’—
as long as this is so, monks, growth is to be expected for the monks, not decline.”
“Bhikkhus, as long as these seven principles of non-decline endure among the bhikkhus,
and as long as the bhikkhus are seen to conform to these seven principles of non-decline, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.”
The Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.24.
3. The Chapter on the Seven Qualities of the Vajjīs.
The Second Sutta on the Septad:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you seven qualities that prevent decline.
Listen to that and attend closely…. ”
And what, monks, are the seven qualities that prevent decline?

As long as, monks, the monks do not delight in worldly activity, do not take pleasure in worldly activity, and are not devoted to delighting in worldly activity—only growth, monks, is to be expected for these monks, not decline.
And as long as, monks, the monks do not delight in talk... [and so on].
They will not delight in sleep… they will not delight in socializing… they will not have evil desires,
nor will they fall under the sway of evil desires.
They will have no evil friends, no evil companions, and no evil associates...
they will not fall into a state of complacency through the attainment of some minor distinction; rather, bhikkhus, growth is to be expected for these bhikkhus, not decline.
As long as, bhikkhus, these seven factors of non-decline endure among the bhikkhus, and in these...
“Monks, when monks are seen to conform to the seven principles that prevent decline, only growth is to be expected for the monks,
not decline. This is the fourth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.25 3. Vajjisattakavagga Tatiyasattakasutta (The Seventh Discourse on the Seven) “Bhikkhus, there are these seven principles of non-decline for the Vajjians. As long as these seven principles of non-decline endure among the Vajjians, and as long as the Vajjians are established in them, they may be expected to prosper and not decline. What are the seven? (1) “As long as the Vajjians meet frequently and hold frequent assemblies, and as long as their assemblies are not dominated by the young, but are attended by the elders, and as long as those who have assembled speak what is beneficial and do not engage in idle chatter, and as long as they rise from their assemblies having accomplished their purpose, these are a principle of non-decline for the Vajjians.

(2) “As long as the Vajjians do not authorize what has not been authorized by their elders, nor abolish what has been authorized, but proceed according to what has been authorized by their elders, this is a principle of non-decline for the Vajjians. (3) “As long as the Vajjians honor, respect, revere, and venerate their elders, and consider them worthy of listening to, this is a principle of non-decline for the Vajjians. (4) “As long as the Vajjians do not abduct women and maidens from their families and force them into slavery, this is a principle of non-decline for the Vajjians. (5) “As long as the Vajjians provide security and protection within their own domains for ascetics and brahmins, for those who are vulnerable and destitute, and for all those who live as wanderers, this is a principle of non-decline for the Vajjians. (6) “As long as the Vajjians do not confiscate the property of those who have died without heirs, this is a principle of non-decline for the Vajjians. (7) “As long as the Vajjians honor, respect, revere, and venerate their traditional shrines, both those that are ancient and those that are new, and do not neglect the offerings made to them, this is a principle of non-decline for the Vajjians. These, bhikkhus, are the seven principles of non-decline for the Vajjians. As long as these seven principles of non-decline endure among the Vajjians, and as long as the Vajjians are established in them, they may be expected to prosper and not decline. In the same way, bhikkhus, there are these seven principles of non-decline for this Saṅgha. As long as these seven principles of non-decline endure in this Saṅgha, and as long as the bhikkhus are established in them, this Saṅgha may be expected to prosper and not decline. What are the seven? (1) “As long as the bhikkhus meet frequently and hold frequent assemblies, and as long as their assemblies are not dominated by the young, but are attended by the elders, and as long as those who have assembled speak what is beneficial and do not engage in idle chatter, and as long as they rise from their assemblies having accomplished their purpose, this is a principle of non-decline for this Saṅgha. (2) “As long as the bhikkhus do not authorize what has not been authorized by the Saṅgha, nor abolish what has been authorized, but proceed according to what has been authorized by the Saṅgha, this is a principle of non-decline for this Saṅgha. (3) “As long as the bhikkhus honor, respect, revere, and venerate their elders, and consider them worthy of listening to, this is a principle of non-decline for this Saṅgha. (4) “As long as the bhikkhus do not abduct women and maidens from their families and force them into slavery, this is a principle of non-decline for this Saṅgha. (5) “As long as the bhikkhus provide security and protection for their fellow monks, whether they are newcomers, those of middle standing, or those who have been ordained for a long time, this is a principle of non-decline for this Saṅgha. (6) “As long as the bhikkhus do not confiscate the requisites of those who have died without heirs, this is a principle of non-decline for this Saṅgha. (7) “As long as the bhikkhus honor, respect, revere, and venerate the training, and do not neglect the rules of conduct, this is a principle of non-decline for this Saṅgha. These, bhikkhus, are the seven principles of non-decline for this Saṅgha. As long as these seven principles of non-decline endure in this Saṅgha, and as long as the bhikkhus are established in them, this Saṅgha may be expected to prosper and not decline.”
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you seven principles that lead to non-decline.
Listen to that and attend closely….
And what, bhikkhus, are the seven principles that lead to non-decline?”
"As long, monks, as the bhikkhus shall have faith, only growth, monks, is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline. As long, monks,
as the bhikkhus shall have a sense of shame … [as they shall have] a sense of moral dread …"
They will be learned;
they will be energetic;
they will be mindful.
They will be possessed of wisdom. Monks, only growth is to be expected for the monks, not decline.

As long as these seven factors of non-decline remain established among the monks, and as long as the monks are seen to conform to these seven factors of non-decline, monks, only growth is to be expected for the monks.
“...is to be expected, not decline.
The fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.26
3. The Chapter on the Seven Qualities of the Vajjis: The Discourse on the Factors of Enlightenment.
“Monks, I shall teach you seven qualities that prevent decline.”
Listen to that and pay close attention...
What, monks, are the seven qualities that prevent decline?
As long as monks develop the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, monks, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.
"And as long, monks, as the bhikkhus will cultivate the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment … the energy factor of enlightenment … the rapture factor of enlightenment …"

They will cultivate the enlightenment factor of tranquility… the enlightenment factor of concentration… the enlightenment factor of equanimity; for these monks, bhikkhus, only growth is to be expected, not decline.
“Bhikkhus, as long as these seven principles of non-decline endure among the bhikkhus,
and as long as the bhikkhus are seen to conform to these seven principles of non-decline, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.27 3.
Vajjisattakavagga (The Chapter on the Seven [Qualities] of the Vajjīs)
The Discourse on Perception:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you seven principles that prevent decline.
Listen to that and attend closely….”
"And what, monks, are the seven qualities that prevent decline?
As long as, monks, the monks cultivate the perception of impermanence, for them, monks, only growth is to be expected, not decline.
And as long as, monks, the monks cultivate the perception of non-self... [and so on].
They will cultivate the perception of foulness;
they will cultivate the perception of danger;
they will cultivate the perception of abandonment.
They will cultivate the perception of dispassion… they will cultivate the perception of cessation;
for as long as this is so, monks, growth is to be expected for these bhikkhus, not decline. And as long as, monks—
"When these seven principles of non-decline are established among the bhikkhus, and when the bhikkhus manifest these seven principles of non-decline,
it can be expected, bhikkhus, that there will be growth for the bhikkhus and not decline.
This is the seventh.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.28 3. Vajjisattakavagga First Discourse on Decline “Monks, there are these seven conditions for the decline and disappearance of a monastic community that has not yet declined. What seven? (1) Here, monks, the monks in this Sangha do not meet frequently, do not meet often, and do not convene in assembly. This is the first condition for the decline and disappearance of a monastic community that has not yet declined. (2) Furthermore, the monks in this Sangha do not meet in harmony, depart in harmony, and conduct their business in harmony. This is the second condition for the decline and disappearance of a monastic community that has not yet declined. (3) Furthermore, the monks in this Sangha do not honor, respect, revere, and venerate those elder bhikkhus who are of long standing, of long duration, fathers and leaders of the Sangha, and who are founders of the training. This is the third condition for the decline and disappearance of a monastic community that has not yet declined.

(4) Furthermore, the monks in this Sangha do not properly learn the Dhamma—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legends, birth stories, marvelous accounts, and classifications—as it has been taught and proclaimed by the Tathāgata. This is the fourth condition for the decline and disappearance of a monastic community that has not yet declined. (5) Furthermore, the monks in this Sangha do not properly learn the discipline—the rules of training, the summaries of the training, the detailed explanations, the matrices, the analysis, the expositions, the regulations, and the collections—as it has been taught and proclaimed by the Tathāgata. This is the fifth condition for the decline and disappearance of a monastic community that has not yet declined. (6) Furthermore, the elders in this Sangha, being themselves luxurious and lax, lead the younger bhikkhus to luxury and laxity. They do not encourage them to be ardent in the higher mind for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, and for the realization of the unrealized. This is the sixth condition for the decline and disappearance of a monastic community that has not yet declined. (7) Furthermore, the monks in this Sangha come under the influence of women and girls, and they frequent the families of such women and girls. This is the seventh condition for the decline and disappearance of a monastic community that has not yet declined. These, monks, are the seven conditions for the decline and disappearance of a monastic community that has not yet declined. Monks, there are these seven conditions for the non-decline and stability of a monastic community that has not yet declined. What seven? (1) Here, monks, the monks in this Sangha meet frequently, meet often, and convene in assembly. This is the first condition for the non-decline and stability of a monastic community that has not yet declined. (2) Furthermore, the monks in this Sangha meet in harmony, depart in harmony, and conduct their business in harmony. This is the second condition for the non-decline and stability of a monastic community that has not yet declined. (3) Furthermore, the monks in this Sangha honor, respect, revere, and venerate those elder bhikkhus who are of long standing, of long duration, fathers and leaders of the Sangha, and who are founders of the training. This is the third condition for the non-decline and stability of a monastic community that has not yet declined. (4) Furthermore, the monks in this Sangha properly learn the Dhamma—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legends, birth stories, marvelous accounts, and classifications—as it has been taught and proclaimed by the Tathāgata. This is the fourth condition for the non-decline and stability of a monastic community that has not yet declined. (5) Furthermore, the monks in this Sangha properly learn the discipline—the rules of training, the summaries of the training, the detailed explanations, the matrices, the analysis, the expositions, the regulations, and the collections—as it has been taught and proclaimed by the Tathāgata. This is the fifth condition for the non-decline and stability of a monastic community that has not yet declined. (6) Furthermore, the elders in this Sangha, being themselves ardent, lead the younger bhikkhus to ardor. They encourage them to be ardent in the higher mind for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, and for the realization of the unrealized. This is the sixth condition for the non-decline and stability of a monastic community that has not yet declined. (7) Furthermore, the monks in this Sangha do not come under the influence of women and girls, nor do they frequent the families of such women and girls. This is the seventh condition for the non-decline and stability of a monastic community that has not yet declined. These, monks, are the seven conditions for the non-decline and stability of a monastic community that has not yet declined.”
(AN 7.28, AN 7.26, PTS AN iv 24) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven qualities that lead to the decline of a bhikkhu in training.
What seven?”
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, lack of restraint over the sense faculties,
and lack of moderation in eating— furthermore, there are communal duties to be performed within the Saṅgha; regarding these, a bhikkhu who is still in training reflects thus:
‘There are indeed elders in the Saṅgha who are long-standing, long-ordained, and bearers of the burden; they will be known by that [act]. Thus, he applies himself to them personally.
These, monks, are the seven qualities that lead to the decline of a bhikkhu in training.
These, monks, are the seven qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu in training.
Which seven?

Not delighting in work, not delighting in talk, not delighting in sleep, not delighting in company, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, and there are indeed communal duties in the Saṅgha; regarding these, a bhikkhu who is still in training reflects thus:

"Furthermore, there are elders in the Saṅgha who have long been ordained, who have long gone forth, and who are bearers of the burden; they will be recognized for that [virtue]. Thus, he does not apply himself to them out of self-interest.
These, monks, are the seven qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu in training.
The eighth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.29 3.
Vajjisattakavagga Dutiyaparihānisutta (The Second Discourse on Decline)
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven qualities that lead to the decline of a lay follower. What seven? [The text continues with the list of seven qualities.]”
He neglects seeing the bhikkhus,
he neglects hearing the true Dhamma,
and he does not train in the higher morality.
He is full of little faith;
he listens to the Dhamma with a critical mind toward the elder, the junior, and the middle-ranking bhikkhus, seeking out faults;
and he looks for objects of offerings outside of this [Sangha].
And therein he performs the first service.
These, monks, are the seven qualities that lead to the decline of a lay follower.
These, monks, are the seven qualities that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower.
Which seven?
He does not neglect seeing bhikkhus;
he does not neglect hearing the true Dhamma.
He trains in the higher virtue;
he is full of confidence;
and among the elder, junior, and middle-ranking bhikkhus, he listens to the Dhamma with a mind free from criticism, not seeking out faults.
He does not seek out those worthy of offerings outside of this [teaching],
and he performs meritorious deeds here [within it].
These, monks, are the seven qualities that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further said this:
“Beholding those who have developed themselves...”
The lay follower who neglects listening to the noble teachings and does not train in higher virtue.
Lack of confidence in the monks increases more and more,
and his mind becomes intent on finding fault.
He desires to hear the true Dhamma,
yet he seeks elsewhere outside of this [teaching] for one worthy of offerings.
And the lay follower who performs meritorious deeds right there—
these indeed are the factors of decline.
A lay follower who practices these seven well-taught qualities does not decline from the true Dhamma.
The lay follower who does not neglect visiting those of developed self,
nor hearing the noble teachings, [is one who has fulfilled his duty].
And he trains in the higher virtue;
his confidence in the bhikkhus increases more and more.
With a mind free from reproach,
one desires to hear the true Dhamma;
not seeking anything else outside of this.
That lay follower who seeks out those worthy of offerings and performs meritorious deeds right here [in this life].
These indeed are the seven well-taught qualities that lead to non-decline;
a lay follower who cultivates them—
“He does not fall away from the true Dhamma.
Thus was the ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.30

3. Vajjisattakavagga: Vipattisutta (The Discourse on Failures) “Monks, there are these seven failures of a noble disciple. What seven? Failure in faith, failure in virtue, failure in learning, failure in generosity, failure in wisdom, failure in lack of shame, and failure in lack of moral dread. These, monks, are the seven failures of a noble disciple.”
"Bhikkhus, there are these seven failures of a lay follower...
[and] there are these seven accomplishments of a lay follower...
Tenth."

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.31 3. Vajjisattakavagga Parābhava Sutta: On Decline “Monks, there are these seven causes and conditions for the decline of a noble clan that has long been established, well-grown, prosperous, and numerous. What seven? Herein, monks, the members of a noble clan do not honor those who are worthy of honor; they do not respect those who are worthy of respect; they do not venerate those who are worthy of veneration; they do not revere those who are worthy of reverence. They do not support their mother and father who have raised them, who have brought them up, who have shown them the world. They do not support ascetics and brahmins who are self-restrained in body, speech, and mind, who live the holy life, and who practice for the sake of the higher realms and the welfare of others. They do not maintain the ancestral shrines, neglecting the offerings and the sacrifices. They do not maintain the true Dhamma, abandoning the teachings of the Buddhas that are wholesome, leading to liberation, and conducive to the goal. They do not maintain the righteous conduct of the noble ones, abandoning the virtuous behavior practiced by the noble ones. These, monks, are the seven causes and conditions for the decline of a noble clan that has long been established, well-grown, prosperous, and numerous. But, monks, there are these seven causes and conditions for the non-decline of a noble clan that has long been established, well-grown, prosperous, and numerous. What seven? Herein, monks, the members of a noble clan honor those who are worthy of honor; they respect those who are worthy of respect; they venerate those who are worthy of veneration; they revere those who are worthy of reverence. They support their mother and father who have raised them, who have brought them up, who have shown them the world. They support ascetics and brahmins who are self-restrained in body, speech, and mind, who live the holy life, and who practice for the sake of the higher realms and the welfare of others. They maintain the ancestral shrines, not neglecting the offerings and the sacrifices. They maintain the true Dhamma, upholding the teachings of the Buddhas that are wholesome, leading to liberation, and conducive to the goal. They maintain the righteous conduct of the noble ones, practicing the virtuous behavior of the noble ones. These, monks, are the seven causes and conditions for the non-decline of a noble clan that has long been established, well-grown, prosperous, and numerous.”
“Monks, there are these seven grounds for the ruin of a lay follower... [as above] ...
Monks, there are these seven grounds for the prosperity of a lay follower.”
Which seven?
He does not neglect seeing the bhikkhus;
he does not neglect hearing the true Dhamma.
He trains in the higher virtue;
he is full of confidence;
and among the elder, junior, and middle-ranking bhikkhus, he listens to the Dhamma with a mind free from criticism, not seeking out faults.
He does not seek those worthy of offerings outside of this [teaching],
and he performs meritorious deeds here.
These, monks, are the seven qualities that arise in a lay follower.
The lay follower who, having seen those of developed self,
neglects both the hearing of the noble Dhamma and—
He does not train in the higher morality,
and his lack of confidence toward the monks increases more and more.
And with a mind intent on finding fault,
he wishes to hear the true Dhamma; and from here,
he seeks something else outside.
The lay follower who seeks out one worthy of offerings and performs an act of merit for that very person first.
These seven factors conducive to decline have been well taught;
a lay follower practicing them—
The lay follower who does not neglect the vision of those whose minds are developed does not fall away from the true Dhamma.
He listens to the noble teachings and trains in the higher morality;
he has confidence in the bhikkhus.
It increases more and more;
with a mind free from malice,
he desires to hear the true Dhamma.
He does not seek another worthy of offerings outside of this [teaching];
he performs meritorious deeds right here.
The lay follower who practices these seven well-taught factors that lead to non-decline.
“The lay follower who practices thus does not fall away from the true Dhamma.
Thus ends the eleventh [sutta].
The third chapter is the Vajjisattaka-vagga.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is: Sāranda and Vassakāra.
The seven triads concerning monks;
the two regarding the perception of enlightenment; decline and ruin.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.32 4. Devatāvagga Appamādagāravasutta (The Discourse on Reverence for Heedfulness) “Bhikkhus, there are these seven kinds of persons found existing in the world. What seven? The person who is heedless and does not honor heedfulness; the person who is heedful and honors heedfulness; the person who is muddle-minded and does not honor mindfulness; the person who is mindful and honors mindfulness; the person who is unlearned and does not honor learning; the person who is learned and honors learning; and the person who is one of little virtue and does not honor virtue. These, bhikkhus, are the seven kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha continued: “Bhikkhus, there are these seven kinds of persons found existing in the world. What seven? The person who is heedless and does not honor heedfulness... [as above] ...and the person who is one of little virtue and does not honor virtue. These, bhikkhus, are the seven kinds of persons found existing in the world.

But, bhikkhus, there are these other seven kinds of persons found existing in the world. What seven? The person who is heedless and honors heedfulness; the person who is heedful and honors heedfulness; the person who is muddle-minded and honors mindfulness; the person who is mindful and honors mindfulness; the person who is unlearned and honors learning; the person who is learned and honors learning; and the person who is one of little virtue and honors virtue. These, bhikkhus, are the seven kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha continued: “Bhikkhus, there are these seven kinds of persons found existing in the world. What seven?
