Then, when the night had advanced, a certain deity of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove,
approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, [she stood] to one side.
She stood to one side. Standing there, that deity addressed the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, these seven qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
What are the seven?”

“Veneration for the Teacher, veneration for the Dhamma, veneration for the Saṅgha, veneration for the training, veneration for concentration, veneration for heedfulness, and veneration for hospitality. These, venerable sir, are the seven qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
This is what that deity said.
The Teacher gave his consent.
Then that deity, thinking, "The Teacher has consented to me," paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to the right, and vanished right there.
Then, when that night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, last night, when the night was far spent, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, having illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, approached me.
Having approached and paid homage to me, she stood to one side.
Standing there to one side, monks, that deity said this to me:”
“Bhante, there are these seven qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
What are the seven?
Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, reverence for concentration, reverence for heedfulness, and reverence for hospitality.”
“Venerable sir, these seven qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
This is what that deity said, monks.
Having said this, she paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to her right, and vanished right there.
Reverent toward the Teacher, reverent toward the Dhamma,
and possessing intense reverence for the Saṅgha;
reverent toward concentration and ardent in effort.
One who has intense reverence for the training,
a bhikkhu who values heedfulness and respects hospitality.
He is incapable of falling away;
he is indeed close to Nibbāna. Thus ends the first [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.33 4.

Devatāvagga Hirigāravasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these seven qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. What seven? He has a sense of moral shame and a sense of moral dread; he is learned; he is content with the four requisites of life; he is one who delights in meditation; he is one who delights in wakefulness; he is one who honors the elders among the bhikkhus—those who are senior, long-standing, long-ordained, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha. These, bhikkhus, are the seven qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee.”
“Monks, this very night, when the night was far spent, a certain deity of surpassing beauty,
having illuminated the entirety of Jeta’s Grove, approached me; having approached and paid homage to me, [she stood] to one side.”
He stood there. Standing to one side, monks, that deity said this to me:
“Venerable sir, these seven qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
Which seven?”

“Veneration for the Teacher, veneration for the Dhamma, veneration for the Saṅgha, veneration for the training, veneration for concentration, veneration for moral shame, and veneration for moral dread. These, Bhante, are the seven qualities that lead to a bhikkhu’s non-decline.
This is what that deity said, monks.
Having said this, he paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to his right, and vanished right there.
Reverent toward the Teacher, reverent toward the Dhamma,
and possessing intense reverence for the Saṅgha;
Reverent toward concentration, ardent,
with intense reverence for the training,
and endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing.
Possessing reverence and respect,
he is incapable of decline and is indeed close to Nibbāna.
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.34 4. Devatāvagga (The Chapter on Deities)
The Discourse on Being Easy to Correct (First) (Paṭhamasovacassatāsutta).
“Monks, last night a certain deity approached me while I was sitting in the open air and spoke to me thus: [The discourse continues as in AN 7.33–34.]
“Bhante, there are these seven qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
What are the seven?
Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, reverence for concentration, being easy to correct, and having virtuous friends.”
“Venerable sir, these seven qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
This is what that deity said, monks.
Having said this, she paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to her right, and vanished right there.
Reverent toward the Teacher, reverent toward the Dhamma,
and possessing intense reverence for the Saṅgha;
reverent toward concentration and ardent in effort—
Having intense reverence for the training,
possessing good friends, being easy to speak with,
respectful, and deferential.
He is incapable of falling away;
he is close to Nibbāna itself. Thus ends the third [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.35 4. Devatāvagga Dutiyasovacassatāsutta (The Second Discourse on Being Easy to Speak To) “Monks, there are these seven qualities that make one easy to speak to. What seven? Here, monks, a monk is endowed with faith; he places trust in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus:

‘Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He has heard much, has retained what he has heard, and has stored up what he has heard. All those teachings that are lovely in the beginning, lovely in the middle, and lovely in the end, which in spirit and in letter proclaim the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure—such teachings as these he has heard much of, retained, recited verbally, investigated with the mind, and penetrated well through view. He is easy to speak to; he is patient and does not become irritated when spoken to. He is gentle in his speech; he speaks words that are blameless, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, reaching the heart, urbane, and liked by many people. He is not envious; he does not envy others’ gain, honor, offerings, respect, reverence, salutations, or the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. He is not miserly; he is not stingy with regard to dwellings, families, or gains. He is open-handed, living as one who gives, delighting in relinquishment, one who makes others happy, and one who enjoys sharing. He is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. These, monks, are the seven qualities that make one easy to speak to.”
“Monks, this very night, when the night was far spent, a certain deity of surpassing beauty approached... [and said]:
‘Venerable sir, there are these seven qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.’”
“What seven?
Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, reverence for concentration, being easy to correct, and having good friends.
These, Bhante, are the seven qualities that lead to a bhikkhu’s non-decline.”
“This is what that deity said, monks.
Having said this, she paid homage to me, circumambulated me with her right side toward me, and vanished right there.
When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I understand the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief in this way:
Here, venerable sir, a bhikkhu himself has reverence for the Teacher and speaks in praise of such reverence for the Teacher.
And those other bhikkhus who lack reverence for the Teacher, he encourages them toward reverence for the Teacher.”
He speaks at the proper time, truthfully and accurately, in praise of those other bhikkhus who have reverence for the Teacher.
He himself possesses reverence for the Dhamma … [and] he possesses reverence for the Saṅgha …
He has reverence for the training;
he has reverence for concentration;
he is easy to correct.
He has good friends, he speaks in praise of having good friends;
he encourages those other monks who do not have good friends to adopt the practice of having good friends;
and he speaks at the proper time, truthfully and accurately, in praise of those other monks who do have good friends.
“Bhante, this is how I understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
It is good, Sāriputta, that you understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief in such a way.”
Here, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu himself has reverence for the Teacher and speaks in praise of having reverence for the Teacher.
He encourages other bhikkhus who lack reverence for the Teacher to develop reverence for the Teacher,
and he speaks at the proper time, truthfully and accurately, in praise of those other bhikkhus who do have reverence for the Teacher.
He himself has reverence for the Dhamma … he has reverence for the Saṅgha … he has reverence for the training …
He has reverence for concentration;
he is easy to speak to;
he has good friends and speaks in praise of having good friends.
“Those other monks who are not good friends, he encourages them toward being good friends.
And those other monks who are good friends, he speaks in praise of them—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time.
“Sāriputta, this is how the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.36 4. Devatāvagga (The Chapter on Devas)
The First Discourse on Friends (Paṭhamamittasutta): “Monks,
a friend endowed with seven factors should be cultivated.

"By which seven? He gives what is hard to give; he does what is hard to do; he endures what is hard to endure; he reveals his secrets; he guards his secrets; he does not abandon him in times of misfortune; he does not despise him when he is destitute.
It is by possessing these seven factors, monks, that a friend should be cultivated."
A friend gives what is hard to give and performs what is difficult to do;
yet even for such a one, harsh words [are uttered].
He endures suffering and insults;
he reveals his secrets to him and keeps his secrets hidden.
He does not abandon one in times of misfortune,
nor does he despise one for what has been consumed.
In whomsoever these qualities reside—
Such individuals are found here in this world;
one who desires friends should associate with such a person as a true friend.
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.37 4.
Devatāvagga (The Chapter on Deities)
The Second Discourse on Friends (Dutiyamittasutta): “Bhikkhus,
a bhikkhu who possesses seven qualities should be cultivated, befriended, and attended upon by a friend, even if he is being sent away.”
Which seven?
He is beloved, pleasing, respected, and worthy of honor; he is one who speaks and is patient with what is said; he is a speaker of profound discourse, yet does not direct one toward what is improper.
Possessing these seven qualities, monks, a monk who is a friend should be served, associated with, and attended upon—even if one is being dismissed.
One who is dear, respected, and inspiring;
one who speaks and is patient with what is said;
and one who delivers profound discourse—
He does not direct one toward what is improper.
In whatever person these qualities are found here, [he is a true teacher].
Thus, a friend who desires a friend,
out of compassion and wishing for their welfare,
should act even if they are being led away.
“Such a person as that should be honored.
The sixth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.38

4. Devatāvagga First Discourse on the Analytical Knowledges (Paṭhamapaṭisambhidāsutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these four analytical knowledges. What four? The analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of language, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence. These, bhikkhus, are the four analytical knowledges.”
“Bhikkhus, endowed with seven qualities, a bhikkhu will, before long, having realized them for himself through direct knowledge, dwell in the possession of the four analytical knowledges.
What are the seven?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is mental sluggishness in myself.’”
When the mind is contracted internally, he understands it as it really is: "My mind is contracted internally.
When the mind is distracted externally, he understands it as it really is: "My mind is distracted externally.
His feelings arise known, they persist known, and they pass away known.
Perceptions arise known, they persist known, and they pass away known;
thoughts arise known, they persist known, and they pass away known.

Furthermore, regarding phenomena that are suitable or unsuitable, inferior or superior, dark or bright, and their counterparts, he has well grasped the sign, attended to it well, retained it well, and penetrated it with wisdom.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these seven qualities will, before long, having realized the four analytical knowledges for himself through direct knowledge, dwell in their possession.
Thus was the seventh [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.39.

4. Devatāvagga Dutiyapaṭisambhidāsutta (AN 7.39, AN 7.37b, PTS AN iv 33) “Monks, there are these four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). What four? The analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*). These, monks, are the four analytical knowledges.”
“Bhikkhus, endowed with seven qualities, Sāriputta dwells having himself realized and attained through direct knowledge the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
With which seven?
Here, bhikkhus, Sāriputta understands as it really is: ‘This is mental sluggishness in myself.’”
When the mind is contracted internally, he understands it as it really is: "My mind is contracted internally.
When the mind is distracted externally, he understands it as it really is: "My mind is distracted externally.
His feelings arise known, they remain present known, and they pass away known.
Perceptions are known...
thoughts arise, are known, persist, and pass away as they are known.

Furthermore, regarding things that are suitable or unsuitable, inferior or superior, dark or bright, and their opposites, he has well grasped the sign, attended to it well, retained it well, and penetrated it well with wisdom.
“Bhikkhus, endowed with these seven qualities, Sāriputta dwells having himself realized and attained through direct knowledge the four analytical knowledges.
Thus was the eighth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.40

4. Devatāvagga Paṭhamavasasutta (AN 7.40, AN 7.38a, PTS AN iv 34) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on the present life but not on the future life; the person who is intent on the future life but not on the present life; the person who is intent on neither the present life nor the future life; and the person who is intent on both the present life and the future life. And how, monks, is one a person intent on the present life but not on the future life? Here, monks, someone dwells pursuing the pleasure of sense pleasures, indulging in the pursuit of sense pleasures, burning with passion for them, infatuated by them, and finding gratification therein. This, monks, is called a person intent on the present life but not on the future life. And how, monks, is one a person intent on the future life but not on the present life? Here, monks, someone dwells pursuing self-mortification, indulging in the pursuit of self-mortification, burning with passion for it, infatuated by it, and finding gratification therein. This, monks, is called a person intent on the future life but not on the present life. And how, monks, is one a person intent on neither the present life nor the future life? Here, monks, someone dwells pursuing neither sense pleasures nor self-mortification, but remains indifferent to both, aloof from them, and finds no gratification therein. This, monks, is called a person intent on neither the present life nor the future life. And how, monks, is one a person intent on both the present life and the future life? Here, monks, someone dwells possessing the fivefold sense-pleasure restraint, endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, enjoying himself with them, delighting in them, and finding gratification therein. And he is one who has developed the mind of loving-kindness, cultivated it, made much of it, established it, maintained it, augmented it, and perfected it. This, monks, is called a person intent on both the present life and the future life. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing seven qualities, a bhikkhu wields mastery over his mind; he does not come under the sway of the mind.
What are the seven?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is skilled in concentration, skilled in the attainment of concentration, skilled in concentration...”
“He is skilled in stability, skilled in emerging from concentration, skilled in the excellence of concentration, skilled in the range of concentration, and skilled in the directing of concentration.
Possessing these seven qualities, monks, a bhikkhu wields mastery over his mind; he does not come under the sway of his mind.”
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.41 4.
Devatāvagga (The Chapter on Devas)
The Second Discourse on Mastery (Dutiyavasasutta):
“Bhikkhus, endowed with seven qualities, Sāriputta wields mastery over his mind; he does not, however, come under the sway of his mind.”
By which seven?

Here, monks, Sāriputta is skilled in concentration; he is skilled in the attainment of concentration, skilled in the maintenance of concentration, skilled in the emergence from concentration, skilled in the excellence of concentration, and skilled in the range of concentration.
He is skilled in the directing of concentration.
Endowed with these seven qualities, monks, Sāriputta wields his mind as he pleases, and Sāriputta does not allow himself to be wielded by his mind.
Thus ends the tenth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.42 4. Devatāvagga Paṭhamaniddasasutta (The First Discourse on the Ten) “Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities of one who is ‘touched’ by the Dhamma. What ten? He is endowed with faith; he has confidence in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus:

‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses a sense of moral shame; he is ashamed of doing evil and unwholesome deeds. He possesses moral dread; he dreads doing evil and unwholesome deeds. He is learned; he has retained in mind what he has heard from the Teacher or his disciples, and by reciting it often and reflecting on it, he has penetrated its meaning through view. He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. He is easy to correct and possesses qualities that make him easy to correct; he is patient and receives instruction respectfully. He is energetic; he possesses firm energy and does not abandon the task of developing wholesome qualities. He is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. He frequents pleasant lodgings: remote jungle-thicket resting places in the forest, at the foot of a tree, in mountain caves, in grottoes, in open spaces, and in charnel grounds. These, bhikkhus, are the ten qualities of one who is ‘touched’ by the Dhamma.”
(AN 7.42, AN 7.39, PTS AN iv 34) Then, in the morning,
the Venerable Sāriputta dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then,
it occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī.
What if I were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?
Then the Venerable Sāriputta went to the park of the wanderers of other sects; having arrived, he exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side.
Now at that time, while those wanderers of other sects were seated together in assembly, this discussion arose among them:
"Friends, anyone who has practiced the complete and pure holy life for twelve years is fit to be called a 'twelve-year monk.'"
Then the Venerable Sāriputta neither approved nor rejected the words of those wanderers of other sects.
Without approving or rejecting them, he rose from his seat and departed, thinking:
"I shall understand the meaning of these words in the presence of the Blessed One."
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from his almsround after the meal, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Then, Bhante, this thought occurred to me:
‘It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī.’”
"What if I were to go to the park where the wanderers of other sects are?
Then, venerable sir, I went to the park where the wanderers of other sects were; having arrived, I exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects.
When we had concluded our polite and courteous conversation, I sat down to one side.
Now at that time, Bhante, while those wanderers of other sects were sitting together in assembly, this discussion arose among them:
"Friends, anyone who has practiced the holy life for twelve years—complete and pure—is fit to be called a 'bhikkhu free from the stains.
Then, Bhante, I neither rejoiced in the words of those wanderers of other sects nor did I reject them.
Without approving and without rejecting it, I rose from my seat and departed, thinking:
"I shall learn the meaning of this in the presence of the Blessed One.
"Is it possible, venerable sir, in this Dhamma and Vinaya, for a monk to be designated as 'one who has reached the tenth year' merely by counting the number of rains?"
“Sāriputta, it is not possible in this Dhamma and Discipline to designate a bhikkhu as ‘of ten years’ seniority’ merely by counting the number of rains.
There are, Sāriputta, these seven grounds for being of ten years’ seniority that have been declared by me after realizing them for myself with direct knowledge.
What are the seven?
"Here, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu has a keen desire for undertaking the training and an undiminished love for undertaking the training in the future;
he has a keen desire for settling in the Dhamma and an undiminished love for settling in the Dhamma in the future;
he has a keen desire for the removal of longing and an undiminished love for the removal of longing in the future; he has a keen desire for seclusion..."
He has a strong desire for future solitude and an undiminished love for it; he has a strong desire for the exertion of energy and an undiminished love for the exertion of energy in the future;
he has a strong desire for mindfulness and discernment and an undiminished love for mindfulness and discernment in the future;
he has a strong desire for the penetration of views and an undiminished love for the penetration of views in the future.
"These, Sāriputta, are the seven grounds for being called 'one who has completed the course,' which I have declared after realizing them for myself through direct knowledge.

Possessing these seven grounds for being called 'one who has completed the course,' a bhikkhu—if he practices the complete and pure holy life for twelve years—is fit to be called 'a bhikkhu who has completed the course';
if he practices the complete and pure holy life for twenty-four years, he is fit to be called 'a bhikkhu who has completed the course.'"
“Even if one practices the holy life (brahmacariya) for thirty-six years, complete and pure, it is sufficient to call such a monk ‘one who has completed the ten-year course’;
even if one practices the holy life for forty-eight years, complete and pure,
it is sufficient to call such a monk ‘one who has completed the ten-year course.’”

The Second Discourse on the Declaration of Purpose (Dutiya-niddesa-sutta).
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kosambī for alms.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
“It is still too early to wander for alms in Kosambī.
What if I were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?
Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the park of the wanderers of other sects; having arrived, he exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries with him, he sat down to one side.
Now at that time, while those wanderers of other sects were seated together in assembly, this discussion arose among them:
"Friends, anyone who has practiced the complete and pure holy life for twelve years is fit to be called a 'bhikkhu of ten years' standing.'"
Then the Venerable Ānanda neither rejoiced in nor rejected the words of those wanderers of other sects.
Without rejoicing or rejecting them, he rose from his seat and departed,
thinking, "I shall understand the meaning of these words in the presence of the Blessed One."
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having walked for alms in Kosambī and returned from his almsround after his meal, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I entered Kosambī for alms.
Then, Bhante, this thought occurred to me:
‘It is still too early to wander for alms in Kosambī.’”
"What if I were to go to the park where the wanderers of other sects are?"...
[he went] and exchanged greetings with them.
When they had concluded their polite and memorable conversation, he sat down to one side.
“Now at that time, Bhante, while those wanderers of other sects were sitting gathered together, this discussion arose among them:
‘Friends, anyone who has practiced the holy life for twelve years—complete and pure—is fit to be called a bhikkhu who has completed his course.
Then, Bhante, I neither rejoiced in the statement of those wanderers of other sects nor did I reject it.”
Without approving and without rejecting it, I rose from my seat and departed, thinking:
“I shall understand the meaning of these words in the presence of the Blessed One.
“Is it possible, venerable sir, in this Dhamma and Discipline, for a monk to be designated as ‘one of ten rains’ merely by counting the number of years?”
“Ānanda, it is not possible in this Dhamma and Discipline to designate a bhikkhu as ‘of ten years’ standing merely by counting the number of rainy-season retreats.
There are, Ānanda, these seven grounds for being of ten years’ standing that have been declared by me after realizing them for myself through direct knowledge.
What are the seven?
“Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith, he is possessed of a sense of shame, he is afraid of wrongdoing, he is learned, he is energetic, he is mindful, and he is wise.
These, Ānanda, are the seven grounds for declaring [one’s seniority], which I have proclaimed after realizing them for myself through direct knowledge.

If a bhikkhu endowed with these seven grounds for declaring [his seniority] should lead the full and pure holy life for twelve years, it is sufficient to call him a ‘bhikkhu who has declared his seniority.’”
If one practices the holy life (brahmacariya) for twenty-four years, fulfilled and pure, it is sufficient to call him a "bhikkhu of ten years' standing";
if one practices the holy life for thirty-six years, fulfilled and pure, it is sufficient to call him a "bhikkhu of ten years' standing";
and if one practices the holy life for forty-eight years, fulfilled and pure, [it is likewise sufficient].
“A bhikkhu who has seen [the truth] is fit for this address.
The twelfth [sutta].
The fourth chapter on Devas is finished.
Its summary verse:
Heedfulness and conscience,
two who are easy to speak with, and two kinds of friends.
Two analytical knowledges, two powers,
and two bases for the destruction of the taints.
