5. The Chapter on the Great Sacrifice:
The Discourse on the Seven Stations of Consciousness (Sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitisutta) (AN 7.44, AN 7.41, PTS AN iv 39)
“Bhikkhus, there are seven stations of consciousness.
What are the seven?
There are beings, bhikkhus, who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as humans, some devas, and some beings in the states of deprivation.
This is the first station of consciousness.
There are, monks, beings who are diverse in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-order who have first reappeared there.
This is the second station of consciousness.
"There are, monks, beings who are uniform in body and diverse in perception, such as the Ābhassara gods.
This is the third station of consciousness.
There are, monks, beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Subhakiṇha gods."
This is the fourth station of consciousness.

There are, monks, beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," have reached the sphere of infinite space.
This is the fifth station of consciousness.
There are, monks, beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," have reached the base of infinite consciousness.
This is the sixth station of consciousness.
There are, monks, beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever," have reached the base of nothingness.
This is the seventh station of consciousness.
These, monks, are the seven stations of consciousness. Thus was the first [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.45 5.
Mahāyaññavagga Samādhiparikkhārasutta (The Requisites for Concentration)
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven requisites for concentration.
What seven?”
“Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness.
That one-pointedness of mind which is fully equipped with these seven factors, monks, is called noble right concentration ‘with its proximate cause’ and ‘with its equipment.
This is the second [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.46 5. Mahāyaññavagga First Discourse on Fire (Paṭhamaaggisutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these seven kinds of fire. What seven? The fire of grass, the fire of wood, the fire of chaff, the fire of dung, the fire of rubbish, the fire of the gods, and the fire of the noble ones. These, bhikkhus, are the seven kinds of fire. Of these seven fires, bhikkhus, the fire of the noble ones is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, is the fire of the noble ones the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among these seven fires?

“Bhikkhu, when a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, he is one who will attain final nibbāna from that very state, without ever returning from that world. This, bhikkhu, is the fire of the noble ones: it is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among these seven fires. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the fire of the noble ones is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among these seven fires? “Bhikkhu, the fire of the noble ones burns with the fuel of faith, burns with the fuel of virtue, burns with the fuel of learning, burns with the fuel of generosity, and burns with the fuel of wisdom. Because it burns with these fuels, bhikkhu, the fire of the noble ones is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among these seven fires. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how does the fire of the noble ones burn with the fuel of faith, how does it burn with the fuel of virtue, how does it burn with the fuel of learning, how does it burn with the fuel of generosity, and how does it burn with the fuel of wisdom? “Bhikkhu, when a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One’—in this way, bhikkhu, the fire of the noble ones burns with the fuel of faith. When a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise’—in this way, bhikkhu, the fire of the noble ones burns with the fuel of faith. When a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world’—in this way, bhikkhu, the fire of the noble ones burns with the fuel of faith. When a noble disciple possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration—in this way, bhikkhu, the fire of the noble ones burns with the fuel of virtue. When a noble disciple has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and consolidates what he has learned; when the teachings he has learned are well-preserved in his mind, well-rehearsed by speech, well-penetrated by view, and well-mastered by the heart—in this way, bhikkhu, the fire of the noble ones burns with the fuel of learning. When a noble disciple is generous, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, one who dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, devoted to charity, ready to give, and delighting in giving—in this way, bhikkhu, the fire of the noble ones burns with the fuel of generosity. When a noble disciple possesses wisdom—wisdom directed toward arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering—in this way, bhikkhu, the fire of the noble ones burns with the fuel of wisdom. Thus, bhikkhu, the fire of the noble ones burns with the fuel of faith, burns with the fuel of virtue, burns with the fuel of learning, burns with the fuel of generosity, and burns with the fuel of wisdom. Because it burns with these fuels, bhikkhu, the fire of the noble ones is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among these seven fires. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the fire of the noble ones is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among these seven fires. Venerable sir, just as the ocean is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among all bodies of water, so too, venerable sir, the fire of the noble ones is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among these seven fires. Venerable sir, just as the river Ganges inclines toward the east, slopes toward the east, and flows toward the east, so too, venerable sir, the fire of the noble ones inclines toward the east, slopes toward the east, and flows toward the east. Venerable sir, just as the river Yamunā, the river Aciravatī, the river Sarabhū, and the river Mahī incline toward the ocean, slope toward the ocean, and flow toward the ocean, so too, venerable sir, the fire of the noble ones inclines toward the ocean, slopes toward the ocean, and flows toward the ocean. Venerable sir, just as the river Gaṅgā, the river Yamunā, the river Aciravatī, the river Sarabhū, and the river Mahī enter the great ocean, reach the great ocean, and become the great ocean, so too, venerable sir, the fire of the noble ones enters the great ocean, reaches the great ocean, and becomes the great ocean. Venerable sir, just as the great ocean is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among all bodies of water, so too, venerable sir, the fire of the noble ones is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among these seven fires. “Bhikkhu, it is because you have been taught by those who know, who see, the arahants, that you speak thus. For indeed, bhikkhu, it is because they were taught by those who know, who see, the arahants, that the fire of the noble ones is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among these seven fires. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, that bhikkhu delighted in the Blessed One’s words. (This concludes the First Discourse on Fire.)
“Bhikkhus, there are these seven fires.
Which seven?
“The fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion, the fire for those worthy of offerings, the fire of the householder, the fire for those worthy of gifts, and the fire of wood—
these, monks, are the seven fires. This is the third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.47 5.
Mahāyaññavagga Dutiyaaggisutta (The Second Discourse on Fire)
Now at that time, a great sacrifice had been prepared by the brahmin Uggatasarīra.
Five hundred bulls had been brought to the sacrificial posts for the sake of the sacrifice, and five hundred young oxen had also been brought to the sacrificial posts.
Five hundred young bulls were brought to the sacrificial post for the sake of sacrifice;
five hundred goats were brought to the sacrificial post for the sake of sacrifice; five hundred rams were brought to the sacrificial post for the sake of sacrifice.
Then the brahmin Uggatasarīra approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the brahmin Uggatasarīra said this to the Blessed One:
"I have heard, Master Gotama, that taking up the sacrificial fire and erecting a sacrificial post brings great fruit and great benefit.
"I too, brahmin, have heard that taking up the sacrificial fire and erecting a sacrificial post brings great fruit and great benefit."
A second time, the brahmin Uggatasarīra...
[and] a third time, the brahmin Uggatasarīra said this to the Blessed One:
"I have heard, Master Gotama, that taking up the fire and raising the sacrificial post brings great fruit and great benefit."
“Indeed, brahmin, I too have heard that taking up the sacrificial fire and raising the sacrificial post is of great fruit and great benefit.
“This, Master Gotama, agrees with you in every respect, exactly as it is for us.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the brahmin Uggatasarīra:
“Brahmin, Tathāgatas should not be asked thus:
‘I have heard this, Master Gotama: the taking up of the fire and the raising of the sacrificial post brings great fruit and great benefit.
Rather, Brahmin, Tathāgatas should be asked thus:”
“Venerable sir, I desire to take up the sacrificial fire and to raise the sacrificial post.
May the Blessed One exhort me, venerable sir;
may the Blessed One instruct me, venerable sir, in a way that will lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time.”
Then the brahmin Uggatasarīra said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, I desire to take up the sacrificial fire and to raise up a sacrificial post.
May Master Gotama exhort me."
“May Master Gotama instruct me in that which would lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time.

“Brāhmaṇa, when one kindles the sacrificial fire and erects the sacrificial post, even before the sacrifice itself, one raises up three unwholesome weapons that have suffering as their outcome and suffering as their result.
What are these three? [The text continues:]”
The weapon of the body, the weapon of speech, and the weapon of the mind.
O Brahmin, when one kindles the sacrificial fire and erects the sacrificial post, even before the sacrifice, one should arouse such a thought:
“Let so many bulls be slain for the sake of the sacrifice; let so many young oxen be slain for the sake of the sacrifice; let so many…”
‘Let female calves be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many goats be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many sheep be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice.

Thinking, ‘I am doing merit,’ he does demerit; thinking, ‘I am doing what is wholesome,’ he does what is unwholesome; thinking, ‘I am seeking the path to a good destination,’ he seeks the path to a bad destination.

Brahmin, when one kindles the fire and erects the sacrificial post, even before the sacrifice itself, this first weapon of the mind is raised up—unwholesome, with suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.
Furthermore, Brahmin, when one kindles the fire and erects the sacrificial post, even before the sacrifice itself, one speaks these words:
“So many bulls should be slaughtered for the sake of the sacrifice; so many heifers should be slaughtered for the sake of the sacrifice; so many...”
"Let female calves be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many goats be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many rams be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice.

Thinking, "I am performing merit," he performs demerit; thinking, "I am performing what is wholesome," he performs what is unwholesome; thinking, "I am seeking the path to a good destination," he seeks the path to a bad destination.

Brāhmaṇa, when one kindles the fire and raises the sacrificial post, even before the sacrifice itself, this is the second sword of speech that one raises—unwholesome, with suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.

Furthermore, Brāhmaṇa, when one kindles the fire and raises the sacrificial post, even before the sacrifice itself, one personally initiates the first action to kill a bull for the sake of the sacrifice; one personally initiates the first action to kill a young ox...
For the sake of sacrifice, he himself first undertakes the task of killing young cows for the sake of sacrifice;

for the sake of sacrifice, he himself first undertakes the task of killing goats for the sake of sacrifice; for the sake of sacrifice, he himself first undertakes the task of killing rams for the sake of sacrifice.

Thinking, “I am doing merit,” he does demerit; thinking, “I am doing what is wholesome,” he does what is unwholesome; thinking, “I am seeking the path to a good destination,” he seeks the path to a bad destination.

“Brāhmaṇa, when one kindles the fire and erects the sacrificial post even before the sacrifice, this is the third weapon of the body that one raises up—unwholesome, with suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.

Brāhmaṇa, when one kindles the fire and erects the sacrificial post even before the sacrifice, these three weapons that one raises up are unwholesome, with suffering as their outcome and suffering as their result.
Brāhmaṇa, these three fires should be abandoned, avoided, and not cultivated.”
Which three?
The fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion.
And why, brahmin, should this fire of lust be abandoned, avoided, and not cultivated?
“Brahmin, one who is lustful, overcome by lust, and whose mind is consumed by it, engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.
Therefore, this fire of lust must be abandoned, avoided, and not cultivated.”
And why, brahmin, should this fire of hatred be abandoned, avoided, and not cultivated?
One who is corrupted, overcome by hatred, and whose mind is consumed by it engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
Therefore, this fire of hatred should be abandoned and avoided; it should not be cultivated.
And why, brahmin, should this fire of delusion be abandoned and avoided, and not cultivated?
Because one who is deluded, brahmin, being overcome by delusion and with mind consumed by it, engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Thus, having practiced misconduct by way of body, having practiced misconduct by way of speech, and having practiced misconduct by way of mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
Therefore, this fire of delusion should be abandoned, avoided, and not cultivated.
These, brahmin, are the three fires that should be abandoned, avoided, and not cultivated.
"There are, brahmin, three fires that should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped, and which should be properly tended for one's own happiness.
Which three?
The fire worthy of offerings, the householder’s fire, and the fire worthy of alms."
And what, brahmin, is the fire worthy of offerings?
Here, brahmin, those who have a mother or a father—this, brahmin, is called the fire worthy of offerings.
For what reason?

Therefore, brahmin, this fire has arisen from an offering; thus, this fire of those worthy of offerings should be properly maintained with happiness by honoring it, respecting it, revering it, and worshipping it.
And what, brahmin, is the householder’s fire?
Here, brahmin, for one who has sons, or wives, or slaves, or messengers, or laborers—this, brahmin, is called the householder’s fire.
Therefore, this householder’s fire should be properly maintained for one’s comfort, after having honored it, revered it, esteemed it, and worshipped it.
And what, brahmin, is the fire worthy of offerings?
Here, brahmin, those ascetics and brahmins who have desisted from the doctrines of others and are established in patience and gentleness.
They tame themselves alone, they calm themselves alone, and they bring themselves alone to final nibbāna;
this, brahmin, is called the fire worthy of offerings.
Therefore, this fire worthy of offerings should be properly maintained in happiness by honoring it, respecting it, revering it, and worshipping it.
“Brahmin, these three fires should be treated with honor, respect, esteem, and worship, and should be properly maintained for one’s own happiness.
Furthermore, brahmin, this fire of wood must from time to time be kindled, from time to time be looked after with equanimity, from time to time be extinguished, and from time to time be set aside.
When this was said, the brahmin Uggatasarīra said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
And so, Master Gotama, I release these five hundred bulls; I grant them their lives. I release these five hundred young oxen.”
"I release them; I grant them their lives! I release five hundred young oxen; I grant them their lives! I release five hundred goats;
I grant them their lives! I release five hundred rams; I grant them their lives!
Let them eat green grass, let them drink cool water, and let a cool breeze blow upon them."
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.48.
5. The Chapter on Great Sacrifices (Mahāyaññavagga).
The Discourse on the First Perceptions (Paṭhamasaññāsutta):
“Bhikkhus, these seven perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their ground and the Deathless as their consummation.”
“What seven?

The perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of repulsiveness in food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, and the perception of non-self in what is suffering.
These seven perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their ground and the Deathless as their consummation.”
The Fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.49.
5. The Chapter on Great Sacrifices (Mahāyaññavagga).
The Second Discourse on Perceptions (Dutiyasaññāsutta):
“Bhikkhus, these seven perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their goal and the Deathless as their consummation.”
Which seven?

The perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, and the perception of non-self in what is suffering.
These seven perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their goal and the Deathless as their consummation.
“Monks, the perception of foulness, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it plunges into the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless.
So it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
Monks, for a monk who dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of foulness, there is no inclination toward sexual intercourse.
The mind recoils, shrinks back, and turns away; it does not extend forward, but rather settles into equanimity or aversion.

Just as, monks, a chicken feather or a strip of sinew thrown into a fire recoils, shrinks back, and turns away, and does not extend forward—just so, monks, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of foulness.
The mind recoils, shrinks back, and turns away from engaging in sexual intercourse;
it does not extend toward it, and either equanimity or revulsion becomes established.

Monks, if, while a monk dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of foulness, his mind still inclines toward engaging in sexual intercourse and non-revulsion becomes established, [he should understand that he has not yet attained mastery].

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should understand this: ‘The perception of foulness has not been developed by me; there is no distinction between my former state and my present one; I have not attained the power of development.
Thus he is fully aware in that regard.
But if, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of foulness, there arises in him an inclination toward sexual intercourse...”
The mind recoils, shrinks back, and turns away; it does not extend forward, and either equanimity or revulsion becomes established.
In this regard, monks, a bhikkhu should understand: "My perception of the foul has been well-developed; there is a distinction between my former state and my present one;
I have attained the power of development. Thus, he is clearly comprehending in that situation.
“Monks, when the perception of foulness is developed and cultivated, it is of great fruit and great benefit; it is immersed in the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless.
This is what was said, and it is on this account that it was said.

“Monks, when the perception of death is developed and cultivated, it is of great fruit and great benefit; it is immersed in the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless. This too has been said, but with reference to what was it said?

“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of death, his mind shrinks away from attachment to life, recoils, turns back, and does not extend toward it; either equanimity or revulsion becomes established.

Just as, bhikkhus, a cock’s feather or a strip of sinew, when thrown into a fire, shrinks away, recoils, turns back, and does not extend toward it—so too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of death...”
The mind recoils, shrinks away, and turns back from attachment to life; it does not extend toward it, but rather settles into equanimity or aversion.
Monks, if, while a monk dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of death, his mind still inclines toward attachment to life and does not settle into aversion;

“Monks, a monk should understand this: ‘The perception of death has not been developed by me; there is no distinction between my former state and my present one; I have not attained the power of development.
Thus he is fully aware in that regard.
But if, monks, while a monk dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of death, there arises in him a craving for life...”
The mind recoils, shrinks back, and turns away; it does not extend forward, but rather equanimity or revulsion becomes established.
In this regard, monks, a bhikkhu should understand: "My perception of death is well-developed; there is a distinction between my former state and my present one;
I have attained the power of development. Thus, he is fully aware in that situation.
“‘Monks, the perception of death, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit;
it has the Deathless as its ground and the Deathless as its consummation’—this is what was said, and it is with reference to this that it was said.

‘Monks, the perception of repulsiveness in food, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it has the Deathless as its ground and the Deathless as its consummation’—this too was said, and with reference to what was it said?”

“Monks, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of repulsiveness in food, his mind shrinks away from craving for flavors... equanimity or revulsion becomes established.
Just as, monks, a chicken feather or a piece of sinew thrown into a fire shrinks away, recoils, turns back, and does not spread out.”

In the same way, monks, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of repulsiveness in food, his mind shrinks away from craving for flavors... [as before] ...or equanimity or revulsion becomes established.

But if, monks, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of repulsiveness in food, his mind still inclines toward craving for flavors and non-repulsion becomes established;
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should understand this: ‘The perception of repulsiveness in food has not been developed by me; there is no distinction between my former state and my present one;
I have not attained the power of development. Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard.

But if, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of repulsiveness in food, his mind recoils from craving for flavors... [and so on] ...or equanimity or revulsion becomes established.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should understand this: ‘The perception of the repulsiveness of food has been well developed by me; there is a distinction between my former state and my present state;
I have attained the power of development. Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard.
‘Bhikkhus, when the perception of the repulsiveness of food is developed and cultivated, it is of great fruit and great benefit; it plunges into the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless.’”

Thus, that which was said—"Monks, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it has the Deathless as its destination and the Deathless as its consummation"—this is what was said.
But with reference to what was this said?
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells with a mind often cultivated by the perception of non-delight in the entire world, his mind shrinks away from the wonders of the world...
Just as, bhikkhus, [a ball of string thrown into the air]... it shrinks back, recoils, and turns back; it does not extend further.
Even so, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells with a mind often cultivated by the perception of non-delight in the entire world...”
As he dwells thus, his mind recoils, shrinks away, and turns back from the world’s diversions;
it does not extend toward them, and either equanimity or revulsion becomes established.

But if, monks, while a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of non-delight in the entire world, his mind still inclines toward the world’s diversions and non-revulsion becomes established;
"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should understand this: 'The perception of non-delight in the entire world has not been developed by me; there is no distinction between my former state and my present one;
I have not attained the power of development. Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard.

But if, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of non-delight in the entire world, his mind recoils from the diversities of the world... and either equanimity or revulsion becomes established."
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should understand this: ‘The perception of non-delight in the entire world has been well developed by me; there is a distinction between my former state and my present state;
I have attained the fruit of the power of development. Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard.
‘Bhikkhus, when the perception of non-delight in the entire world is developed and cultivated, it is of great fruit and great benefit; it plunges into the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless.’”

Thus, that which was said—"Monks, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it is grounded in the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless"—this is what was said.
But with reference to what was this said?
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells with a mind often cultivated by the perception of impermanence, his mind shrinks away from gain, honor, and fame... equanimity or revulsion becomes established.
Just as, bhikkhus, a cock’s feather or a strip of sinew, when thrown into a fire, shrinks away, recoils, turns back, and does not stretch out.”

In the same way, monks, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of impermanence, his mind shrinks away from gain, honor, and fame... [as before] ...or equanimity or revulsion becomes established.
But if, monks, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of impermanence, his mind still inclines toward gain, honor, and fame, and non-revulsion becomes established;

"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should understand this: 'My perception of impermanence is undeveloped; there is no distinction between my former state and my present one; I have not attained the power of development.
Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard.
But if, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of impermanence, gain, honor, and fame [arise]..."
The mind recoils, shrinks back, and turns away; it does not extend forward, but rather equanimity or revulsion becomes established.
In this regard, monks, a bhikkhu should understand: "My perception of impermanence is well-developed; there is a distinction between my former state and my present one;
I have attained the power of development. Thus, he is clearly comprehending in that situation.
“Monks, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it has the deathless as its ground and the deathless as its consummation.
It was with reference to this that this was said.

“Monks, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it has the deathless as its ground and the deathless as its consummation. This too was said.
And with reference to what was this said? Monks,
for a monk who frequently dwells with a mind cultivated by the perception of suffering in the impermanent,
a keen perception of danger arises toward indolence, laziness, negligence, heedlessness, lack of application, and lack of reflection.
It is, monks, just like a murderer with his sword raised.

If, monks, for a bhikkhu who dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of suffering in the impermanent, a keen perception of danger does not arise toward laziness, indolence, negligence, heedlessness, lack of application, and lack of reflection; [then he is well-established in that perception].
It is like, monks, a murderer with his sword drawn. A monk should understand this:
"The perception of suffering in what is impermanent has not been developed by me; there is no distinction between my former state and now; I have not attained the power of development.
Thus, he is fully aware in that regard.
But if, monks, for a monk who dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of suffering in the impermanent,
a keen perception of danger arises toward laziness, indolence, negligence, heedlessness, lack of application,
and lack of reflection— just as it would, monks, toward an executioner with his sword raised— then he is one who has truly entered upon the way.
"It should be known by a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, that: 'The perception of suffering in the impermanent has been well developed by me; there is a distinction between my former state and my present state;
I have attained the power of development. Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard.
'The perception of suffering in the impermanent, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it is grounded in the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless.'"

Thus, that which was said—"Monks, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it has the deathless as its destination and the deathless as its consummation"—this is what was said.
But with reference to what was this said?
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of non-self in what is suffering,
his mind becomes free from the notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ and from the conceit ‘I am’ regarding this conscious body and all external signs;
it transcends discrimination and is peaceful and well-liberated.”
If, monks, for a bhikkhu who dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of non-self in suffering, his mind—
regarding this conscious body and all external signs— is free from the notions of "I" and "mine," devoid of the conceit of "I am," has transcended differentiation,
and is peaceful and well-liberated.

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should understand this: ‘The perception of non-self in what is suffering has not been developed by me; there is no distinction between my former state and my present one; I have not attained the power of development.
Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard.
But if, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of non-self in what is suffering...”

And in regard to this conscious body and all external signs, the mind becomes free from the notions of "I" and "mine," free from the conceit of "I am," transcending discrimination, peaceful, and well-liberated.

A bhikkhu should understand: "The perception of non-self in suffering has been well-developed by me; there is a distinction between my former state and my present one; I have attained the power of development."
Thus he is fully aware therein.
"Monks, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit;
it is grounded in the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless"—this is what was said, and it is on this account that it was said.
“Monks, these seven perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their ground and the Deathless as their consummation.
The sixth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 7.50.
5. Mahāyaññavagga Methunasutta (AN 7.50, AN 7.47, PTS AN iv 54)
Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said this to the Blessed One:
"Does Master Gotama also claim to be a practitioner of the holy life?"
“For if anyone, O Brahmin, speaking rightly were to say:
‘He leads a holy life that is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, unblemished, complete, and pure,’ it is of me alone, O Brahmin, that one could rightly say this.
For I, O Brahmin, lead a holy life that is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, unblemished, complete, and pure.”
“But what, Master Gotama, is a fracture, a flaw, a blemish, and a crack in the holy life?
“In this case, brahmin, a certain ascetic or brahmin, while claiming to be one who lives the holy life correctly, does not indeed engage in the union of the two organs with a woman;
yet he consents to her being rubbed, massaged, bathed, and kneaded by her. This, brahmin, is a fracture, a flaw, a blemish, and a crack in the holy life.”
Thus he relishes it, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it.
This, brahmin, is a fracture, a flaw, a blemish, and a scar in the holy life.
This, brahmin, is called one who leads an impure holy life, fettered by the bond of sexual intercourse.
He is not liberated from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
he is not liberated from suffering, I say.
Furthermore, Brahmin, here some ascetic or brahmin, claiming to be one who lives the holy life correctly...
Not only does he not engage in sexual intercourse with a woman, nor does he consent to being rubbed, massaged, bathed, or anointed by a woman;
but rather, he laughs, plays, and dallies with a woman... [and so forth].
Nor does he laugh with a woman, play with her, or joke with her;
yet he gazes and stares at a woman with his own eyes...
nor does he gaze and stare at a woman with his own eyes.
Furthermore, he hears the sound of women from beyond a wall or beyond a fence—whether they are laughing, speaking, singing, or weeping...
Or he does not hear the sound of women from beyond a wall or beyond a fence—whether they are laughing, speaking, singing, or weeping;
rather, he recollects those former instances of laughing, talking, and playing with women... [and so on].
Nor does he recollect those things that he formerly laughed at, talked over, and played with together with women;
rather, he sees a householder or a householder’s son endowed with and possessed of the five cords of sensual pleasure, diverting himself with them...
nor does he see a householder or a householder’s son endowed with and possessed of the five cords of sensual pleasure, diverting himself with them.
Furthermore, one leads the holy life aspiring for some particular class of devas, thinking: "By this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, may I become a deva, or some kind of deva.
He relishes that, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it.
This too, Brahmin, is a flaw, a crack, a blemish, and a stain in the holy life.
This, brahmin, is called one who leads an impure holy life, bound by the bond of sexual intercourse;
he is not liberated from birth, aging, and death, nor from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
he is not liberated from suffering, I say.
"Brāhmaṇa, as long as I perceived even one of these seven bonds of sexual intercourse as unabandoned within myself,

I did not, Brāhmaṇa, claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brāhmaṇas, its devas and humans."
But when, brahmin, I did not perceive even one of these seven bonds of sexual union as unabandoned within myself,

then, brahmin, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.
“Furthermore, knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no further becoming.
When this was said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
This is the seventh [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.51 5.

Mahāyaññavagga Saṁyogasutta (The Discourse on Bonds) “Bhikkhus, there are these seven bonds. What seven? The bond of gain, the bond of fame, the bond of honor, the bond of pleasure, the bond of views, the bond of precepts and observances, and the bond of ignorance. These, bhikkhus, are the seven bonds.”
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you a discourse on the Dhamma concerning bondage and liberation.
Listen to that... [as above] ...”
And what, monks, is that discourse on the Dhamma concerning bondage and liberation?
A woman, monks, attends internally to the female faculty—
the feminine gestures, the feminine deportment, the feminine appearance, the feminine desire, the feminine voice, and feminine adornments.
She becomes attached there and finds delight therein.
Being attached and finding delight therein, she directs her mind toward the male faculty externally—
the male gestures, the male appearance, the male mannerisms, the male inclinations, the male voice, and the male ornaments.
There she becomes attached and finds delight therein.
Being attached and finding delight therein, she longs for union with the external.
And she also longs for whatever pleasure and joy arise for her on account of that union.
“Monks, beings who delight in femininity have entered into bondage with men.
In this way, monks, a woman does not transcend femininity.
A man, monks, attends to the male faculty within himself.”
He adopts the gestures of a man, the deportment of a man, the behavior of a man, the desires of a man, the voice of a man, and the adornments of a man.
He takes delight in that and finds pleasure therein.
Being attached to that and finding pleasure therein, he directs his attention externally toward the female faculty.
The gestures of a woman, the attire of a woman, the appearance of a woman, the desire for a woman, the voice of a woman, and the ornaments of a woman.
He becomes attached to these, he delights in them.
Being attached to them and delighting in them, he longs for union with the external.
And he desires that pleasure and joy which arise for him through the condition of union.
Monks, beings who delight in manhood enter into union with women.
In this way, monks, a man does not transcend his manhood.
"Thus, monks, there is bondage. And how, monks, is there liberation?
A woman, monks, does not attend to the female faculty within herself."
She does not delight in feminine gestures, feminine attire, feminine manners, feminine desires, feminine voices, or feminine ornaments.
Not being attached to those things and not finding pleasure therein,
she does not direct her mind toward the male faculty externally.
She does not take delight in male gestures, male manners, male ways, male desires, male voices, or male ornaments;
she does not find pleasure therein. Being unattached to those things and finding no pleasure in them, she does not long for external union.
And she does not desire that pleasure and joy which arise for her through the condition of union.
Monks, beings who are dissatisfied with their femininity have attained disunion from men.
In this way, monks, a woman transcends her femininity.
“Monks, a man does not attend to the internal faculty of masculinity—the male gait, the male deportment, the male manner, the male desire, the male voice, and the male adornment.
He is not enamored with it; he does not take delight in it.”
Thus, being unattached there and finding no delight therein, he does not direct his mind toward the female faculty externally—
the feminine gestures, feminine attire, feminine appearance, feminine desire, feminine voice, or feminine ornaments. He is not enamored by them,
nor does he find pleasure therein.
Thus, being dispassionate toward that and finding no delight therein, he does not long for external union.
And whatever pleasure or joy arises conditioned by that union, he does not long for that either.
Monks, beings who find no delight in masculinity have attained dissociation from women.
"In this way, monks, a person transcends the state of being a mere man.
In this way, monks, there is disjunction.
This, monks, is the discourse on the Dhamma concerning conjunction and disjunction."
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.52.
5. The Chapter on Great Sacrifices (Mahāyaññavagga).
The Discourse on the Great Fruit of Giving (Dānamahapphalasutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond.
Then a number of lay followers from Campā approached the Venerable Sāriputta;
having approached, they paid homage to the Venerable Sāriputta and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the lay followers from Campā said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“It has been a long time, Bhante, since we have heard a discourse on the Dhamma from the Blessed One’s own presence.
It would be well, Bhante, if we might receive a discourse on the Dhamma from the Blessed One’s own presence.
“In that case, friends, you should come on the Uposatha day.”
“Perhaps you might obtain the opportunity to hear a discourse on the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One.

“Very well, venerable sir,” the lay followers of Campā replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. Having risen from their seats, they paid homage to the Venerable Sāriputta, circumambulated him keeping him to their right, and departed.
Then, on that very Uposatha day, the lay followers of Campā approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, they paid homage to the Venerable Sāriputta and stood to one side.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, together with those lay followers from Campā, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, could it be that for someone here, such a gift as that, when given, is not of great fruit and does not have great benefit?
And could it be, venerable sir, that for someone else here, such a gift as that, when given, is of great fruit and has great benefit?
“It could be so, Sāriputta, that for someone here, such a gift as that, when given, is not of great fruit and does not have great benefit.”
“But it may be, Sāriputta, that here someone gives such a gift as that, and it becomes of great fruit and great benefit.
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why here someone gives such a gift as that, and it does not become of great fruit and great benefit?
Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why here someone gives such a gift as that, and it becomes of great fruit and great benefit?”

“Here, Sāriputta, someone gives a gift out of attachment; they give a gift with a mind bound [to the recipient]; they give a gift looking for a store of merit; they give a gift thinking, ‘I shall enjoy this after death.
They give that gift—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps—to a recluse or a brahmin.
What do you think, Sāriputta, would anyone here give such a gift?”
“Yes, venerable sir. “In this regard, Sāriputta,

one who gives a gift while being full of longing, gives a gift with a mind attached, gives a gift while looking for a store, and gives a gift thinking, ‘I shall enjoy this after I have passed away,’ having given that gift,
at the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the gods of the Four Great Kings.
Having exhausted that karma, that psychic power, that fame, and that sovereignty, he becomes one who goes on, one who comes back to this state of being.

But here, Sāriputta, a certain person does not give a gift out of longing, does not give a gift with a bound mind, does not give a gift seeking a store, nor does he give a gift thinking, ‘I shall enjoy this after passing away’;
rather, he gives a gift thinking, ‘Giving is good’ … [and so forth] …”
Nor does he give a gift thinking, “Giving is good”;
rather, he gives a gift thinking, “It was given before, it was done before by my father and grandfather; I ought not to let the ancient family lineage decline.

… [as above] … Nor does he give a gift thinking, “It was given before, it was done before by my father and grandfather; I ought not to let the ancient family lineage decline”; [but rather, he gives for the sake of heaven].
Furthermore, one gives a gift thinking: “I cook, but these others do not cook; it is not right for me, while cooking, not to give a gift to those who do not cook.
… [as before] … Nor does one give a gift thinking: “I cook, but these others do not cook; it is not right for me, while cooking, not to give a gift to those who do not cook”;
rather, one gives a gift thinking: “Just as those ancient seers had those great sacrifices, namely—”

‘Just as this was the gift and distribution of Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamadaggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu, so shall this gift and distribution of mine be’—thus one gives a gift...
Nor does one give thinking, ‘Just as those ancient seers had those great sacrifices, namely—’

‘By this gift and distribution of mine, may there be [merit] for Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamadaggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu’—one gives a gift with such a thought.
Nor does one give a gift thinking, ‘As I give this gift, my mind becomes serene, and gladness and joy arise within me.
…pe… Nor does one give a gift thinking, ‘As I give this gift, my mind becomes serene, and gladness and joy arise within me.’
Moreover, one gives a gift that is an adornment for the mind and an equipment for the mind.
One gives that gift—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lighting—to a recluse or a brahmin.
What do you think, Sāriputta, would anyone here give such a gift?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In this regard, Sāriputta, there is one who gives a gift not out of longing,
nor does he give a gift with a mind of attachment.
One does not give a gift with the expectation of storing it up;
one does not give a gift thinking, “I shall enjoy this after passing away”;
nor does one give a gift merely because “giving is good.”
Nor does one give a gift thinking, "This was not given before, nor performed before by my father and grandfather; I ought not to let this ancient family lineage decline";
nor does one give a gift thinking, "I cook, but these others do not cook; it is not right that I, while cooking, should not give a gift to those who do not cook";
nor does one give a gift thinking, "Just as those ancient seers had those great sacrifices, namely—"
‘May this gift of mine be shared with Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamadaggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu’—thus one gives a gift;
nor does one give a gift thinking, ‘As I give this gift, my mind becomes serene, and gladness and joy arise within me’;
rather, one gives a gift as an adornment of the mind and an equipment for the mind.
Having given that gift, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the gods of Brahmā’s retinue.
Having exhausted that karma, that psychic power, that fame, and that sovereignty, he becomes a non-returner, one who does not come back to this state of being.
This, Sāriputta, is the cause, this is the condition, why for some here even such a gift as that is not of great fruit and does not have great benefit.
"But this, Sāriputta, is the cause, this is the reason why a gift given by someone here, though being exactly the same [as another], becomes of great fruit and great benefit.
Thus it was said. The ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.53
5. The Chapter on Great Sacrifices:
The Discourse to Nandamātā (AN 7.53, AN 7.50, PTS AN iv 63)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were wandering on tour among the Southern Hills together with a large community of bhikkhus.
Now at that time, the female lay follower Veḷukaṇḍakī Nandamātā, having risen at the time of dawn during the night, was reciting the *Pārāyana* in a melodic chant.
Now at that time, the Great King Vessavaṇa was traveling from the northern direction toward the southern direction on some business.
The Great King Vessavaṇa heard the laywoman Nandamātā reciting the *Pārāyana* in a melodic chant; having heard it, he stood waiting for the conclusion of her discourse.
Then, after the laywoman Nandamātā had finished reciting the *Pārāyana* in a melodic chant, she became silent.
Then the Great King Vessavaṇa, perceiving that the discourse with the female lay follower Nandamātā had reached its conclusion, expressed his approval:
“Excellent, sister! Excellent, sister!
“But who is this, O gentle-faced one?”
“I am your brother, sister, Vessavaṇa the Great King.
“Excellent, good sir! In that case, let this discourse on the Dhamma which has been spoken by me be your hospitality.
“Excellent, sister! Let this indeed be my hospitality.”
“Tomorrow the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna, will come to Veḷukaṇḍaka before their morning meal; having served that Saṅgha of bhikkhus, you should dedicate the gift to me.
This shall be my hospitality.
Then, at the end of that night, the female lay follower Nandamātā had exquisite hard and soft food prepared in her own residence.
Then the community of monks, headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna, arrived at Veḷukaṇḍaka before their morning meal had been taken.
Then the female lay follower Nandamātā addressed a certain man:
“Come, good man, go to the monastery and announce the time to the community of monks:”
“Venerable sir, it is time; the meal is ready at the residence of the noble lady Nandamātā.
“Very well, madam,” that man replied to the female lay follower Nandamātā. Having gone to the monastery, he announced the time to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus:
“Venerable sirs, it is time; the meal is ready at the residence of the noble lady Nandamātā.”

Then, in the morning, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna, dressed themselves, took their bowls and robes, and went to the residence of the female lay follower Nandamātā. Having arrived, they sat down on the seats prepared for them.
Then the female lay follower Nandamātā, with her own hands, personally satisfied and served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna, with excellent hard and soft foods.
Then the female lay follower Nandamātā sat down to one side after the Venerable Sāriputta had finished his meal and withdrawn his hand from the bowl.
As she was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the female lay follower Nandamātā:
“But who informed you, Nandamātā, of the arrival of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?”
“Here, venerable sir, having risen at the time of dawn during the night and recited the *Pārāyana* in a melodic chant, I became silent.
Then, venerable sir, the Great King Vessavaṇa, perceiving the conclusion of my speech, expressed his approval:
‘Excellent, sister! Excellent, sister!’”
“Who is this, good sir?
“I am your brother Vessavaṇa, the Great King, sister.
“Excellent, good sir! In that case, let this discourse on the Dhamma which you have spoken for me be your hospitality.”
“Excellent, sister! Let this be my hospitality.

Tomorrow the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna, will come to Veḷukaṇḍaka before their morning meal; after you have served that Saṅgha of bhikkhus, you should dedicate the merit to me.
This indeed shall be my hospitality.”
“Venerable sir, may this merit and the great ground of merit arising from this gift be for the happiness of the Great King Vessavaṇa.
“It is wonderful, Nandamātā! It is marvelous, Nandamātā!
That you should converse face to face with the Great King Vessavaṇa, a son of the gods so powerful and so majestic!”
“Venerable sir, this is not the only wonderful and marvelous quality for me.
There is another wonderful and marvelous quality as well.
Here, venerable sir, I have an only son named Nanda, who is dear and beloved.”
"In some legal matter, kings seized him by force and took his life.

Yet, Bhante, whether that child had been seized or was being seized, whether he had been sentenced to death or was being sentenced, whether he had been killed or was being killed, I do not recall any alteration of my mind.
"It is wonderful, Nandamātā! It is marvelous, Nandamātā!"
"For you will even purify the arising of a thought!
"Venerable sir, this is not the only wonderful and marvelous quality I possess.
I have another wonderful and marvelous quality as well."
"Venerable sir, my husband has passed away and has been reborn in a certain class of *yakkhas*.
He appeared to me in that very same former body.
Yet, venerable sir, I do not recall any change of mind on my part because of that."
“It is wonderful, Nandamātā! It is marvelous, Nandamātā!
That you should purify even a single thought-occurrence!
“Venerable sir, this is not the only wonderful and marvelous quality of mine.”
“I have another wonderful and marvelous quality, Venerable Sir.
Since I was brought here as a young girl to my husband when he was still a youth, I do not recall ever having transgressed against my husband even in thought, much less in body.
“It is wonderful, Mother of Nanda! It is marvelous, Mother of Nanda!”
"For you will even purify a single thought-occurrence!
"Venerable sir, this is not the only wonderful and marvelous quality I possess;
I have another wonderful and marvelous quality as well."
“Venerable sir, as a female lay follower who has confessed her faults, I do not recall ever intentionally transgressing any training rule.
“It is wonderful, Nandamātā! It is marvelous, Nandamātā!
“But, venerable sir, this is not the only wonderful and marvelous quality of mine.”
"I have another wonderful and marvelous quality.

Here, venerable sir, as far as I desire, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, I enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and pleasure born of concentration."
“With the fading away of rapture, I dwell equanimous and, mindful and clearly comprehending, I experience happiness with the body;
I enter and dwell in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous.

With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.”
“It is wonderful, Nandamātā! It is marvelous, Nandamātā!
“Venerable sir, this is not the only wonderful and marvelous thing for me.
There is another wonderful and marvelous thing as well.”
“Venerable sir, regarding these five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One, I do not see any of them that have not been abandoned within myself.
“It is wonderful, Nandamātā! It is marvelous, Nandamātā!
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the female lay follower Nandamātā with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat and departed.

6. Abyākatavagga Abyākatasutta (AN 7.54, AN 7.51, PTS AN iv 67)
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why doubt does not arise in a learned noble disciple regarding the undeclared points?
“With the cessation of views, bhikkhu, doubt does not arise in a learned noble disciple regarding the undeclared points.”
‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ bhikkhu, is a speculative view;
‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death’ is a speculative view;
‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ is a speculative view.
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—this, bhikkhu, is a speculative view.
The uninstructed worldling, bhikkhu, does not understand this view; he does not understand the origin of views, the cessation of views, or the practice leading to the cessation of views.
His view increases, and he is not freed from birth, aging, and death; he is not freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not freed from suffering, I say.
But the learned noble disciple, bhikkhu, understands view, understands the origin of view, understands the cessation of view, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of view.
That view of his ceases; he is liberated from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is liberated from suffering, I say.
Knowing thus, bhikkhu, and seeing thus, the learned noble disciple does not declare: “The Tathāgata exists after death.”
‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ he does not declare;
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ he does not declare;
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,’ he does not declare.
“Knowing thus, bhikkhu, and seeing thus, the instructed noble disciple does not make a declaration regarding the undeclared points.
Knowing thus, bhikkhu, and seeing thus, the instructed noble disciple is not terrified, does not tremble, does not shake, and does not fall into fear regarding the undeclared points.
‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ bhikkhu, is a state of craving... [and so on].”
This is included within perception...
this is a mental fabrication...
this is a conceptual proliferation... [and so on].
This belongs to the sphere of clinging...
"A Tathāgata exists after death," bhikkhu, is a state of remorse;
"A Tathāgata does not exist after death," bhikkhu, is a state of remorse.
“‘The Tathāgata exists after death and does not exist after death’—this, bhikkhu, is remorse.
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—this, bhikkhu, is remorse.

The uninstructed worldling, bhikkhu, does not understand remorse; he does not understand the origin of remorse, he does not understand the cessation of remorse, and he does not understand the way leading to the cessation of remorse.”
His remorse increases; he is not freed from birth, aging, and death, nor from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not freed from suffering, I say.

But the learned noble disciple, bhikkhu, understands remorse, understands the origin of remorse, understands the cessation of remorse, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of remorse.
His remorse ceases; he is liberated from birth... [and so on] ...from suffering, I say.

Knowing thus, bhikkhu, and seeing thus, the learned noble disciple does not declare: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’; nor does he declare: ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’; nor does he declare:
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’; nor does he declare: ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’
“Knowing thus, bhikkhu, and seeing thus, the learned noble disciple is one who does not make declarations regarding the undeclared points.
Knowing thus, bhikkhu, and seeing thus, the learned noble disciple is not startled, does not tremble, does not shake, and does not fall into terror regarding the undeclared points.
This, bhikkhu, is the cause, this is the reason why doubt does not arise in the learned noble disciple regarding the undeclared points.”

Chapter 6: The Unexpounded (Abyākata-vagga).
Purisagatisutta: “Monks,
I shall teach you the seven destinations for persons and unbinding through non-clinging.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, are the seven destinations for persons?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu practices thus:
‘May there be nothing for me, and may I have nothing; may it not come to be for me, and may it not be mine; whatever exists, whatever has come to be—that I abandon. Thus he attains equanimity.”
Thus, one does not delight in existence; one does not delight in becoming. One sees with right wisdom the state that is peaceful, which transcends the eightfold [worldly conditions].
Yet, for such a person, that state has not been fully realized in every respect;

the underlying tendency to conceit has not been entirely abandoned, the underlying tendency to lust for existence has not been entirely abandoned, and the underlying tendency to ignorance has not been entirely abandoned.
Thus, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval.
Just as, monks, when an iron pan has been heated all day and is struck, a spark might arise and be extinguished;
even so, monks, a bhikkhu practicing in this way [becomes an antarāparinibbāyī].

‘May there be nothing for me, and may nothing be mine; may it not come to be, and may nothing be mine in the future; whatever exists, whatever has come to be—that I abandon,’ thus he attains equanimity.
He does not delight in existence, he does not delight in becoming; he sees with right wisdom that there is a further state which is peaceful.
Yet that state has not been fully realized by him in every respect, and thus the underlying tendency to conceit is not entirely abandoned in every respect.

The underlying tendency to sensual lust has not been abandoned in every way; the underlying tendency to existence has not been abandoned in every way; the underlying tendency to ignorance has not been abandoned in every way.
Yet, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final nibbāna in the interval.
Furthermore, monks, a monk here practices in this way:

‘May there be nothing for me, and may nothing be mine; may there not come to be anything for me, and may nothing be mine in the future; whatever exists, whatever has come to be—that I abandon. Thus he attains equanimity.
He does not delight in existence, nor does he delight in becoming; he sees with right wisdom that further state which is peaceful.
Yet that state is not fully realized by him in every respect, and thus the underlying tendency to conceit is not entirely abandoned in every respect.
The underlying tendency to sensual lust has not been entirely abandoned, nor has the underlying tendency to ignorance been entirely abandoned.
With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final nibbāna in the interval.

Just as, monks, when an iron pan heated all day is struck, a spark might be produced, fly up, and go out; even so, monks, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final nibbāna in the interval.
In the same way, monks, a monk practices thus:
‘May there be nothing for me,
and may I have nothing…’ … through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains nibbāna in the interval.
But here, monks, a bhikkhu practices thus: ‘May there be nothing for me,
and may I have nothing…’ … Through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final nibbāna in the interval.
“Just as, monks, when an iron pan has been heated all day and is struck, a spark might be produced, fly up, and go out without reaching the ground;
even so, monks, a monk who practices in this way thinks:
‘May there be nothing for me, and may nothing be mine... [and so on].
Thus, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final nibbāna in the interval.
Furthermore, monks, a monk here practices in this way:
‘May there be nothing for me, and may nothing be mine... [as before].
Thus, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who attains final nibbāna upon landing.
Just as, monks, when an iron pan has been heated all day and a spark is struck from it, having arisen and flown up, it might attain final extinction upon reaching the surface;
even so, monks, a monk practicing in this way becomes such a one.
‘May there be nothing for me, and may nothing be mine...
...Through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains nibbāna upon landing.
Furthermore, monks, a monk here practices in this way:
‘May there be nothing for me, and may I have nothing of anything...
...With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final nibbāna without exertion.
Monks, it is just as if a red-hot iron pan, heated all day, were struck and a spark were produced, which, having flown up, should fall upon a small heap of straw or a small heap of wood.
There he might produce fire and produce smoke; having produced fire and produced smoke, after consuming that very same small heap of grass or wood, it would go out for lack of fuel.
In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu practices thus:
‘May there be neither I nor mine... [and so on].
Thus, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final nibbāna without exertion.
Furthermore, monks, a monk here practices in this way:
"May there be nothing for me, and may nothing be mine... [as before].
Thus, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who attains final nibbāna with exertion.
Monks, it is just as if an iron pan heated all day were struck, and a spark were produced and fly off, falling upon a large heap of grass or a large heap of wood.
There it might produce fire and produce smoke; having produced fire and produced smoke, and having consumed that very large heap of grass or heap of wood, it would go out for lack of fuel.
In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu practices thus:
‘May it be neither for me,
nor may there be anything that is mine’ … [as before] … through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who attains final nibbāna with exertion.
But here, monks, a bhikkhu practices thus: ‘May there be nothing for me, may nothing be mine;
may there not come to be anything for me, may nothing belong to me in the future; whatever exists, whatever has come to be—that I abandon. Thus he attains equanimity.
He does not delight in existence, he does not delight in becoming; he sees with right wisdom the further state that is peaceful.
But that state has not been fully realized by him in every respect;

the underlying tendency to conceit has not been entirely abandoned by him, the underlying tendency to lust for existence has not been entirely abandoned, and the underlying tendency to ignorance has not been entirely abandoned.
With the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who flows upwards, bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.
“Monks, it is just as if an iron pan, heated all day long, were struck and a spark were produced, which, having flown up, were to fall upon a large heap of grass or a large heap of wood.
There it would produce fire and produce smoke;
and having produced fire and produced smoke, after consuming that very large heap of grass or heap of wood, it would burn down the forest and burn down the grove.”

"Even as a fire, having burned up its supply of logs and having burned up its supply of faggots, might go out upon reaching the edge of a green field, or the edge of a path, or the edge of a rock, or the edge of water,
or upon reaching a delightful spot of ground; even so, monks,
a monk who practices in this way is one who has entered upon the right path."
‘May there be nothing for me,
and may I have nothing of anything…’ … through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who goes upstream bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm.
These, monks, are the seven destinations for persons.
And what, monks, is final Nibbāna without clinging?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu practices thus:

“Let there be nothing for me, and may nothing be mine; let there be no future existence for me, and may no future existence be mine; whatever exists, whatever has come to be—that I abandon. Thus he attains equanimity.
Thus one does not delight in existence, nor does one delight in non-existence; one sees with right wisdom the state that is beyond both as peaceful.
And that state has been fully realized by him in every respect;

the underlying tendency to conceit has been abandoned by him in every respect, the underlying tendency to lust for existence has been abandoned by him in every respect, and the underlying tendency to ignorance has been abandoned by him in every respect.
Thus, with the destruction of the taints... having realized it for himself and entered upon it, he dwells therein.
This, monks, is called final nibbāna through non-clinging.
These, monks, are the seven destinations for persons and final nibbāna through non-clinging.”

Tissabrahmāsutta (AN 7.56, AN 7.53, PTS AN iv 74):
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then two deities, at a late hour of the night, having illuminated the entirety of Vulture Peak Mountain with their surpassing beauty, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
They stood to one side. Standing there, one deity said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, these bhikkhunīs are liberated.
Another deity said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, these bhikkhunīs are well-liberated, with no residue remaining.
This is what those deities said.
The Teacher gave his approval.
Then those deities, thinking, "The Teacher has consented," paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to their right, and vanished right there.
Then, at the end of that night, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, during this night, two deities of surpassing beauty approached me when the night was far spent, illuminating the entire extent of the area."
Having illuminated Vulture Peak, they approached me; having approached, they paid homage to me and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, bhikkhus, a certain deity said this to me:
“Venerable sir, these bhikkhunīs are liberated.”
Another deity said this to me:
“Venerable sir, these bhikkhunīs are well-liberated, without remainder.
This is what those deities said, monks.
"Having said this, they paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to their right, and vanished right there.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was sitting not far from the Blessed One.
Then, it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Of which deities, then, does such knowledge arise as this:
‘One with a residue remaining is one with a residue remaining; one without a residue remaining is one without a residue remaining’?
Now at that time, a bhikkhu named Tissa, who had recently passed away, had been reborn in a certain Brahma-world.
There too they know him thus:
"The Brahmā Tissa is of great psychic power and great majesty.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—just as a strong man might bend his drawn-in arm...
Just as one might stretch out an arm, or bend back an arm that had been stretched out, even so, having vanished from Vulture Peak Mountain,
he reappeared in that Brahma world.
The Brahmā Tissa saw the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna coming from afar.
Having seen the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, he said this to him:
“Come, dear Moggallāna!
Welcome, dear Moggallāna!”
"It has been long indeed, worthy Moggallāna, since you made this occasion for coming here.
Sit down, worthy Moggallāna; this seat is prepared.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna sat down on the prepared seat.
Then Brahmā Tissa also paid homage to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to him:
“Tissa, for which deities does such knowledge arise as this:”
“‘With a residue remaining, one has a residue remaining; or without a residue remaining, one has no residue remaining’?
“Indeed, dear Moggallāna, among the gods of the Brahma-body, such knowledge arises:
‘With a residue remaining, one has a residue remaining; or without a residue remaining, one has no residue remaining.’”
“Tissa, do all the gods of the Brahma-body possess this knowledge:
‘One with a residue remaining is one with a residue remaining; one without a residue remaining is one without a residue remaining’?
“No indeed, venerable Moggallāna, not all the gods of the Brahma-body possess such knowledge.”
‘With residue remaining, with residue remaining,’ or ‘without residue remaining,
without residue remaining. Now, dear Moggallāna, those gods of the Brahma-body who are satisfied with their Brahma-life,
satisfied with their Brahma-form, Brahma-happiness, Brahma-fame, and Brahma-sovereignty— furthermore...
They do not understand escape as it really is.
Thus, they do not have the knowledge:
"With a residue remaining, there is a residue remaining; or with no residue remaining, there is no residue remaining."
But those gods of the Brahma-body, dear Moggallāna, who are dissatisfied with their Brahma-like lifespan,
and who are dissatisfied with their Brahma-like beauty, Brahma-like happiness, Brahma-like glory, and Brahma-like sovereignty,
they understand the further escape as it really is.
They have this knowledge:
‘With residue remaining, there is residue remaining; without residue remaining, there is no residue remaining.
Here, dear Moggallāna, a bhikkhu is one liberated in both ways.
The gods know of him thus:
“This venerable one is liberated both ways;
as long as his body remains, so long will gods and humans behold him.”
‘With the breakup of the body, gods and humans will not see him.
In this way too, dear Moggallāna, those devas possess knowledge:
‘One with residue remaining is one with residue remaining; one without residue remaining is one without residue remaining.’”
But here, dear Moggallāna, there is a bhikkhu who is liberated by wisdom.
Those devas know of him thus:
"This venerable one is indeed liberated by wisdom."
‘As long as his body remains, so long will gods and humans behold him;
with the breakup of the body, gods and humans will no longer behold him.
In this way too, dear Moggallāna, those devas possess such knowledge:
‘With residue remaining, he has residue remaining; or, with no residue remaining, he has no residue remaining.
But here, dear Moggallāna, there is a bhikkhu who is a body-witness.
Of him the devas know thus:
‘This venerable one is indeed a bodily witness. Perhaps,
as this venerable one resorts to favorable lodgings, associates with good friends, and harmonizes his faculties, he might—

having personally realized through direct knowledge in this very life the supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness— dwell having attained it.’
In this way too, dear Moggallāna, those devas possess knowledge:
‘One with a residue remaining is “one with a residue remaining,” and one without a residue remaining is “one without a residue remaining.
But here, dear Moggallāna, a bhikkhu is one who has attained vision... [and so on].
