He is one liberated by faith …pe… he is a follower of the Dhamma.
Those devas know of him thus:
‘This venerable one is a follower by Dhamma. Perhaps,
as this venerable one resorts to suitable lodgings, associates with good friends, and harmonizes his faculties, he might—

having realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life the supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness— dwell having attained it.’
“In this way too, dear Moggallāna, those devas possess knowledge:
‘One with a residue remaining is “one with a residue remaining,” and one without a residue remaining is “one without a residue remaining.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the words of the Brahmā Tissa, just as...
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, even so, having disappeared from the Brahma-world, he reappeared on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with the Brahmā Tissa.
"But, Moggallāna, did the Brahmā Tissa teach you about the seventh person, the one who dwells in the signless?
"It is the time for this, Blessed One; it is the time for this, Sugata."
“If the Blessed One would teach about the seventh type of person who dwells in the signless, the bhikkhus, having heard it from the Blessed One, will remember it.
“In that case, Moggallāna, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In this case, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu, through non-attention to all signs, enters and dwells in the signless concentration of mind.
Regarding him, those devas know thus:”
‘This venerable one, by not attending to any signs, dwells having entered upon the signless concentration of mind. May it be that this venerable one,
resorting to favorable lodgings, associating with good friends, and harmonizing his faculties, might—

having realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life— enter and dwell in that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.’
“In this way, Moggallāna, those devas have knowledge:
‘One with a residue remaining is one with a residue remaining; one without a residue remaining is one without a residue remaining.
This is the third [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.57 6. The Chapter on the Undeclared (Abyākatavagga) The Discourse to Siha the General (Sīhasenāpati-sutta) At Sāvatthī. Then Siha the general approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: "Siha, if a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has reached the ultimate conclusion, one for whom there is no further state beyond this. What four? Here, Siha, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. If a noble disciple possesses these four things, Siha, he is one who has reached the ultimate conclusion, one for whom there is no further state beyond this. When this was said, Siha the general said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!

Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward, for as long as life shall last. Then Siha the general addressed the bhikkhus: “Venerable sirs, may the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus accept tomorrow’s meal from me. The Blessed One consented by silence. Then Siha the general, having understood the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Now when the night had passed, Siha the general had various kinds of excellent food prepared in his own residence and had the time announced to the Blessed One: “It is time, venerable sir; the meal is ready. Then, it being morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and outer robe, and went together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to the residence of Siha the general. On arrival, he sat down on the appointed seat. Then Siha the general, with his own hand, served and satisfied the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with various kinds of excellent food. When the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, Siha the general took a low seat, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, there are some ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings spontaneously reborn; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins of right conduct and right practice who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, make them known to others. What does the Blessed One say about this? “Siha, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view, are either influenced by ignorance or they speak out of delusion. Why is that? Because, Siha, the giving of alms exists, the offering of alms exists, the sacrifice of alms exists; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world and the other world; there is mother and father; there are beings spontaneously reborn; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins of right conduct and right practice who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, make them known to others. Furthermore, Siha, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view, are either influenced by ignorance or they speak out of delusion. Why is that? Because, Siha, there are beings who are born, have become, and have come to be in this world who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, are due to reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. Furthermore, Siha, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view, are either influenced by ignorance or they speak out of delusion. Why is that? Because, Siha, there are beings who are born, have become, and have come to be in this world who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, are due to reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. Furthermore, Siha, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view, are either influenced by ignorance or they speak out of delusion. Why is that? Because, Siha, there are beings who are born, have become, and have come to be in this world who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, are due to reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. Furthermore, Siha, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view, are either influenced by ignorance or they speak out of delusion. Why is that? Because, Siha, there are beings who are born, have become, and have come to be in this world who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, are due to reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. Furthermore, Siha, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view, are either influenced by ignorance or they speak out of delusion. Why is that? Because, Siha, there are beings who are born, have become, and have come to be in this world who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, are due to reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. Furthermore, Siha, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view, are either influenced by ignorance or they speak out of delusion. Why is that? Because, Siha, there are beings who are born, have become, and have come to be in this world who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, are due to reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. Furthermore, Siha, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view, are either influenced by ignorance or they speak out of delusion. Why is that? Because, Siha, there are beings who are born, have become, and have come to be in this world who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, are due to reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. Furthermore, Siha, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view, are either influenced by ignorance or they speak out of delusion. Why is that? Because, Siha, there are beings who are born, have become, and have come to be in this world who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, are due to reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. Furthermore, Siha, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view, are either influenced by ignorance or they speak out of delusion. Why is that? Because, Siha, there are beings who are born, have become, and have come to be in this world who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, are due to reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. Furthermore, Siha, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain this doctrine, hold this view
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.

Then Sīha the general approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Sīha the general said this to the Blessed One:
“Is it possible, Bhante, to point out the visible fruit of giving?
“In that case, Sīha, I shall question you about this very matter; answer as you see fit.”
What do you think, Sīha?
Suppose there were two men here:
one man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive; and another man who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts. Which of these two would be the more praiseworthy?
“What do you think, Sīha? Whom would the Arahants first show compassion to out of their compassion:
the man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive, or the man who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts?

“Venerable sir, as for the man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive—why would the Arahants show him compassion first out of their compassion? [They would show compassion first to the other.]”
“But, Bhante, as for that person who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in continuous generosity—it is him that the Arahants, out of compassion, would approach first.
“What do you think, Sīha? When approaching first, whom would the Arahants approach:
the man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive, or the man who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in continuous generosity?”
“Venerable sir, that man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive—how could the Arahants approach him first when they go for alms?
Rather, venerable sir, the Arahants would approach first that man who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts.
“What do you think, Sīha? Whom would the Arahants accept first when they receive offerings?”
“Whether it be that man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive, or that man who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts?
“Venerable sir, as for the man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive—how could the Arahants accept from him first when they receive alms?
But, venerable sir, it is from that man who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts that the Arahants would accept first when they receive alms.”
“What do you think, Sīha? When the Arahants first teach the Dhamma, to whom would they first teach it:
to the man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive, or to the man who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts?
“Venerable sir, as for the man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive—what would the Arahants have to teach him first when they teach the Dhamma?”
“But, Bhante, as for that person who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts—it is to him that the Arahants would first teach the Dhamma.
“What do you think, Sīha? Whose good reputation would spread abroad:
that of the man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive, or that of the man who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts?”
“Venerable sir, as for that man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive—how could a good report of him spread abroad?
But as for that man, venerable sir, who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts—it is of him that a good report would spread abroad.
“What do you think, Sīha? Suppose a man were to approach whatever assembly it might be—whether an assembly of khattiyas...”
“Whether it be an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics, would one approach it with confidence and without timidity, thinking:
‘Whether that person be faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive, or whether that person be faithful, a master of giving, and delighting in distribution’?
“Venerable sir, as for that person who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive—what [difference does he make] regarding whichever assembly [one approaches]?”
He will approach— whether it be an assembly of khattiyas, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders,
or an assembly of ascetics— he will approach with confidence and without timidity.
And as for that person, Bhante, who is faithful, a patron of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts, whichever assembly he enters...
He would approach with confidence and without timidity whether it be an assembly of kṣatriyas, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics.
What do you think, Sīha, who would, upon the breakup of the body after death, be reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world?
“Whether it be that man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive, or that man who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts?
“Venerable sir, as for that man who is faithless, stingy, miserly, and abusive—how could he, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world?

But as for that man, venerable sir, who is faithful, a master of giving, and delights in bestowing gifts—he would, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.”
“Venerable sir, as for these visible fruits of giving that have been declared by the Blessed One, I do not follow them out of faith in the Blessed One;
I know them myself.
Venerable sir, I am a donor, a master of giving; it is me that the arahants first show compassion toward when they show compassion.”
“Venerable sir, I am a donor, a master of giving; it is to me that the Arahants first approach when they come.
Venerable sir, I am a donor, a master of giving; it is from me that the Arahants first accept when they receive.
Venerable sir, I am a donor, a master of giving; it is to me that the Arahants first teach the Dhamma when they teach.”
“Venerable sir, I am a donor, a master of giving; a fine reputation for me has spread abroad:
‘General Sīha is a donor, a benefactor, an attendant upon the Saṅgha.

Venerable sir, as a donor and master of giving, whenever I approach an assembly—whether it be an assembly of kṣatriyas... or an assembly of ascetics—I approach it with confidence and without timidity.”
“Venerable sir, as for these visible fruits of giving that have been declared by the Blessed One, I do not follow them out of faith in the Blessed One;
I know them myself.
And as for what the Blessed One has said to me thus:”
‘Sīha, a donor, a master of giving, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
This I do not know; yet in this matter, Sīha, I proceed by faith in the Blessed One.
“It is so, Sīha, it is so, Sīha.”
“Sīha, a donor, a master of giving, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. Thus it was said.
The fourth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.58
6. The Chapter on the Indeterminate:
The Discourse on What Should Not Be Guarded (Araṅkheyyasutta)
“Bhikkhus, there are these four things that the Tathāgata need not guard against, and he is beyond reproach in three respects.
What are the four things that the Tathāgata need not guard against?
Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is pure in his bodily conduct.”
There is no bodily misconduct of the Tathāgata that he would need to guard, thinking:
"Lest another should know this of me.
Monks, the Tathāgata’s verbal conduct is utterly pure.
There is no verbal misconduct of the Tathāgata that he would need to guard, thinking:
"Lest another should know this of me.
Monks, the Tathāgata is pure in his mental conduct.
There is no mental misconduct of the Tathāgata that he would need to guard against, thinking:
"Lest others should know this of me.
Monks, the Tathāgata is pure in livelihood.
There is no wrong livelihood of the Tathāgata that the Tathāgata would need to guard, thinking:
"Lest others should know this of me.
These are the four things that the Tathāgata has no need to guard.
By what three [qualities] is he beyond reproach?
Monks, the Tathāgata has well-expounded the Dhamma.
In this regard, indeed, no ascetic or brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could rightfully challenge me, saying:
‘In this way, you are one whose Dhamma is not well-proclaimed’—
I do not perceive any such ground for this, monks. Not perceiving any such ground,
monks, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained intrepidity.
Furthermore, monks, I have well-proclaimed to my disciples the practice leading to Nibbāna.

By practicing accordingly, my disciples—through the destruction of the taints—realize for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained them, they dwell therein.
In this regard, no ascetic or brahmin, no god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, could rightfully challenge me thus:

‘In such a way, you have not well-proclaimed the practice leading to Nibbāna for your disciples, such that by practicing it, your disciples, through the destruction of the taints... having realized it for themselves, enter and dwell in [the state of liberation].
Monks, I do not perceive any such ground for this.
Not perceiving any such ground, monks, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence.

Moreover, monks, my assembly of disciples numbering many hundreds dwell having realized for themselves, attained, and entered upon the destruction of the taints through the exhaustion of the taints...
In this regard, indeed, no ascetic or brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could rightfully challenge me, saying:

"In such a way, your assembly of disciples numbering many hundreds does not dwell having realized for themselves, attained, and entered upon the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life through direct knowledge and the destruction of the taints."
"I do not see, monks, any ground for this.
Not seeing such a ground, monks, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-confidence.
In these three respects, I am beyond reproach."
“Monks, these are the four things that a Tathāgata need not guard against, and by means of these three he is beyond reproach.
Thus was the fifth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.59.
6. Abyākatavagga Kimilasutta (AN 7.59, AN 7.56, PTS AN iv 84)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kimilā in the Nicula Grove.

Then the Venerable Kimila approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Kimila said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the true Dhamma does not endure long after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna?
“Here, Kimila, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, monks, nuns, male lay followers, and female lay followers dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Teacher;
they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Dhamma; they dwell without reverence toward the Saṅgha.”
“They dwell without deference, disrespectful toward the training; they dwell without deference, disrespectful toward concentration;
they dwell without deference, disrespectful toward heedfulness; they dwell without deference, disrespectful toward hospitality.
This, Kimila, is the cause, this is the reason why, after a Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the true Dhamma does not endure for long.”
“But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why the true Dhamma endures for a long time after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna?
“Here, Kimila, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen followers, and laywomen followers dwell with reverence and deference toward the Teacher;
they dwell with reverence and deference toward the Dhamma; they dwell with reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha.”
They dwell with reverence; they dwell with reverence and deference toward the training; they dwell with reverence and deference toward concentration;
they dwell with reverence and deference toward heedfulness; they dwell with reverence and deference toward hospitality.
“This, Kimila, is the cause, this is the reason why the true Dhamma endures for a long time after a Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.60

6. Abyākatavagga Sattadhammasutta (AN 7.60, AN 7.57, PTS AN iv 85) “Monks, there are these seven things that are undeclared by me. Which seven? ‘The world is eternal’—this, monks, is undeclared by me. ‘The world is not eternal’—this, monks, is undeclared by me. ‘The world is finite’—this, monks, is undeclared by me. ‘The world is infinite’—this, monks, is undeclared by me. ‘The soul and the body are the same’—this, monks, is undeclared by me. ‘The soul is one thing and the body another’—this, monks, is undeclared by me. ‘After death, a Tathāgata exists’—this, monks, is undeclared by me. ‘After death, a Tathāgata does not exist’—this, monks, is undeclared by me. ‘After death, a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist’—this, monks, is undeclared by me. ‘After death, a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist’—this, monks, is undeclared by me. And why, monks, are these seven things undeclared by me? Because they are not connected with the goal, not fundamental to the holy life, and do not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and nibbāna. Therefore, these seven things are undeclared by me. But, monks, there are these four things that are declared by me. Which four? ‘This is suffering’—this, monks, is declared by me. ‘This is the origin of suffering’—this, monks, is declared by me. ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—this, monks, is declared by me. ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—this, monks, is declared by me. And why, monks, are these four things declared by me? Because they are connected with the goal, fundamental to the holy life, and lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and nibbāna. Therefore, these four things are declared by me.”

“Bhikkhus, possessing seven qualities, a bhikkhu might, before long, through the destruction of the taints, realize for himself with direct knowledge, and having entered upon it, dwell in the state of arahantship.
What are the seven?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith, he is virtuous, he is learned, he is secluded, he is energetic, he is mindful, and he is wise.”

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these seven qualities will, before long, by the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge, enter and dwell in the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom that are taintless, having realized them in this very life.
Thus it was said. The seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.61

6. Abyākatavagga Pacalāyamānasutta (AN 7.61, AN 7.58a, PTS AN iv 85) “Monks, when one is nodding off, the mind becomes unsteady; when the mind is unsteady, one does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering. One does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. One does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. One does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “When one is nodding off, the mind becomes unsteady; when the mind is unsteady, one does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the origin of suffering’ … ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will not nod off while standing, nor while walking, nor while sitting, nor while lying down; we will not nod off even while leaning against a wall or a tree, nor while reclining on a couch or a seat. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, in the Deer Park.
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was sitting dozing in Kallavāḷaputta village among the Magadhans.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Blessed One saw the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna sitting nodding in the village of Kallavāḷaputta among the Magadhans.
Having seen him—
just as a strong man might stretch out his drawn-in arm, or draw in his stretched-out arm— [he approached].
In this very way, having vanished from the Bhesakaḷā Grove deer park at Susumāragira among the Bhaggas,
the Blessed One appeared before the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the village of Kallavāḷaputta among the Magadhans.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Are you nodding off, Moggallāna? Are you nodding off, Moggallāna?
“Yes, Bhante.”
“Therefore, Moggallāna, as you dwell with such a perception, do not attend to that perception, do not cultivate that perception, so that the drowsiness which comes over you may be abandoned.
It is possible, Moggallāna, that while dwelling thus, that drowsiness will be abandoned.

But if, while dwelling thus, that drowsiness is not abandoned, then you, Moggallāna, should mentally reflect upon, examine, and contemplate with your mind the Dhamma as you have heard it and mastered it.”
It is possible that while you are dwelling in this way, that drowsiness will be abandoned.
If, while dwelling in this way, that drowsiness is not abandoned, then you, Moggallāna, should recite in detail the Dhamma as you have heard it and mastered it.
It is possible that while you are dwelling in this way, that drowsiness will be abandoned.
If that drowsiness is not abandoned while you dwell in this way, then, Moggallāna, you should pull at both your earlobes and rub your limbs with your hand.
It is possible that while you dwell in this way, that drowsiness will be abandoned.

If that drowsiness is still not abandoned while you dwell in this way, then, Moggallāna, having risen from your seat, you should rub your eyes with water, look around at the quarters, and gaze up at the constellations and the forms of the stars.
It is possible that as you dwell in this way, that drowsiness will be abandoned.

If, while dwelling in this way, that drowsiness is not abandoned, then you, Moggallāna, should attend to the perception of light and resolve upon the perception of day—just as by day, so by night; just as by night, so by day.
Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, you should develop a radiant mind.
It is possible that as you dwell in this way, that drowsiness will be abandoned.

But if it is not abandoned while you dwell in this way, then, Moggallāna, you should maintain walking meditation, perceiving the succession of before and after, with your sense faculties withdrawn within and your mind not directed outward.
It is possible that as you dwell in this way, that drowsiness will be abandoned.

But if, while dwelling in this way, that drowsiness is not abandoned, then, Moggallāna, you should lie down on your right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed your mind on the perception of rising.
And once awakened, Moggallāna, you should rise quickly.
‘I shall dwell without being devoted to the pleasure of reclining, the pleasure of lying down, or the pleasure of sloth.
In this way, Moggallāna, you should train yourself.
Therefore, Moggallāna, you should train yourself thus:
‘I will not approach families with my head held high.
Thus, Moggallāna, should you train yourself.
For if, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu approaches families with his head held high, there are indeed duties and obligations to be performed within those families.
When people do not pay attention to a bhikkhu who has arrived, the thought occurs to that bhikkhu:
"Who now has caused a rift between me and this family? These people have become indifferent toward me.
Through this lack of gain, he becomes dejected; being dejected, he becomes restless; being restless, he lacks restraint; and lacking restraint, his mind is far from concentration.
Therefore, Moggallāna, you should train yourself thus:
"I will not engage in contentious talk.
In this way, Moggallāna, should you train yourself.

“Moggallāna, when there is contentious talk, an abundance of talk is to be expected; when there is an abundance of talk, there is agitation; for one who is agitated, there is no restraint; for one who lacks restraint, the mind is far from concentration.
Moggallāna, I do not praise association with everyone, nor do I refrain from praising association with everyone.”
"Moggallāna, I do not praise association with householders and those who have gone forth.
However, I praise association with such lodgings as are quiet, free from noise, secluded from people, remote from human habitation, and suitable for seclusion.
When this was said, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to the Blessed One:

“To what extent, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu, in brief, liberated by the destruction of craving, one who has reached the ultimate end, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and realized the ultimate goal—the foremost among gods and humans?
“In this case, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu has heard:
‘All phenomena are not fit for adherence.’”
And when, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu has heard thus:
“All phenomena are not worth adhering to,” he directly knows all phenomena;

having directly known all phenomena, he fully understands them. Having fully understood all phenomena, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—[he dwells contemplating impermanence, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment in regard to those feelings].

Thus he dwells contemplating impermanence in those feelings, he dwells contemplating dispassion in those feelings, he dwells contemplating cessation in those feelings, he dwells contemplating relinquishment in those feelings.

Dwelling thus contemplating impermanence in those feelings, dwelling contemplating dispassion in those feelings, dwelling contemplating cessation in those feelings, dwelling contemplating relinquishment in those feelings, he does not cling to anything in the world.
Not clinging, he is not agitated; being unagitated, he personally attains Nibbāna.
‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.

It is in this way, Moggallāna, that a bhikkhu is, in brief, liberated by the destruction of craving; he has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and realized the ultimate consummation; he is the best among gods and humans. This was the eighth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.62 6. The Chapter on the Undeclared (Abyākatavagga) The Discourse on Loving-kindness (Mettasutta) "Monks, one who possesses these seven qualities is not reborn in hell, nor in the animal realm, nor in the sphere of afflicted spirits, nor in the realm of the asuras;

rather, having abandoned the four states of deprivation, he is certain for the higher realms, assured of happiness, and destined for enlightenment. What are the seven? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith; he places faith in the Tathāgata’s awakening thus: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He has heard much, has retained what he has heard, accumulated what he has heard; those teachings that are lovely at the beginning, lovely in the middle, and lovely at the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings he has heard much of, retained, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well by view. He is a speaker on the Dhamma; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma and the Discipline; his speech is timely, grounded in facts, purposeful, and connected with the goal. He is one who encourages, inspires, and gladdens his fellow monks with talk on the Dhamma. He is a forest-dweller, one who resorts to remote lodgings such as forests, the roots of trees, mountains, mountain caves, grottoes, open spaces, heaps of straw, and cemeteries. He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites. He is one who dwells with a mind of loving-kindness, free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, and without ill will. One who possesses these seven qualities, monks, is not reborn in hell, nor in the animal realm, nor in the sphere of afflicted spirits, nor in the realm of the asuras; rather, having abandoned the four states of deprivation, he is certain for the higher realms, assured of happiness, and destined for enlightenment."
“Do not fear merit, monks. This, monks, is a designation for happiness: namely, ‘merits.’”
"I recall, monks, experiencing for a long time the desirable, lovely, and pleasing ripening of merits performed over a long period.
For seven years I cultivated a mind of loving-kindness.
Having cultivated a mind of loving-kindness for seven years, I did not return to this world for seven aeons of dissolution and evolution."
“Monks, when the world was contracting, I went to the Ābhassara realm;
when the world was expanding, I was reborn in an empty Brahmā palace.
There, monks, I was Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power.”
Furthermore, monks, thirty-six times I was Sakka, lord of the devas;
and many hundreds of times I was a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dhamma, conqueror of the four quarters, stabilizer of the land, endowed with the seven treasures.
Monks, these were my seven treasures, namely:
The wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Moreover, monks, I had more than a thousand sons, brave, heroic in form, crushers of enemy armies.
Having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean without punishment or sword, but by righteousness, they dwelt therein.
Behold the ripening of merits,
of wholesome deeds for one seeking happiness;
having cultivated a mind of loving-kindness,
For seven years, O monks,
throughout seven aeons of world-dissolution and evolution,
I did not return to this world again.
When the world was contracting,
I became one who has attained the Ābhassara realm; when the world was expanding, I [became one who has attained the Subhakinhā realm].
I became one who has attained the Brahma-world of emptiness.
Seven times I was Mahābrahmā,
a wielder of power at that time.
Thirty-six times I exercised the sovereignty of the gods as Lord of Devas;
I was also a universal monarch.
I was the lord of Jambumaṇḍa,
an anointed kshatriya,
a ruler over men.
One should conquer this earth without the rod, without the sword,
and without violent action.
You have governed with impartiality.
Having ruled this circle of the earth according to the Dhamma, you have done so justly.
I was born into a family of great wealth and great enjoyments,
affluent and endowed with all desirable things.
And by means of the seven treasures;
the Buddhas are the sustainers in the world,
and by them this has been well-taught.
This is the cause of my greatness:
the earth does not fail me;
I possess abundant wealth and requisites.
He becomes a king of majestic splendor,
possessed of supernormal power and renown,
the lord of the realm of Jambudīpa.
Who, even one of dark birth, would not have confidence upon hearing this?
Therefore, by one who desires their own welfare...
By one desiring the highest greatness,
the True Dhamma should be held in high esteem,
remembering the instruction of the Buddhas.
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.63 6.
The Chapter on the Undeclared (Abyākatavagga)
The Discourse on Wives (Bhariyāsutta).
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Now at that time, there were loud noises and great clamor in the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, why is there such a loud noise and clamor in your house, like fishermen over a haul of fish?
“Venerable sir, this daughter-in-law Sujātā was brought here from a wealthy family.
She does not respect her mother-in-law, she does not respect her father-in-law, she does not respect her husband; nor does she honor, revere, esteem, or worship the Blessed One.”
Then the Blessed One addressed his daughter-in-law Sujātā:
“Come, Sujātā.
“Yes, venerable sir,” Sujātā the daughter-in-law replied to the Blessed One, and she approached him.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As Sujātā, the daughter-in-law, was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to her:
"Sujātā, there are these seven kinds of wives for a man."
Which seven?
One who is like an executioner, one who is like a thief, one who is like a mistress, one who is like a mother, one who is like a sister, one who is like a friend, and one who is like a slave-girl.
These, Sujātā, are the seven kinds of wives for a man.
“Of these, which one are you?
“I do not understand, venerable sir, the detailed meaning of this brief statement spoken by the Blessed One.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement spoken by the Blessed One.”
“In that case, Sujātā, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the house-daughter-in-law Sujātā replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
With a corrupted mind, lacking compassion,
she is infatuated with others and despises her husband;
eager for his death, she seeks to kill him whom she purchased with wealth.
Such a wife as this is called a wife for slaughter. Whatever wealth the husband acquires from his wife, [he must give it back].
A wife such as this, who desires to seize away even a little of a man's craft, trade, or farming— even though he is intent upon them— [is not a true wife].
She is called a "thieving wife" and a "burdening wife":
one who is unwilling to work, lazy, gluttonous,
harsh, fierce, and a speaker of evil words.
She who prevails over those who rise early,
such a wife as this is called by a man "a lady and a wife."
She who is always compassionate for his welfare,
who protects her husband as a mother protects her son,
safeguards the wealth he has accumulated.
Such a wife as this is called both "mother" and "wife.
Just as an elder sister is to a younger brother, so too is she.
She who is full of respect for her own husband,
modest, and obedient to her husband’s will—
such a wife as this is a blessing to a man.
"She is called both 'sister' and 'wife.
Having seen her husband here,
she rejoices like a female friend meeting a male friend after a long time."
A wife who is well-behaved, virtuous, and devoted—
such a woman as this is called both a "friend" and a "wife" by a man.
Unprovoked and peaceful, though threatened by the rod of execution,
she endures her husband with a mind free from malice;
free from anger, she follows the will of her lord.
Such a wife as this is called a man’s “slave-wife.
And she who is called here a “murderous wife,”...
Those who are called "noble ladies" though they are thieves— immoral,
harsh, and disrespectful—
they go to hell after the breakup of the body.
She who was formerly called "mother," "sister," or "friend," and "slave" or "wife"—
because she is established in virtue and has long been restrained, she is now so described.
"With the breakup of the body, they go to a happy destination.
These, Sujātā, are the seven kinds of wives for a man.
Which one among them are you?"
“From this day forward, Bhante, may the Blessed One consider me as a wife equal to a slave belonging to my husband.
Tenth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.64

6. Abyākatavagga Kodhanasutta (AN 7.64, AN 7.60, PTS AN iv 94) “Bhikkhus, one who is angry is not one who has acted in accordance with the Dhamma; one who is not angry is one who has acted in accordance with the Dhamma. One who is angry is not one who has lived in accordance with the Dhamma; one who is not angry is one who has lived in accordance with the Dhamma. One who is angry does not attain the goal; one who is not angry attains the goal. One who is angry is not dear and beloved to many; one who is not angry is dear and beloved to many. One who is angry is hard to support; one who is not angry is easy to support. One who is angry does not bring about the welfare of many people; one who is not angry brings about the welfare of many people. One who is angry is not one who has entered the path of the noble ones; one who is not angry is one who has entered the path of the noble ones. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will abandon anger whenever it arises. It is in this way that you should train yourselves.”
“Bhikkhus, these seven things, which are pleasing to an enemy and serve to make one an enemy, come upon a man or a woman who is prone to anger.
What seven?
Here, bhikkhus, an enemy wishes for an enemy thus:”
‘Oh, may this person be ugly!
For what reason?
Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in the beauty of his enemy.
“Monks, when a person is prone to anger, overcome by anger, and possessed by anger, even though he may be well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, and clothed in white garments,
yet because he is overcome by anger, he remains ugly. Monks,
this is the first quality that is pleasing to an enemy and conducive to enmity that comes upon an angry woman or man.”
Furthermore, monks, an enemy wishes this of his enemy:
"Oh, may he sleep in discomfort!
For what reason?
“Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in the comfortable sleep of his enemy.
Monks, when a person is angry, overcome by anger, and possessed by anger,
even though he may lie on a couch spread with a woolen coverlet, a cotton coverlet, and a choice antelope-skin rug, provided with a canopy above and red pillows at both ends;”
Then, overcome by anger, he lies in suffering alone.
This, monks, is the second thing that is pleasing to an enemy and conducive to an enemy’s purpose that comes upon an angry woman or man.
Furthermore, monks, an enemy desires this for his enemy:
‘Oh, may this person not have abundant wealth!
For what reason?
Monks, an enemy does not rejoice at the abundance of wealth belonging to his enemy.

“Monks, this angry person, overcome by anger and possessed by anger, thinks, ‘I have gained what is beneficial,’ even when he has gained what is harmful; and he thinks, ‘I have gained what is harmful,’ even when he has gained what is beneficial.
These things, grasped as mutually contradictory, lead for a long time to his harm and suffering for one who is overcome by anger.
This, monks, is the third thing that is pleasing to an enemy and conducive to making an enemy, which comes upon an angry woman or man.”
Furthermore, monks, an enemy wishes this of his enemy:
“Oh, may he not possess wealth!
For what reason?
“Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in the wealth of his enemy.
Monks, for a person who is angry, overcome by anger, and possessed by anger—
even those possessions of his that were acquired through exertion and effort, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned through sweat, and obtained righteously and lawfully— ”
Those kings, overcome by anger, cause [the offender's] wealth to enter the royal treasury.
This, monks, is the fourth quality that is pleasing to an enemy and conducive to an enemy’s success that comes upon an angry woman or man.
Furthermore, monks, an enemy desires this for his enemy:
‘Oh, may this person not be famous!
Why is that? Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in the fame of an enemy.
“Monks, this person who is prone to anger, overcome by anger, and possessed by anger—even that reputation he had acquired through diligence—he loses because he is overcome by anger.
Monks, this is the fifth thing pleasing to an enemy and conducive to an enemy’s purpose that comes upon an angry man or woman.
Furthermore, monks, an enemy desires for his enemy as follows:”
‘Oh, may this person not have friends!
For what reason?
Because, monks, an enemy does not rejoice in an enemy’s having friends.

“Monks, when a person is angry, overcome by anger, and possessed by anger, even those who are his friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relations avoid him from afar because he is overcome by anger.
This, monks, is the sixth quality that is pleasing to an enemy and conducive to making one an enemy, which comes upon an angry man or woman.
Furthermore, monks, an enemy desires this for an enemy:”
‘Oh, may this person, with the breakup of the body after death, be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell!
Why is that? Because, monks, an enemy does not rejoice at an enemy’s going to a good destination.
“Monks, this angry person, overcome by anger and possessed by anger, engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.
Having engaged in misconduct by body, by speech, and so forth...
with the breakup of the body, after death, he—overcome by anger—is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell.”
“Monks, this seventh thing is pleasing to an enemy and creates enmity; it comes upon a woman or a man who is prone to anger.
Monks, these seven things are pleasing to an enemy and create enmity; they come upon a woman or a man who is prone to anger.
One who is prone to anger is ugly.”
Furthermore, he lies in suffering;
furthermore, having grasped what is beneficial,
he falls into what is harmful.
Then, having committed an act of killing with body or speech,
the angry man is overcome by anger.
One incurs the loss of wealth.
Intoxicated by the madness of anger,
one incurs misfortune.
Relatives, friends, and companions avoid one who is prone to anger;
anger is the producer of misfortune.
Anger is a disturber of the mind;
people do not realize that this fear has arisen from within themselves.
One who is angry does not know the goal;
one who is angry does not see the Dhamma.
Then there is blinding darkness.
Anger overcomes the man whom it seizes;
when one is angry, even that which is easy becomes difficult to do.
Later, when his anger has passed,
he burns like one consumed by fire;
he displays a state of wickedness.
Like fire with smoke,
wherever anger spreads,
there young men become enraged.
In one who is overcome by anger, there is no shame, no fear of wrongdoing, nor is there any reverence in speech.
There is no lamp whatsoever.
There are deeds that bring remorse,
which are far removed from the true Dhammas.
I shall declare those things;
listen to them as they truly are.
For one who is angry slays even his father.
An angry person slays even his own mother;
for one who is angry slays a brahmin,
and an angry person slays an ordinary man.
The mother who supports and nourishes the person,
by whom this world is looked upon—
even her, the giver of life, one should honor.
An angry worldling destroys [himself],
for those beings are like themselves,
and the self is indeed most dear.
One who is angry slays the manifold [objects of perception],
being infatuated with various forms;
he slays himself with a sword.
Deluded, they eat poison;
bound by a rope, they die even in mountain caves.
Performing deeds that destroy living beings and those that lead to their own destruction,
they do not realize it.
Born of anger is ruin.
This snare of Death, dwelling in the cave of the heart, has come here in the form of anger.
One should utterly cut off that [defilement] by means of self-control,
wisdom, energy, and right view,
so that this unwholesome state may cease.
The wise person should utterly cut it off;
likewise, one should train in the Dhamma,
lest there be wickedness in us.
Free from anger, free from weariness,
free from greed, and without longing;
tamed, having abandoned anger—
“Those free from taints attain final Nibbāna.
The eleventh [sutta].
The sixth chapter on the Undeclared (Abyākata-vagga).
Its summary verse:
The Indeterminate, the Destination of Men,
Tissa, Sīha, and the Unprotected.
Kimila, the seven beings, Pacālā,
Mettā as wife, and the eleven types of anger.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.65)

7. Mahāvagga Hirīottappasutta (AN 7.65, AN 7.61, PTS AN iv 99) “Monks, there are these two qualities that lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. What two? A lack of moral shame and a lack of moral dread. These, monks, are the two qualities that lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. There are, monks, these two qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. What two? Moral shame and moral dread. These, monks, are the two qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee.”
“Bhikkhus, when there is no sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, for one devoid of shame and fear of wrongdoing, the prerequisite for restraint of the faculties is destroyed.
When there is no restraint of the faculties, for one devoid of restraint of the faculties, the prerequisite for virtuous conduct is destroyed.
When there is no virtuous conduct, for one devoid of virtuous conduct, the prerequisite for right concentration is destroyed.”
When right concentration is absent, for one deficient in right concentration, the supporting condition for knowledge and vision of things as they really are is destroyed.

When knowledge and vision of things as they really are are absent, for one deficient in knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the supporting condition for disenchantment and dispassion is destroyed.
When disenchantment and dispassion are absent, for one deficient in disenchantment and dispassion, the supporting condition for the knowledge and vision of liberation is destroyed.
Just as, monks, when a tree is deprived of its branches and foliage,
its shoots do not reach full development, nor does its bark, its inner bark, or its heartwood reach full development; even so, monks,
when there is no moral shame and dread of wrongdoing, for one devoid of moral shame and dread of wrongdoing, the restraint of the sense faculties lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no restraint of the sense faculties, for one who has failed in the restraint of the sense faculties, virtue lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no virtue, for one who has failed in virtue, right concentration lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no right concentration, for one who has failed in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are lacks its proximate cause.

When there is no knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one who has failed in knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the proximate cause for disenchantment and dispassion is destroyed.
When there is no disenchantment and dispassion, for one who has failed in disenchantment and dispassion, the proximate cause for the knowledge and vision of liberation is destroyed.
Monks, when there is moral shame and moral dread, for one endowed with moral shame and moral dread, the restraint of the sense faculties is endowed with its proximate cause.
When there is restraint of the sense faculties, for one who is accomplished in restraint of the sense faculties, virtue is fully supported by its proximate cause.
When there is virtue, for one who is accomplished in virtue, right concentration is fully supported by its proximate cause.
When there is right concentration, for one who is accomplished in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is fully supported by its proximate cause.

When there is knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one endowed with knowledge and vision of things as they really are, disenchantment and dispassion are fulfilled as their supporting condition.
When there is disenchantment and dispassion, for one endowed with disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation is fulfilled as its supporting condition.
Just as, monks, when a tree is endowed with branches and foliage, its bark reaches full development, its inner bark, its softwood, and its heartwood also reach full development.
"In the same way, monks, when there is moral shame and moral dread, for one endowed with moral shame and moral dread, the supporting conditions are fulfilled...
[and so on] ...up to the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.66 7. Mahāvagga Sattasūriyasutta (The Discourse on the Seven Suns) “Bhikkhus, suppose there were seven suns to appear in the world. With the appearance of those seven suns, the great earth, together with its mountains and its forests, would be consumed and burnt up, leaving behind only ashes and dust. Just as, bhikkhus, when seven suns appear in the world, the great earth, together with its mountains and its forests, is consumed and burnt up, leaving behind only ashes and dust; so too, bhikkhus, this body consists of the four great elements. It is not yours, nor does it belong to others. It should be regarded as it actually is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When one sees it thus as it actually is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the body, dispassionate toward the body, and liberated from the body. One becomes disenchanted with form, dispassionate toward form, and liberated from form. One becomes disenchanted with feeling, dispassionate toward feeling, and liberated from feeling. One becomes disenchanted with perception, dispassionate toward perception, and liberated from perception. One becomes disenchanted with volitional formations, dispassionate toward volitional formations, and liberated from volitional formations. One becomes disenchanted with consciousness, dispassionate toward consciousness, and liberated from consciousness. Through this liberation, one is liberated by final knowledge. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
(AN 7.66, AN 7.62, PTS AN iv 100) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in Ambapālī’s Grove.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Monks, conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
monks, conditioned phenomena are unstable.”
“Monks, conditioned phenomena are not a source of consolation.
To this extent, monks, it is indeed sufficient to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, sufficient to become dispassionate toward them, and sufficient to be liberated from them.
Monks, Sineru, the king of mountains, is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and eighty-four thousand yojanas [in width].”
In detail, it is submerged eighty-four thousand yojanas into the great ocean and rises eighty-four thousand yojanas above the great ocean.
There comes a time, monks, when after the lapse of a long period— after many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years— the rain does not fall.
Furthermore, monks, when it rains, whatever seed-life and plant-life there is—herbs, grasses, and forest trees—they wither away, dry up, and cease to exist.
Thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are unstable … [and so on] …
It is enough to be liberated.
There comes a time, monks, when after the passing of a long period, a second sun appears at some point.
With the appearance of the second sun, monks, whatever small rivers and pools there are, they dry up and evaporate; they no longer exist.
"Thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are impermanent... [as before] ...
they are sufficient for liberation.
There comes a time, monks, when after the passing of a long period, at some point, a third sun appears."
“Monks, with the appearance of the third sun, whatever great rivers there are—namely, the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī—they dry up and evaporate; they no longer exist.
Thus, monks, are conditioned phenomena impermanent... [and so on]”
It is enough for liberation.
There comes a time, monks, when after the lapse of a long period, a fourth sun appears.
With the appearance of the fourth sun, monks, those great lakes from which these great rivers flow—namely:
The Anotatta Lake, the Sīhapapāta Falls, the Rathakāra Lake, the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa Lake, the Kuṇāla Lake, the Chaddanta Lake, and the Mandākinī River—all these dry up, wither away, and cease to exist.
Thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are impermanent...
enough to be liberated.
There comes a time, monks, when after the passing of a long period, at some point, a fifth sun appears.
With the appearance of the fifth sun, monks, the waters in the great ocean recede by a hundred yojanas;
they recede by two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, and four hundred yojanas.
The waters of the great ocean recede by five hundred yojanas, six hundred yojanas, and even seven hundred yojanas;
the water in the great ocean remains at a depth of seven palm trees, six palm trees, five palm trees, four palm trees, three palm trees, two palm trees, and even at the height of a single palm tree;
the water in the great ocean remains at a depth of seven fathoms, six fathoms, five fathoms, and four fathoms.
The water in the great ocean remains standing at the depth of three men, two men, one man, half a man, even as deep as the waist, as deep as the knees, or as deep as the ankles.

Just as, monks, in the autumn season when the rain falls in large drops, pools of water remain here and there in the hoofprints of cattle; so too, monks, the water in the great ocean remains standing at the depth of three men, two men, one man, half a man, even as deep as the waist, as deep as the knees, or as deep as the ankles.
In the same way, monks, there remain only waters as deep as the ankle here and there in the great ocean.
With the appearance of the fifth sun, monks, not even water as deep as a finger-joint remains in the great ocean.
Thus, monks, are conditioned phenomena impermanent... [and so on].
Enough with [seeking] liberation.
There comes a time, monks, when after the passing of a long period, at some point, a sixth sun appears.
With the appearance of the sixth sun, monks, this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, smoke, fume, and billow with smoke.
“Just as, monks, a potter’s kiln, when first plastered, smokes, fumes, and billows with smoke;
even so, monks, with the appearance of the sixth sun, this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, smoke, fume, and billow with smoke.
Thus, monks, are conditioned phenomena impermanent... [as before] ...”
Enough with the thought of liberation.
There comes a time, monks, when after the passing of a long period, at some point, a seventh sun appears.
With the appearance of that seventh sun, monks, this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, ignite, blaze up, and become a single mass of flame.
And, monks, when this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, are burning and blazing, the flame, driven by the wind, goes even as far as the Brahma-world.
When Sineru, the king of mountains, is burning, blazing, perishing,
and overwhelmed by a great mass of fire, its peaks a hundred yojanas high crumble away, and those two hundred yojanas high do likewise.
Summits measuring three hundred yojanas, four hundred yojanas, and even five hundred yojanas crumble away.
And, monks, as this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, burn and blaze, neither ash nor soot is perceived.
Just as, monks, when ghee or oil burns and blazes, neither ash nor soot is perceived.
In the same way, monks, when this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, are burned and consumed by fire, neither ash nor soot is perceived.
So impermanent, monks, are conditioned phenomena;
so unstable, monks, are conditioned phenomena.
"Thus, monks, conditioned phenomena are not to be relied upon.
To this extent, monks, it is indeed enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them.
In this regard, monks, who would have confidence? Who would have faith?"
"Except for those who have seen the Truth, who would think: ‘This earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will burn up, perish, and cease to exist’?
Once upon a time, monks, there was a teacher named Sunetta, a founder of a school who was free from passion for sensual pleasures.
That teacher Sunetta, monks, had many hundreds of disciples."
"Bhikkhus, the Teacher Sunetta taught the Dhamma to his disciples for the sake of companionship with the Brahmā-world.

Those who fully understood the entire teaching of the Teacher Sunetta as he was teaching it for the sake of companionship with the Brahmā-world, at the breaking up of the body, after death, were reborn in a good destination, in the Brahmā-world.
Those who did not fully understand the entire teaching, at the breaking up of the body, after death, some were reborn among the Paranimmitavasavatti devas."
Some were reborn in the company of the gods; some were reborn in the company of the Nimmānarati gods;
some were reborn in the company of the Tusita gods; some were reborn in the company of the Yāma gods;
some were reborn in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa gods; and some were reborn in the company of the Cātumahārājika gods.
Some were reborn in the company of the devas; some were reborn in the company of wealthy kshatriyas;
some were reborn in the company of wealthy brahmins; and some were reborn in the company of wealthy householders.
Then, monks, it occurred to the teacher Sunetta:
“It is not fitting for me that my disciples should have an equal destination in the future life; what if I were to develop further loving-kindness?
Then, monks, the teacher Sunetta developed a mind of loving-kindness for seven years.
Having developed a mind of loving-kindness for seven years, he did not return to this world for seven aeons of dissolution and evolution.
Monks, when the world was dissolving, he went to the Ābhassara realm;
when the world was evolving, he was reborn in an empty Brahma-palace.
In that regard, monks, he was indeed Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the conqueror unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power.
Furthermore, monks, thirty-six times he was Sakka, lord of the devas.
Many hundreds of times he was a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dhamma, victorious over the four quarters, a stabilizer of the land, and possessed of the seven treasures.
Moreover, he had more than a thousand sons who were brave, heroic in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
Having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean, he dwelt therein, ruling by righteousness, without rod or sword.
Yet, monks, even though that teacher Sunetta was so long-lived and remained for such a long time, he was not liberated.
‘One is not yet freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; one is not yet freed from suffering,’ I say. And why is that?
Because of the non-awakening and non-penetration of four things.

Of which four? Of noble virtue, monks, through lack of full understanding and non-penetration; of noble concentration, through lack of full understanding and non-penetration; of noble wisdom, through lack of full understanding and non-penetration; and of noble liberation, through lack of full understanding and non-penetration.
But this noble virtue, monks, has been fully understood and penetrated; noble concentration has been fully understood and penetrated.
“Noble wisdom has been awakened to and penetrated; noble liberation has been awakened to and penetrated. Craving for existence is cut off;
the conduit to existence is exhausted; there is now no further becoming.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
"Virtue, concentration, wisdom,
and supreme liberation;"
"These phenomena have been fully understood by the illustrious Gotama.
Thus, having realized this through direct knowledge, the Buddha—
He proclaimed the Dhamma to the bhikkhus;
the Teacher, the Seer who brings an end to suffering, has attained final Nibbāna.
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.67 7. Mahāvagga
The Discourse on the City-like King (Nagaropamasutta): “Bhikkhus,
when a king’s frontier city is well-provided with the seven requisites of a city, and he obtains the four kinds of food at will, without difficulty, and without hardship.”
This, monks, is called a king’s frontier city that cannot be overcome by external enemies or adversaries.
By what seven fortifications is it well-fortified?
Here, monks, in the king’s frontier city there is a pillar that is deep-based, firmly planted, immovable, and unshakable.
By this first city requisite, the king’s frontier city is well-fortified for the protection of those within and for the repelling of those without.
Furthermore, monks, the moat surrounding the king’s frontier city is both deep and wide.
By this second city requisite, the king’s frontier city is well-fortified for the protection of those within and for the repelling of those without.
Furthermore, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is a patrol road that is both high and wide.
By this third city requisite, the king’s frontier city is well-provided for the protection of those within and the warding off of those without.
Furthermore, monks, in a king’s frontier city much weaponry is stored, both for missiles and for hand-to-hand combat.
With this fourth city requisite, a king’s frontier city is well-provided for the protection of those within and the repelling of those without.
Furthermore, monks, in a king’s frontier city there dwells a large body of troops, such as:

elephant-riders, cavalry, chariot-warriors, archers, standard-bearers, banner-carriers, messengers, high-born nobles, princes, elite warriors, great leaders, heroes, shield-bearers, and sons of slaves.
With this fifth requisite for a city, a king’s frontier city is well-provided for the protection of those within and the warding off of those without.
Furthermore, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is a gatekeeper who is wise, competent, and intelligent, who keeps out strangers and admits those he knows.
With this sixth requisite for a city, a king’s frontier city is well-provided for the protection of those within and the warding off of those without.
Furthermore, monks, a king’s frontier city has a rampart that is high, wide, and well-plastered.
By this seventh city-requisite, the king’s frontier city is well-fortified for the protection of those within and for the warding off of those without.
Thus it is well-fortified by these seven city-requisites.
Of which four kinds of nutriment is he one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble?
Here, monks, in a king’s frontier city, much grass, wood, and water are stored up for the pleasure, non-distress, and comfortable dwelling of those within, and for the warding off of those without.
Furthermore, monks, in a king’s frontier city, much rice and barley are stored up for the pleasure, non-distress, and comfortable dwelling of those within, and for the warding off of those without.

Furthermore, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is stored much sesame, mung beans, kidney beans, and other grains for the enjoyment, freedom from distress, and comfortable living of those within, and for the warding off of those without.
Furthermore, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is stored much medicine, namely:
ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, and salt, for the enjoyment, freedom from distress, and comfortable living of those within, and for the warding off of those without.
Monks, one obtains these four kinds of sustenance at will, without difficulty, and without hardship. Monks,
when a king’s frontier city is well-provided with these seven requisites for a city and one obtains these four kinds of sustenance at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, this, monks,
is called a king’s frontier city that cannot be overcome by external enemies or adversaries.
In the same way, monks, when a noble disciple is endowed with seven true qualities and is one who obtains at will,
without difficulty, and without hardship, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life,
he is called, monks, a noble disciple who cannot be done anything to by Māra, who cannot be done anything to by the Evil One.
Endowed with what seven true qualities does he possess them?

Just as, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is a pillar that has deep foundations, is well-planted, immovable, and unshakable, for the protection of those within and the warding off of those without;
even so, monks, the noble disciple is endowed with faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
‘Such indeed is he... [as before] ...the Buddha, the Blessed One.
With faith as his guide, monks, the noble disciple abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome;
he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless.
He maintains himself in purity.
He is thus endowed with this first true quality.
Just as, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is a moat, both deep and wide, for the protection of those within and to ward off those from without.
In the same way, monks, a noble disciple possesses a sense of shame; he feels shame for misconduct of body, speech, and mind, and he feels shame for the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states.
With a sense of shame as his rampart, monks, the noble disciple abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome;
he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless.
He maintains himself in purity.
By this second true quality he is endowed.
Just as, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is a circumvallation that is both high and wide, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without.

In the same way, monks, a noble disciple is conscientious; he is conscientious regarding bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he is conscientious regarding the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states.
By means of the path of conscientiousness, monks, the noble disciple abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome;
he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless.

He maintains himself in purity. He is endowed with this third true quality. Just as, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is a great store of weapons—both for immediate use and for reserve—for the protection of those within and to ward off those without; so too, monks, is this the case for a noble disciple who possesses these seven factors of enlightenment. This, monks, is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment.

Furthermore, monks, a king’s frontier city has many provisions of food, both for immediate consumption and for storage, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. So too, monks, a noble disciple who possesses these seven factors of enlightenment has much food for the journey, both for immediate consumption and for storage, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. What, monks, is the food for the journey that is for immediate consumption? It is the four foundations of mindfulness. And what, monks, is the food for the journey that is for storage? It is the seven factors of enlightenment. Just as, monks, a king’s frontier city has many provisions of food, both for immediate consumption and for storage, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without; so too, monks, a noble disciple who possesses these seven factors of enlightenment has much food for the journey, both for immediate consumption and for storage, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. This, monks, is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. Furthermore, monks, a king’s frontier city is well-fortified with ramparts and moats, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. So too, monks, a noble disciple who possesses these seven factors of enlightenment is well-fortified with the rampart of mindfulness and the moat of contentment, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. This, monks, is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. Furthermore, monks, a king’s frontier city has many weapons stored up, both for immediate use and for reserve, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. So too, monks, a noble disciple who possesses these seven factors of enlightenment has many weapons stored up, both for immediate use and for reserve, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. What, monks, are the weapons for immediate use? They are the four right endeavors. And what, monks, are the weapons for reserve? They are the seven factors of enlightenment. Just as, monks, a king’s frontier city has many weapons stored up, both for immediate use and for reserve, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without; so too, monks, a noble disciple who possesses these seven factors of enlightenment has many weapons stored up, both for immediate use and for reserve, for the protection of those within and to ward off those without. This, monks, is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment.
In the same way, monks, a noble disciple is learned … [as before] … has well penetrated right view.
Armed with the weapon of learning, monks, the noble disciple abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome;
he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless.
He maintains himself in purity.
He is endowed with this fourth true quality.
Just as, monks, in a king’s frontier city there dwells a large military force, namely:

Elephant riders, cavalrymen, charioteers, archers, standard-bearers, banner-carriers, providers of provisions, high-born nobles, princes, impetuous warriors, great heroes, brave men, shield-bearers, and sons of slaves—all for the protection of those within and the warding off of those without.
In the same way, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states;
he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not lay down the burden regarding wholesome states.
“Monks, a noble disciple who possesses the power of energy abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome;
he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless;
he maintains himself in purity.”
Thus he is endowed with this fifth true quality.

Just as, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is a gatekeeper who is wise, competent, and intelligent—one who keeps out strangers and admits those he knows, for the protection of those within and the warding off of those without—just so, monks, the noble disciple is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recalls what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago.
