Bhikkhus, the noble disciple who has mindfulness as his doorkeeper abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome;
he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless;
he maintains himself in purity.
In this way, he is endowed with this sixth true quality.
Just as, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is a rampart that is both high and wide, well-plastered and finished, for the protection of those within and the warding off of those without;
even so, monks, the noble disciple is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
“Bhikkhus, an noble disciple who is endowed with the plastering of the dwelling-place of wisdom abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome;
he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless;
he maintains himself in purity.”
He is endowed with this seventh true quality.
He is endowed with these seven true qualities.
Of which four jhānas—those pertaining to the higher mind, providing a pleasant dwelling in this very life—is he one who obtains them at will, without difficulty, and without trouble?

"Just as, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is stored much grass, wood, and water for the pleasure, lack of anxiety, and comfortable dwelling of those within, and for the warding off of those without;

even so, monks, a noble disciple, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna for his own pleasure, lack of anxiety, comfortable dwelling, and for the entering upon Nibbāna."

“Just as, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is a great store of rice and barley accumulated for the pleasure, the lack of anxiety, and the comfortable dwelling of those within, and for the warding off of those without;
even so, monks, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a noble disciple enters and dwells in the second jhāna...
for his own pleasure, for his lack of anxiety, for his comfortable dwelling, and for the entering upon Nibbāna.”

“Just as, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is stored much sesame, mung beans, and other cooked food for the delight, lack of anxiety, and comfortable dwelling of those within, and for the warding off of those without;

even so, monks, with the fading away of rapture, a noble disciple dwells having attained the third jhāna—free from joy—with equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, experiencing in himself that joy of which the Noble Ones say:
‘Happy is he who dwells with equanimity and mindfulness’—for his own delight, lack of anxiety, comfortable dwelling, and for the descent into Nibbāna.”
“Just as, monks, in a king’s frontier city there is stored up much medicine,
namely: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, and salt— for the pleasure, lack of distress, and comfortable dwelling of those within,
and for the warding off of those from without— even so, monks, a noble disciple, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, having previously [abandoned joy and dejection]...”
With the subsiding of both joy and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity;
this is for his own delight, for his lack of agitation, for his comfortable dwelling, and for the descent into Nibbāna.
He becomes one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, these four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
Monks, when a noble disciple is endowed with these seven true qualities and obtains at will,
without difficulty, and without trouble, these four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life, [he is called a stream-enterer].
“Monks, this is called a noble disciple who is beyond the reach of Māra, beyond the reach of the Evil One.
The third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.68

7. Mahāvagga Dhammaññūsutta (AN 7.68, AN 7.64, PTS AN iv 113) [The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who knows the Dhamma; the person who does not know the Dhamma; the person who pretends to know the Dhamma when he does not know it; and the person who does not pretend to know the Dhamma when he does not know it. And how, monks, is one a person who knows the Dhamma? Here, monks, a noble disciple understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who knows the Dhamma. And how, monks, is one a person who does not know the Dhamma? Here, monks, a noble disciple does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... [etc]... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who does not know the Dhamma. And how, monks, is one a person who pretends to know the Dhamma when he does not know it? Here, monks, a certain person does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... [etc]... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ yet he claims: ‘I understand as it really is: “This is suffering”... [etc]... “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who pretends to know the Dhamma when he does not know it. And how, monks, is one a person who does not pretend to know the Dhamma when he does not know it? Here, monks, a certain person does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... [etc]... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ and he does not claim: ‘I understand as it really is: “This is suffering”... [etc]... “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who does not pretend to know the Dhamma when he does not know it. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world."* *The sutta continues with a detailed exposition on the nature of the Dhamma and the consequences for those who misrepresent it.*
“Bhikkhus, possessing seven qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
What seven?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who knows the Dhamma, knows the meaning, knows himself, knows moderation, knows the right time, knows the assembly, and knows the superior and inferior qualities of individuals.
And how, monks, is a monk one who knows the Dhamma?
Here, monks, a monk knows the Dhamma:

the discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), "Thus it was said" (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical treatises (vedalla).
If, monks, a monk did not know the Dhamma—
the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legends, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and questions-and-answers—
he would not be called here ‘one who knows the Dhamma. But because, monks, a monk does know the Dhamma—

The discourses, the mixed prose and verse, the expositions, the verses, the utterances in prose and verse, the legends, the birth stories, the marvelous qualities, and the analyses—therefore one is called "one who knows the Dhamma.
Thus is one who knows the Dhamma.
And how is one "one who knows the meaning"?
“Here, monks, a monk understands the meaning of this or that statement:
‘This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement.
If, monks, a monk did not understand the meaning of this or that statement:”
‘This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement’—if one were to speak thus, one would not here be called ‘one who knows the meaning.
But because, monks, a monk knows the meaning of each and every statement:
‘This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement,’ therefore he is called ‘one who knows the meaning.’
Thus he is one who knows the Dhamma and knows the meaning.
And how is he one who knows himself?
Here, monks, a monk knows himself thus:
‘I am thus much in terms of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence.
Monks, if a monk did not know himself thus:
‘I am thus much in terms of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence,’ he would not be called here ‘one who knows himself.’
And because, monks, a bhikkhu knows himself thus:
“I am so much in terms of faith, virtuous behavior, learning, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence,” therefore he is called “one who knows himself.
Thus he is one who knows the Dhamma, one who knows the meaning, and one who knows himself.
And how is one moderate?
Here, monks, a monk knows the proper measure in accepting robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

If, monks, a monk did not know the proper measure in accepting robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he would not be called "one who knows the proper measure" in this world.
But because, monks, a monk knows the proper measure in accepting robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, he is therefore called "one who knows the measure.
Thus he is one who knows the Dhamma, one who knows the meaning, one who knows himself, and one who knows the measure.
And how is he one who knows the right time?
In this case, monks, a monk knows the proper time:
“This is the time for recitation; this is the time for questioning; this is the time for yoga; this is the time for seclusion.
Monks, if a monk were not to know the proper time:

‘This is the time for recitation, this is the time for questioning, this is the time for yoga, this is the time for seclusion’—if one were to speak thus, one would not be called “one who knows the proper time.
But because, monks, a bhikkhu knows the time, thinking:
‘This is the time for recitation, this is the time for questioning, this is the time for yoga, this is the time for seclusion,’ therefore he is called “one who knows the proper time.”
Thus he is one who knows the Dhamma, who knows the meaning, who knows himself, who knows the proper measure, and who knows the right time.
And how does he come to know the assembly?
Here, monks, a monk knows the assembly: [text continues]
‘This is an assembly of khattiyas, this is an assembly of brahmins, this is an assembly of householders, this is an assembly of ascetics.
Therein one should approach in such a way, stand in such a way, act in such a way, sit in such a way, speak in such a way, and remain silent in such a way.
If, monks, a monk does not know the assembly:
‘This is an assembly of khattiyas’ … [and so on] … ‘one should remain silent in this way,’ yet he would not be called ‘one who knows assemblies’ in this regard.
But because, monks, a bhikkhu knows an assembly thus:
‘This is an assembly of khattiyas, this is an assembly of brahmins, this is an assembly of householders, this is an assembly of ascetics.

Therein one should approach in such a way, stand in such a way, act in such a way, sit in such a way, speak in such a way, and remain silent in such a way. Therefore, one is called ‘one who knows assemblies.
Thus he is one who knows the Dhamma, one who knows the meaning, one who knows himself, one who knows moderation, one who knows the right time, and one who knows assemblies.
And how is one a knower of the higher and lower qualities of persons?
Here, monks, a monk has understood two types of persons by means of a dyad. What are the two persons? [The text continues:
Two persons...
One desires to see the noble ones; one does not desire to see the noble ones.
That person who does not desire to see the noble ones is, for that reason, to be censured.

One person desires to hear the true Dhamma; another does not desire to hear the true Dhamma.
That person who does not desire to hear the true Dhamma is, for that reason, blameworthy.

This person who desires to hear the true Dhamma is to be praised for that quality. There are two persons who desire to hear the true Dhamma: [the one who hears it with attention and the one who hears it without attention].
One listens to the Dhamma with an attentive ear; another listens to the Dhamma without an attentive ear.
That person who listens to the Dhamma without an attentive ear is, for that reason, to be censured.
This person who listens to the Dhamma with an attentive ear is praiseworthy in that respect.
There are two persons who listen to the Dhamma with an attentive ear:
One person, having heard the Dhamma, retains it; another, having heard the Dhamma, does not retain it.
That person who, having heard the Dhamma, does not retain it, is to be criticized for that reason.
This person who, having heard the Dhamma, retains it,
is thus praiseworthy in that respect.
There are two persons who, having heard the Dhamma, retain it:
One person examines the meaning of the phenomena of the elements, while another does not examine the meaning of the phenomena of the elements.
That person who does not examine the meaning of the phenomena of the elements is,
for that reason, to be censured.
When this person examines the meaning of the teachings he has learned,
he is thus praiseworthy in that respect.
There are two kinds of persons who examine the meaning of the teachings they have learned:

One person, having understood the goal and having understood the Dhamma, practices in accordance with the Dhamma; another, having understood the goal and having understood the Dhamma, does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
That person who, having understood the goal and having understood the Dhamma, does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma, is to be blamed for that reason.
This person who, having understood the goal and understood the Dhamma, practices in accordance with the Dhamma—
by that factor, he is praiseworthy. There are two persons who,
having understood the goal and understood the Dhamma, practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
One person practices for their own benefit but not for the benefit of others; another practices both for their own benefit and for the benefit of others.
That person who practices for their own benefit but not for the benefit of others is, in that respect, to be censured.
This person who practices for his own welfare and for the welfare of others is,
in that respect, praiseworthy. Thus, monks,
by means of these two, persons are known by a monk.
"In this way, monks, a monk is one who knows the higher and lower qualities of persons.
Possessing these seven qualities, monks, a monk is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Thus was the fourth [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.69 7. Mahāvagga Pāricchattakasutta “Monks, suppose there were a great banyan tree standing possessed of heartwood;

it would be impossible for anyone to come along and cut off its root, or its trunk, or its branches and foliage, or to burn it with fire, or to carry it away, or to reduce it to ashes, or to do with it as they please, without first having exhausted its heartwood. In the same way, monks, if a bhikkhu is possessed of the heartwood of the higher training in the higher mind, it is impossible for anyone to come along and cut off his virtue, or his concentration, or his wisdom, or his liberation, or his knowledge and vision of liberation, or to burn him with fire, or to carry him away, or to reduce him to ashes, or to do with him as they please, without first having exhausted his heartwood of the higher training in the higher mind. And what, monks, is the heartwood of the higher training in the higher mind? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This, monks, is called the heartwood of the higher training in the higher mind. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall possess the heartwood of the higher training in the higher mind. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has turned yellowish-white, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are elated at that time, thinking:
‘The Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree is now yellowish-white; before long it will have leafed out.’”
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has foliage, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are elated at that time, thinking:
‘The Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree now has foliage; it will not be long before it becomes covered with buds.
Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas is covered with buds, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are elated at that time, thinking:”
‘Now that the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree has produced its network of buds, it will not be long before it produces its shoots.
Monks, when the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has produced its shoots, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are uplifted at that time, thinking:
‘Now that the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree has produced its shoots, it will not be long before it produces its flower buds.’
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has produced buds, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are elated at that time, thinking:
‘The Pāricchattaka koviḷāra has now produced buds; it will not be long before it has formed flower buds.
Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas has formed flower buds, the Tāvatiṃsa devas are elated at that time, thinking:”
‘The coral tree has now produced buds; before long, it will be in full bloom with all its fruits.
Monks, when the coral tree of the Tāvatiṃsa gods is in full bloom, the Tāvatiṃsa gods are uplifted at the foot of the coral tree, amidst divine [splendor].
For four months, they sport, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Furthermore, monks, the radiance of the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree, when all its fruits and flowers are in bloom, pervades fifty yojanas all around;
its fragrance travels a hundred yojanas downwind.
This is the majestic power of the *pāricchattaka* coral tree.
In the same way, monks, at whatever time a noble disciple intends to go forth from the home life into homelessness,
at that time the noble disciple is like a withered leaf, just as [the fallen leaves] are for the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
The *pāricchattaka* coral tree. Monks,
at whatever time a noble disciple, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes,
goes forth from the home life into homelessness, at that time, monks, the noble disciple is like a leafless branch.
Just as there is the Pāricchattaka coral tree belonging to the Tāvatiṃsa gods,
so too, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple, secluded from sensual pleasures... attains and dwells in the first jhāna,
on that occasion the noble disciple is like the Pāricchattaka coral tree of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, covered in blossoms.
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion a noble disciple, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought,
enters and dwells in the second jhāna … at that time the noble disciple is like a *pāricchattaka* coral tree among the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion a noble disciple, with the fading away of rapture, enters and dwells in the third jhāna …”
“Monks, at that time a noble disciple has become like a *kūṭumalaka* bud on the *pāricchattaka* coral tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Monks, when a noble disciple, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain...
[as above] ...enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, at that time, monks, the noble disciple has become like a *koraka* bud on the *pāricchattaka* coral tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.”
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion a noble disciple, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge the state of liberation … on that occasion,
bhikkhus, the noble disciple is in full bloom like the pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
On that occasion, bhikkhus, the earth-dwelling devas raise a cry:”
‘This venerable one of such-and-such a name is the co-resident pupil of that venerable one of such-and-such a name;
having gone forth from the home life into homelessness from such-and-such a village or town, through the destruction of the taints,
he has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein.’
Having heard the sound of the earth-dwelling devas, the Cātumahārājika devas...
[and so on] ...the Tāvatiṃsa devas...
the Yāma devas...
the Tusita devas … the Nimmānarati devas … the Paranimmitavasavatti devas …
The gods of the Brahma-world raise their voices, saying:
“This venerable one of such a name, the co-resident disciple of that venerable one of such a name, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from such a village or town;
through the destruction of the taints, he has realized for himself, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.”
‘Having realized it for oneself through direct knowledge in this very life, one enters and dwells therein.
Thus, at that moment, at that instant, the sound rose up as far as the Brahma-world;
such is the power of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed.”

The Great Division (Mahāvagga).
Sakkaccasutta: Then,
while the Venerable Sāriputta was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“Monk, by honoring, respecting, and relying upon whom could one abandon what is unwholesome and develop what is wholesome?
Then it occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“By honoring, respecting, and relying upon the Teacher, monk, one could abandon what is unwholesome and develop what is wholesome.”
The Dhamma, bhikkhu …pe… the Saṅgha,
bhikkhu …pe… the training, bhikkhu …pe…

“Monk, by honoring, respecting, and relying upon concentration… by honoring, respecting, and relying upon heedfulness… by honoring, respecting, and relying upon hospitality, one may abandon what is unwholesome and develop what is wholesome.”
Then it occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"These teachings of mine are indeed pure and bright; what if I were to go and report these teachings to the Blessed One?
In this way, these teachings of mine will not only remain pure, but will become even more highly regarded as pure."
Just as if a man were to find a gold coin that was perfectly pure and bright, and he thought to himself:
"This gold coin of mine is perfectly pure and bright; what if I were to take this gold coin and show it to the smiths?"
"Just as this gold coin of mine, having gone to a goldsmith's workshop, will become both pure and even more highly regarded for its purity;
even so, these states of mine are pure and bright. What if I were to go and report these states to the Blessed One?
In this way, these states of mine will become both pure and even more highly regarded for their purity."
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
‘What is it that a bhikkhu, by honoring, revering, and relying upon, might abandon the unwholesome and develop the wholesome?
Then, Bhante, this occurred to me:”
“Monk, by honoring, respecting, and relying upon the Teacher, one would abandon what is unwholesome and cultivate what is wholesome.
By honoring the Dhamma … [and so on] … by honoring hospitality, monk …”
‘I shall develop what is wholesome.
Then, venerable sir, it occurred to me:
‘These states of mine are indeed pure and bright; what if I were to go and report these states to the Blessed One?’”
"In this way, these states of mine will become both purified and more thoroughly regarded as purified.
It is just as if a man were to obtain a gold coin that was pure and bright;
it would occur to him:"
"This gold coin of mine is indeed pure and bright. Suppose I were to take this gold coin and show it to the smiths?
In this way, once it has gone to the smiths, this gold coin of mine will become even purer and more highly regarded as pure.
In the same way, these states of mine are pure and bright; suppose I were to go and report these states to the Blessed One?"
"In this way, these states of mine will become purified and even more thoroughly regarded as purified.
"Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
A monk, Sāriputta, by honoring, respecting, and relying upon the Teacher, should abandon what is unwholesome and cultivate what is wholesome."

"Sāriputta, by honoring, revering, and relying upon the Dhamma, a bhikkhu would abandon what is unwholesome and develop what is wholesome. By honoring, revering, and relying upon the Saṅgha... [and] by honoring, revering, and relying upon the training..."
“Sāriputta, by honoring, respecting, and relying upon concentration, heedfulness, and hospitality, a bhikkhu may abandon what is unwholesome and develop what is wholesome.”
When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I understand the detailed meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken in brief in this way:
‘Venerable sir, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who lacks respect for the Teacher could have respect for the Dhamma.’”
"Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who has no respect for the Teacher has no respect for the Dhamma as well.
Indeed, venerable sir, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who has no respect for the Teacher and no respect for the Dhamma should have respect for the Saṅgha.
Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who has no respect for the Teacher and no respect for the Dhamma has no respect for the Saṅgha either."
"Indeed, Bhante, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who lacks respect for the Teacher, lacks respect for the Dhamma, and lacks respect for the Saṅgha, should possess respect for the training.
Bhante, whichever bhikkhu lacks respect for the Teacher, lacks respect for the Dhamma, and lacks respect for the Saṅgha, he also lacks respect for the training.

Indeed, Bhante, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who lacks respect for the Teacher, lacks respect for the Dhamma, lacks respect for the Saṅgha, and lacks respect for the training, should possess respect for concentration."

"Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who is disrespectful toward the Teacher, disrespectful toward the Dhamma, disrespectful toward the Saṅgha, and disrespectful toward the training is also disrespectful toward concentration.

Indeed, venerable sir, it is impossible for a bhikkhu who is disrespectful toward the Teacher, disrespectful toward the Dhamma, disrespectful toward the Saṅgha, disrespectful toward the training, and disrespectful toward concentration to be respectful toward heedfulness."
“Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who lacks respect for the Teacher, lacks respect for the Dhamma, lacks respect for the Saṅgha, lacks respect for the training, lacks respect for concentration,

and lacks respect for heedfulness— he surely lacks respect for hospitality as well. Venerable sir, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who lacks respect for the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, concentration, and heedfulness could possess respect for hospitality.”
“Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who lacks respect for the Teacher... [as above] ...lacks respect even for hospitality.

Indeed, venerable sir, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who has respect for the Teacher would lack respect for the Dhamma. Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who has respect for the Teacher also has respect for the Dhamma...
[as above] .... Indeed, venerable sir, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who has respect for the Teacher... [as above] ...and has respect for heedfulness would lack respect for hospitality.”
“Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher... [as above] ...is also one who has reverence for hospitality.

It is indeed possible, venerable sir, that a bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher will also have reverence for the Dhamma. Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher is also one who has reverence for the Dhamma...
[as above] .... It is indeed possible, venerable sir, that a bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher... [as above] ...and reverence for heedfulness will also have reverence for hospitality.”

“Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, reverence for concentration, reverence for heedfulness, and reverence for hospitality—he is one who possesses reverence.
This, venerable sir, is how I understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!”
"It is good, Sāriputta, that you understand in such detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief.
Indeed, Sāriputta, it is impossible for a bhikkhu who is disrespectful toward the Teacher to be respectful toward the Dhamma...

[as before] ...Sāriputta, that bhikkhu who is disrespectful toward the Teacher, disrespectful toward the Dhamma, disrespectful toward the Saṅgha, disrespectful toward the training, and disrespectful toward concentration is also disrespectful toward heedfulness."
Indeed, Sāriputta, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who lacks respect for the Teacher,

lacks respect for the Dhamma, lacks respect for the Saṅgha, lacks respect for the training, lacks respect for concentration, and lacks respect for heedfulness, should possess respect for hospitality. Sāriputta,

whatever bhikkhu lacks respect for the Teacher, lacks respect for the Dhamma, lacks respect for the Saṅgha, lacks respect for the training, lacks respect for concentration, and lacks respect for heedfulness, he also lacks respect for hospitality.

Indeed, Sāriputta, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher should lack reverence for the Dhamma … [and so on] … Sāriputta, that bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher also has reverence for the Dhamma … [and so on] … Indeed,
Sāriputta, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, and reverence for heedfulness should lack reverence for hospitality.
“Sāriputta, that bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher... [and so on] ...who has reverence for heedfulness will also have reverence for hospitality;
this is possible. Sāriputta, it is indeed possible that a bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher will also have reverence for the Dhamma...
[and so on] .... Sāriputta, it is indeed possible that a bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher... [and so on] ...who has reverence for heedfulness will also have reverence for hospitality.”
"Sāriputta, that bhikkhu who has reverence for the Teacher... [as before] ...and who has reverence for hospitality—he too has reverence.
Sāriputta, this is how the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail.
The sixth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.71 7. Mahāvagga Bhāvanāsutta (The Discourse on Development) “Monks, there are these seven things that are to be developed. What seven? (1) Loving-kindness is to be developed; when developed and cultivated, it leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life and to a happy destination after death. (2) Compassion is to be developed; when developed and cultivated, it leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life and to a happy destination after death. (3) Sympathetic joy is to be developed; when developed and cultivated, it leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life and to a happy destination after death. (4) Equanimity is to be developed; when developed and cultivated, it leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life and to a happy destination after death. (5) Mindfulness of breathing is to be developed; when developed and cultivated, it leads to the cessation of identification and to the destruction of craving. (6) The perception of foulness is to be developed; when developed and cultivated, it leads to the removal of lust for sensual pleasures. (7) The perception of impermanence is to be developed; when developed and cultivated, it leads to the removal of the conceit ‘I am. These, monks, are the seven things that are to be developed.”
“Monks, for a monk who dwells without being devoted to spiritual development, even though such a wish might arise in him: ‘O,
may my mind be liberated from the taints through non-clinging,’ [it will not be so].”
Yet his mind was not liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Why is that? It should be said: "Because it was not cultivated."
Due to the non-cultivation of what?

Of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
Just as, monks, there might be eight, ten, or twelve eggs of a hen...
Those eggs were not properly sat upon by that hen, nor properly incubated, nor properly nurtured.
Even though that hen might have the wish:
"Oh, that my chicks would pierce their shells with the tips of their claws or with their beaks and emerge safely!"
In that case, those chicks would indeed be incapable of breaking out of the eggshell with their claws or beaks and emerging safely. Why is that?
Because, monks, the eggs were not properly incubated by the hen, nor properly warmed, nor properly nurtured.
In the same way, monks, when a monk dwells without being devoted to meditation, even though the wish may arise in him:
"O, that my mind might be liberated from the taints through non-clinging," yet his mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
For what reason is that?
It should be said: “Because of non-cultivation.
Because of the non-cultivation of what?

For a monk, bhikkhus, who dwells devoted to the development of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path—even if the wish should not arise in him:
"O, may my mind be liberated from the taints through non-clinging! [it nevertheless will be so].
Then his mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
For what reason?
It should be said: "Because of its having been developed."
By the cultivation of what?

Of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
Just as, monks, there might be eight, ten, or twelve eggs of a hen...
Suppose those eggs were properly sat upon by the hen, properly incubated, and properly brooded over.
Even though it might not occur to that hen:
“Oh, that my chicks would pierce their shells with the points of their claws or with their beaks and hatch out safely!”
Then those chicks are indeed capable of breaking out of the eggshell with the tip of their claws or with the point of their beaks and emerging safely. Why is that?
Because, monks, the eggs were properly incubated by the hen, properly warmed, and properly brooded.
In the same way, monks, when a monk dwells devoted to meditation, even if no such wish arises in him as,
‘O, may my mind be liberated from the taints through non-clinging,’ nevertheless his mind becomes liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
For what reason is that?
It should be said: "Because of its having been developed.
Because of the development of what?
Of the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on] ...of the Noble Eightfold Path.
Just as, monks, when a carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice sees the finger-marks on his adze-handle and the thumb-mark, yet he does not have the knowledge:
“So much of this has been worn away by me today...”
“‘So much of the oil has been used up today, so much yesterday, and so much before that,’ yet when it is actually exhausted, he knows: ‘It is exhausted.

In the same way, monks, for a monk who dwells devoted to meditation, although such knowledge does not arise—‘So much of my taints has been exhausted today, so much yesterday, and so much before that’—nevertheless, when they are exhausted, he knows: ‘They are exhausted.’”
When it is exhausted, his knowledge is that "it is exhausted.
Bhikkhus, it is just as if a sea-going ship, bound with cordage, had its water supply exhausted after six months and was then hauled onto dry land during the winter;
its moorings, overcome by wind and sun, would be loosened by the rainy season.
“Just as things that have been rained upon by a cloud wither away easily and become rotten,
even so, monks, for a monk who dwells devoted to meditation, the fetters easily subside and become rotten. This is the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.72 7. Mahāvagga Aggikkhandhopamasutta (The Simile of the Mass of Fire) “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a mass of fire burning on all four sides. A person would come along wishing for his own welfare, seeking his own welfare, desiring his own welfare. They would think: ‘I will cross over this mass of fire by leaping from one side to the other.

But they would not leap from that mass of fire until they had reached dry ground, a safe place, free from danger. “So too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has abandoned the five lower fetters, he is like one who has leaped across the mass of fire. He is one who will reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna without ever returning from that world. “Suppose, bhikkhus, there was a great mountain torrent coming down with a swift current. A person would come along wishing for their own welfare, seeking their own welfare, desiring their own welfare. They would think: ‘I will cross over this great mountain torrent by swimming from one bank to the other. But they would not swim across that great mountain torrent until they had reached dry ground, a safe place, free from danger. “So too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has abandoned the five lower fetters, he is like one who has swum across the great mountain torrent. He is one who will reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna without ever returning from that world. “Suppose, bhikkhus, there was a dense jungle thicket. A person would come along wishing for their own welfare, seeking their own welfare, desiring their own welfare. They would think: ‘I will cut through this dense jungle thicket by cutting a path through it from one side to the other. But they would not cut through that dense jungle thicket until they had reached dry ground, a safe place, free from danger. “So too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has abandoned the five lower fetters, he is like one who has cut through the dense jungle thicket. He is one who will reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna without ever returning from that world.”
(AN 7.72, AN 7.68, PTS AN iv 128) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large community of monks.
While traveling along a highway, the Blessed One saw in a certain place a great mass of fire, blazing, flaming, and glowing.
Having seen it, he stepped down from the path and sat down on a seat prepared at the foot of a tree.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, do you see that great mass of fire burning, blazing, and glowing?”— “Yes,
venerable sir.”—
“What do you think, bhikkhus?”
"Now which would be better: that one should embrace and sit down or lie down beside that great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing;
or that one should embrace and sit down or lie down beside a Kṣatriya maiden, or a Brāhmaṇa maiden, or a householder’s daughter, with soft and tender hands and feet?"

“Venerable sir, this alone would be better: that I might embrace and sit down beside or lie down next to a noble maiden, or a brahmin maiden, or a householder’s daughter, with their soft and delicate hands and feet.
For it would be painful, venerable sir, to embrace and sit down beside or lie down next to that great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing.”
“Or it might fall upon him.

“I declare to you, bhikkhus, I make known to you, bhikkhus: for that immoral person of evil nature, of impure and suspicious conduct, of concealed actions, who is not a recluse though claiming to be a recluse—this alone would be better for him.”
For one who is unchaste, yet claims to be chaste, who is internally rotten, lustful, and of impure nature—
to have him embrace that great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing,
and then sit down or lie down beside it.

And why is that? Because on that account, monks, he might meet death or experience suffering amounting to death; yet for that reason alone, with the breakup of the body after death, he would not be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, or hell.
But as for that person, monks, who is immoral, of evil nature, of impure and suspicious conduct... [as above] ...who is like dregs—
If he embraces a noble maiden, a brahmin maiden, or a householder’s daughter— whose hands and feet are soft and tender—
and sits near her or lies down near her, that, monks, leads to his harm and suffering for a long time;
after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
"What do you think, monks? Which would be better:
that a strong man, having wound a stout hair-rope around both your shanks, should rub it so as to cut through the outer skin;
having cut through the outer skin, he should cut through the inner hide; having cut through the inner hide, he should cut through the flesh?"
"Would one cut through the sinews, and having cut through the sinews, cut through the bones, and having cut through the bones,
stand striking right to the marrow; or would one accept the salutation of wealthy kshatriyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders?"
“Venerable sir, this indeed is better: that I should accept the salutation of wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders.
For it would be painful, venerable sir, if a strong man were to strike me with a stout hair-rope...
[and so on] ...until he stood pressing against the very marrow of my bones.”
"I announce to you, bhikkhus; I declare to you, bhikkhus: it would be better for that immoral person...
for that one who is like rotten wood, that a strong man should wrap a stout hair-rope around both his shanks...
and stand pressing against his very marrow."

And why is that? Because on that account, monks, he might meet death or suffering amounting to death; yet for that reason alone, with the breakup of the body after death, he would not be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, downfall, or hell.
But as for that immoral person... [as before] ...who is like rotten grain among the wealthy kṣatriyas or the wealthy brahmins—
or if he accepts salutations from wealthy householders, that, monks, leads to his long-term harm and suffering;
with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
"What do you think, monks?"

“Which would be better: that a strong man should strike one on the chest with a sharp spear polished with oil, or that one should accept the reverential salutation of wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders?
“This alone, Bhante, would be better: that one should accept the reverential salutation of wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders.”
“Or if he were to accept the salutation with joined palms—this, venerable sir, would be painful, as if a strong man were to strike one on the breast with a sharp spear polished with oil.

“I declare to you, bhikkhus, I announce to you, bhikkhus: it would be better for that immoral person... [down to] ...for that person born of filth, if a strong man were to strike him on the breast with a sharp spear polished with oil.”
For what reason?

Because on that account, monks, he might meet death or suffer pain amounting to death; yet for that reason alone, with the breakup of the body after death, he would not be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, downfall, or hell.
But as for that person, monks, who is immoral, of evil nature... [and so forth] ...who is like dregs among wealthy kṣatriyas—
Or if he accepts the salutation with joined palms from great brahmins or great householders, that, monks,
leads to his long-term harm and suffering; after the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation,
a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
"What do you think, monks?
Which is better: that a strong man should wrap one's body with a red-hot iron sheet, burning, blazing, and glowing, or [that one should receive] from wealthy kṣatriyas or wealthy brahmins..."
“Or would one enjoy a robe given in faith by great householders?

“This, Bhante, is better—that one should enjoy a robe given in faith by great kṣatriyas... [as above] ...for it is painful, Bhante, that a strong man should wrap one’s body in a glowing iron sheet, burning, blazing, and incandescent.”
“I declare to you, bhikkhus, I announce to you, bhikkhus: it would be better for that immoral person...
[as before] ...who is like dregs, that a strong man should wrap his body in a red-hot iron sheet, burning, blazing, and glowing.
For what reason?

Because, monks, on that account he might meet death or suffer pain amounting to death; yet it is not because of that that, with the breakup of the body after death, he would be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
But as for that person, monks, who is immoral... [and] a mere dregs among wealthy kṣatriyas or wealthy brahmins...
Or if he makes use of a robe given in faith by wealthy householders, that, monks, leads to his long-term harm and suffering;
with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
What do you think, monks?
Now, which is better: that a strong man should pry open one’s mouth with a red-hot iron spike and thrust into the mouth a glowing,
blazing, incandescent iron ball, which would burn the lips,
burn the mouth, burn the tongue, burn the throat, burn the chest, and burn the intestines?
“Would it be better, Bhante, to take even an ant’s leg and carry it out through the lower part [of the body],

or to consume almsfood given in faith by wealthy kshatriyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders?”— “Venerable sir, this alone is better: that one should consume almsfood given in faith by wealthy kshatriyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders.”
Or if one were to consume almsfood given out of faith, this would indeed be painful, venerable sir,
as if a strong man were to pry open one’s mouth with a red-hot iron spike and thrust into the mouth a red-hot iron ball, burning, blazing, and glowing;
it would burn the lips, it would burn the mouth, it would burn the tongue, and it would burn the throat.
“It might burn his chest, it might burn his intestines, and having taken up even the mesentery, it would exit through the lower part.
“I declare to you, monks, I announce to you, monks: for that immoral person...
[as above] ...who is born of corruption, this alone would be better—that a strong man, having forced open his mouth with a red-hot iron spike, should pour in heated copper.”
Suppose one were to throw a glowing iron ball, burning, blazing, and incandescent,
into one’s mouth— it would burn the lips, burn the mouth, burn the tongue, burn the throat, and burn the chest; then,
taking hold of the intestines and the mesentery, it would pass out through the lower part.

And why is that? Because on that account, monks, he might meet death or experience pain amounting to death; yet it is not because of that, upon the breakup of the body after death, that he would be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, ruin, or hell.
But as for that person, monks, who is immoral, of evil nature... [pe] ...a mere dreg among wealthy kṣatriyas—
Or if he consumes almsfood given in faith by great brahmins or great householders,
that leads to his long-term harm and suffering; with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation,
a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
"What do you think, monks, which would be better:

that a strong man, having seized one by the head or by the shoulder, should force one to sit down or lie down upon a red-hot iron bed or an iron bench; or [that one should attend upon] the great wealthy kṣatriyas?"
“Or would one enjoy a bed and chair given in faith by great wealthy kshatriyas, great wealthy brahmins, or great wealthy householders?

“Venerable sir, it is better indeed that one should enjoy a bed and chair given in faith by great wealthy kshatriyas, great wealthy brahmins, or great wealthy householders; for this, venerable sir, is painful—that a strong man [should drag one away].”
“Or, seizing him by the head or by the shoulder, they would make him sit down or lie down upon a heated iron bed or an iron chair.
“I declare to you, bhikkhus, I make known to you, bhikkhus: it would be better for that immoral person [to undergo] this very thing.”
...pe... as with one who is rotten, a strong man might seize him by the head or by the shoulder and force him to sit down or lie down upon a red-hot iron bed or an iron chair.
For what reason?

For on that account, monks, he might meet death or suffering amounting to death; yet because of that, upon the breakup of the body after death, he would not be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.

But as for that immoral person of evil nature... [as before] ...who, being like a mere rotten reed, uses beds and chairs given in faith by wealthy kshatriyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders.
For that, monks, leads to his long-term harm and suffering; with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
What do you think, monks?

Which indeed is better: that a strong man should seize one by the feet and head, turn one upside down, and throw one into a glowing iron cauldron—blazing, aflame, and incandescent—wherein one is cooked amidst a mass of foam, rising up at one moment, sinking down at another, and drifting sideways at another; or rather...
"Would you enjoy a monastery given in faith by wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders?
"Venerable sir, this alone is better: that [one should enjoy] what is given in faith by wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders."
Or if he were to enjoy a monastery given out of faith: this would indeed be painful, venerable sir, as if a strong man were to seize one by the feet and head, turn one upside down,
and throw one into a glowing iron cauldron that is heated,
blazing, and aflame— where, being cooked amidst a mass of froth, one might go up for a moment and go down for a moment.
“...or he might go sideways.
“I announce to you, bhikkhus, I declare to you, bhikkhus: it would be better for that immoral person of evil nature—[as previously described]...
who is like rotten wood—that a strong man should seize him by his feet and head, turn him upside down, and…”
...pe... he might even go across [the ocean].

Why is that? Because on that account, monks, he might meet death or suffering amounting to death; yet for that reason, with the breakup of the body after death, he would not be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
But when, monks, that immoral person of evil nature— pe—
born of the dregs of the community enjoys a monastery given in faith by wealthy kshatriyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders, that, monks,
leads to his long-term harm and suffering, and after the breakup of the body, after death, it results in his downfall.
He is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"Whatever robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick we may enjoy..."
‘Their acts of service will be of great fruit and great benefit; and this going forth of ours shall not be in vain, but shall be fruitful and productive.
It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves.
“Monks, for one who considers their own welfare, it is indeed sufficient to strive with diligence;
for one who considers the welfare of others, it is indeed sufficient to strive with diligence;
and for one who considers the welfare of both, it is indeed sufficient to strive with diligence.”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
And while this exposition was being delivered, warm blood gushed from the mouths of about sixty bhikkhus.
About sixty bhikkhus renounced the training and returned to the lower life.
“It is a great hardship, Blessed One! It is a very great hardship, Blessed One!
At these words, the minds of about sixty bhikkhus were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Thus ends the eighth [discourse].

“Formerly, monks, there was a teacher named Sunetta, a founder of a sect who was free from passion for sensual pleasures.
That teacher, monks, had many hundreds of disciples.”
The Teacher Sunetta taught the Dhamma to his disciples for the sake of companionship with the Brahmā-world.
But those, monks, who did not place confidence in the minds of the Teacher Sunetta as he was teaching the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahmā-world,
at the breaking-up of the body, after death, were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, even in hell.

"Furthermore, monks, those who placed their faith in the mind of the Teacher Sunetta while he was teaching the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma-world, at the breaking-up of the body after death, were reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.
Once in the past, monks, there was a teacher named Mūgapakkha...
[and so on] ...there was a teacher named Aranemi..."
There was a teacher named Kuddālaka …pe… there was a teacher named Hatthipāla …pe… there was a teacher named Jotipāla …pe…
There was a teacher named Araka, a founder of a spiritual order who was free from passion for sensual pleasures.
Now, monks, that teacher Araka had many hundreds of disciples.
The teacher named Araka taught the Dhamma to his disciples for the sake of companionship with the Brahma-world.
“Monks, those who did not gain confidence of heart while the Teacher Araka was teaching the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma-world,
at the breaking-up of the body, after death, were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, hell. But those, monks,

who gained confidence of heart while the Teacher Araka was teaching the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma-world, at the breaking-up of the body, after death, were reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.”
“What do you think, bhikkhus,

if someone with a corrupt mind were to revile and abuse these seven teachers, founders of sects who are free from lust for sensual pleasures and have retinues of many hundreds along with their assemblies of disciples, would he produce much demerit?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”

“Monks, whoever with a malicious mind should revile and abuse these seven teachers, founders of sects, who are free from passion for sensual pleasures and have retinues of many hundreds along with their assemblies of disciples, that person would produce much demerit.
Whoever with a malicious mind reviles and abuses a single person endowed with right view produces even more demerit than that.
Why is that? [Because]...”
“Monks, I do not speak of such forbearance toward those outside this teaching as I do toward my fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘Our minds shall not become corrupted toward our fellow practitioners of the holy life.’”
“In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus [ends] the ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.74
7. Mahāvagga:
The Discourse on the Araṇa [State] (AN 7.73–74, AN 7.69–70, PTS AN iv 135)
“Bhikkhus, in the past there was a teacher named Araka, a founder of a spiritual order who was free from lust for sensual pleasures.
Bhikkhus, that teacher Araka had many hundreds of disciples.
Teacher Araka taught the Dhamma to his disciples in this way:”

“Brahmin, the life of human beings is short, limited, fleeting, full of suffering, and full of despair. One must understand this through wisdom; one must do what is wholesome; one must lead the holy life. For one who is born, there is no escaping death.

Just as, Brahmin, a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass quickly vanishes when the sun rises and does not last long, even so, Brahmin, the life of human beings is like a drop of dew—short, limited, fleeting, and full of suffering.”
Much must be understood through reflection; what is wholesome must be done; the holy life must be lived; for one who is born, there is no escaping death.
Just as, brahmin, when rain falls in heavy drops, a water bubble quickly vanishes and does not last long, even so, brahmin, human life is like a water bubble—limited, fleeting, and full of suffering.
"Much must be done with wisdom: what is wholesome must be realized, the holy life must be lived, for there is no escaping death for one who is born.
Just as, brahmin, a line drawn on water quickly vanishes and does not remain long, even so, brahmin, human life is like a line drawn on water—brief, limited, and fragile."
"There is no death for one who is born.

Just as, brahmin, a mountain river flowing from a high peak, far-reaching, swift-flowing, and carrying away all that it meets—there is no moment, no instant, no brief space in which it turns back, but rather it only goes on, flows on, and rushes on—just so, brahmin, is human life like a mountain river: limited, fleeting..."
"There is no deathlessness for one who is born.

Just as, brahmin, a strong man might gather a lump of spittle on the tip of his tongue and spit it out without difficulty, even so, brahmin, human life is like a lump of spittle—brief... [and so forth]."
"There is no immortality for one who is born.

Just as, brahmin, a piece of meat thrown into an iron cauldron heated all day quickly dissolves and does not remain for long, even so, brahmin, human life is like a piece of meat—brief... [and so on]."
"There is no deathlessness for one who is born.

Just as, brahmin, a cow condemned to death being led to the slaughterhouse—whichever foot it lifts up, it is ever closer to the slaughter, ever closer to death—even so, brahmin, is the life of humans like a cow condemned to death: limited, fleeting, and full of suffering."
"Much must be understood through wisdom; what is wholesome must be done; the holy life must be lived;
for one who is born, there is no escaping death.
Now at that time, monks, the lifespan of human beings was sixty thousand years, and a maiden of five hundred years was marriageable.
Now at that time, monks, humans had only six afflictions:
cold, heat, hunger, thirst, excrement, and urine.
For indeed, monks, the Teacher Araka, among humans who were so long-lived, so long-enduring, and so free from affliction, would teach the Dhamma to his disciples thus:
“Brahmin, the life of human beings is short, limited, fleeting, full of suffering, and full of despair; one must wake up to this, one must do what is wholesome, and one must lead the holy life;
for there is no escaping death for one who is born. Monks, it is of this that one speaking rightly would say today:

“The life of human beings is short, limited, fleeting, full of suffering, and full of despair; one must wake up to this, one must do what is wholesome, and one must lead the holy life; for there is no escaping death for one who is born.”
At present, monks, whoever lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more.
But living for a hundred years, monks, one lives for only three hundred seasons:
a hundred seasons of winter, a hundred seasons of summer, and a hundred seasons of the rains.
“Monks, living for three hundred autumns, one lives for exactly twelve hundred months—
four hundred months of winter, four hundred months of summer, and four hundred months of the rainy season.
Monks, living for twelve hundred months, one lives for exactly twenty-four hundred fortnights.”
There are eight hundred and fifty half-months of winter, eight hundred and fifty half-months of summer, and eight hundred and fifty half-months of the rainy season.
Monks, living for twenty-four hundred and fifty half-months, one lives for only thirty-six thousand nights:
twelve thousand nights of winter, twelve thousand nights of summer, and twelve thousand nights of the rainy season.

“Monks, one who lives for thirty-six thousand nights eats only seventy-two thousand meals—twenty-four thousand meals during the winter, twenty-four thousand meals during the summer, and twenty-four thousand meals during the rainy season—counting the time spent nursing at the mother’s breast and including the occasions when eating is interrupted.
These are the interruptions to eating: even when afflicted by hunger, one does not eat; even when suffering from illness, one does not eat.”
Even when ill, he does not eat a meal; even when observing the Uposatha, he does not eat a meal; even when receiving no alms, he does not eat a meal.

Thus, monks, for a human being with a lifespan of a hundred years, I have calculated the life-span, I have calculated the measure of that life-span, I have calculated the seasons, I have calculated the years, I have calculated the months, and I have calculated the fortnights.
"Night has been reckoned, day has been reckoned, mealtime has been reckoned, and the obstacles to meals have been reckoned.
Monks, whatever should be done by a Teacher who seeks the welfare of his disciples and is compassionate, out of compassion—this has been done for you by me.
Here, monks, are the roots of trees; here are empty huts. Meditate, monks; do not be negligent, lest you later fall into regret. This is my instruction to you."
The tenth.

The Discourse on the First Vinaya-Holders (Paṭhamavinayadharasutta):

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with seven qualities is a bearer of the Vinaya. What seven? [He knows the origin of an offense, he knows the manifestation of an offense, he knows the classification of an offense, he knows the removal of an offense, he knows the light offense, he knows the heavy offense, and he knows the offense that is both light and heavy.]”
Which seven?
He knows what is an offense;
he knows what is not an offense.
He knows a light offense and he knows a heavy offense;
he is virtuous, dwelling restrained by the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and training himself by undertaking the rules of training.
“He is one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without toil, the four jhānas that constitute higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life;

and, with the destruction of the taints, he enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself through direct knowledge in this very life.
It is, monks, when a bhikkhu possesses these seven qualities that he is a bearer of the Vinaya.”
First.

The Discourse on the Fourth Holder of the Discipline (Catutthavinayadharasutta):
“Bhikkhus, possessing seven qualities, a bhikkhu is a holder of the discipline.”
Which seven?
He knows what is an offense;
he knows what is not an offense.
He knows a light offense;
he knows a grave offense;
he recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say, one birth, two births … [and so on] … thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he understands beings according to their karma.

Through the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon them.
It is, monks, when a monk is endowed with these seven qualities that he is a bearer of the Vinaya.”

Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“Upāli, as for those qualities that you would know thus:
‘These qualities do not lead exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna’—[you should abandon them].”
“Upāli, you should categorically hold:
‘This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher’s instruction.
And as for those teachings, Upāli, that you should know as the Dhamma...”
‘These things lead to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna’—
you should, Upāli, remember this categorically:
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.’”

The Discourse on the Settlement of Legal Issues (Adhikaraṇasamathasutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these seven principles for the settlement of legal issues, for the settling and pacification of legal issues as they arise.”

Which seven? The settlement in the presence should be granted; the settlement through recollection should be granted; the settlement for one no longer insane should be granted; acting according to what has been admitted should be granted; the majority decision should be granted; the further penalty should be granted; the covering over as with grass should be granted.
These, monks, are the seven principles for the settling of legal issues, for the settling and pacification of legal issues as they arise.”
